Implement Blending Techniques for Camouflage Concealment and Decoys (CCD)
High Priority Source: FM 20 3 Camouflage Concealment and Decoys
Overview

Blending is trying to alter a target's appearance so that it becomes part of the background. Generally, it is arranging or applying camouflage material on, over, and/or around a target to reduce its contrast with the...
Overview

Blending is trying to alter a target's appearance so that it becomes part of the background. Generally, it is arranging or applying camouflage material on, over, and/or around a target to reduce its contrast with the background.

Implementation Steps

1. Consider Terrain Patterns: Analyze the terrain patterns in the vicinity to determine appropriate camouflage materials and techniques that match the surrounding environment.
2. Apply Camouflage Material: Arrange or apply camouflage material on, over, and/or around a target to reduce its contrast with the background. This includes using paint, foam, lights, vegetation, and LCSS (Lightweight Camouflage Support System).
3. Adjust for Target Characteristics: Consider the size, shape, texture, color, EM signature, and background of the target when applying camouflage materials.

Additional Considerations

• Ensure that the camouflage material used matches the terrain patterns in the vicinity to avoid detection by enemy sensors.
• Adjust the application of camouflage materials based on the specific characteristics of the target (e.g., size, shape, texture) for optimal blending.
blending camouflage concealment tactical operations terrain patterns target characteristics
Implement Camouflage Concealment and Decoy (CCD) Techniques
High Priority Source: FM 20 3 Camouflage Concealment and Decoys
Overview

Camouflage Concealment and Decoys (CCD) is an essential part of tactical operations. It must be integrated into METT-TC analyses and the IPB process at all echelons. CCD is a primary consideration when planning OPSEC. The skillful use...
Overview

Camouflage Concealment and Decoys (CCD) is an essential part of tactical operations. It must be integrated into METT-TC analyses and the IPB process at all echelons. CCD is a primary consideration when planning OPSEC. The skillful use of CCD techniques is necessary if a unit is to conceal itself and survive.

General Techniques of Employing CCD

There are five general techniques of employing CCD:

1. Hiding: Screening a target from an enemy's sensors by using barriers that hide it from a sensor's view. Examples include burying mines, placing vehicles beneath tree canopies, and covering vehicles and equipment with nets.
2. Blending: Altering a target's appearance so that it becomes part of the background. This is done by arranging or applying camouflage material on, over, and/or around a target to reduce its contrast with the background. Considerations include terrain patterns, size, shape, texture, color, EM signature, and background.
3. Disguising: Applying materials on a target to mislead the enemy as to its true identity. This changes a target's appearance so that it resembles something of lesser or greater significance (e.g., a missile launcher disguised to resemble a cargo truck).
4. Disrupting: Altering or eliminating regular patterns and target characteristics. Techniques include pattern painting, deploying camouflage nets over selected portions of a target, and using shape disrupters (such as camouflage sails) to eliminate regular target patterns.
5. Decoying: Deploying false or simulated targets within a target's scene or in a position where the enemy might conclude that it has found the correct target(s). Decoys generally draw fire away from real targets, enhancing survivability.

Sensor Systems Considerations

• Optical Sensors: Use earth cover, earth embankments, vegetation, LCSS (Lightweight Camouflage Support System), screens, and smoke for hiding; paint, foam, lights, vegetation, and LCSS for blending; reshaping, paint, and LCSS for disguising; camouflage sails, FOS (False Object Simulation), pyrotechnics, smudge pots, balloons, strobe lights, tracer simulators, and smoke for disrupting; decoy targets, lights, and smoke for decoying.
• Thermal Sensors: Use earth cover, earth embankments, vegetation, LCSS, and RAM (Rapidly Deployable Antiradiation Material) for hiding; thermal paint, foam, air conditioning/heating, and vegetation for blending; vegetation, LCSS, RAM, reshaping, and textured mats for disrupting; decoy targets, flares, and smoke for decoying.
• Radar Sensors: Use chaff, earth cover, earth embankments, vegetation, nets, RAM, and LCSS for hiding; vegetation, LCSS, RAM, reshaping, and textured mats for blending; chaff and corner reflectors for disrupting; decoy targets, corner reflectors, and signal generators for decoying.

Additional Considerations

• Use conditions of limited visibility for movement and terrain masking to enhance hiding efforts.
• Hiding roads and obstacles with linear screens can also be an effective technique.
• Battlefield obscurants such as smoke should be used when appropriate.
camouflage concealment decoy hiding blending disguising disrupting tactical operations sensor systems
Implement Hiding Techniques for Camouflage Concealment and Decoys (CCD)
High Priority Source: FM 20 3 Camouflage Concealment and Decoys
Overview

Hiding is screening a target from an enemy's sensors. The target is undetected because a barrier hides it from a sensor's view. Every effort should be made to hide all operations; this includes using conditions of limited visibility...
Overview

Hiding is screening a target from an enemy's sensors. The target is undetected because a barrier hides it from a sensor's view. Every effort should be made to hide all operations; this includes using conditions of limited visibility for movement and terrain masking.

Implementation Steps

1. Bury Mines: Use earth cover to conceal mines effectively, ensuring they are not detectable by enemy sensors.
2. Place Vehicles Beneath Tree Canopies: Utilize natural cover such as tree canopies to hide vehicles from enemy detection.
3. Position Equipment in Defilade Positions: Place equipment in positions that are protected from direct line of sight or fire, using terrain features for concealment.
4. Cover Vehicles and Equipment with Nets: Use camouflage nets to obscure the view of vehicles and equipment from enemy sensors.
5. Hide Roads and Obstacles with Linear Screens: Deploy linear screens (e.g., fences, vegetation barriers) along roads and obstacles to prevent detection by enemy forces.
6. Use Battlefield Obscurants: Employ battlefield obscurants such as smoke to obscure the view of operations or equipment from enemy sensors.

Additional Considerations

• Use conditions of limited visibility (e.g., fog, night) for movement and terrain masking to enhance hiding efforts.
• Ensure that all operations are hidden as much as possible to avoid detection by enemy forces.
hiding camouflage concealment tactical operations battlefield obscurants defilade positions linear screens

Objective: Minimize the visibility of light and heat signatures during nighttime operations to avoid detection.

### Key Actions
1. Black Out Lights: All lights must be extinguished or covered at night, as they can be seen from great distances (e.g., campfires visible up to 8 kilometers, vehicle lights up to 20 kilometers).
2. Use Ground Guides and Blackout Lights: When movement is necessary at night, use ground guides and blackout lights in forward combat areas.
3. Minimize Thermal Signatures: If heat sources are unavoidable, employ techniques such as terrain masking, exhaust baffling, or other methods to reduce thermal signatures from fires, stoves, or heaters.

Identify and Understand Terrain Patterns for Camouflage Concealment and Decoys (CCD)
Standard Source: FM 20 3 Camouflage Concealment and Decoys
Objective: Recognize and understand the five general terrain patterns to enhance CCD effectiveness without disturbing the natural environment.

### Terrain Pattern Types
1. Agricultural: Characterized by a checkerboard pattern when...
Objective: Recognize and understand the five general terrain patterns to enhance CCD effectiveness without disturbing the natural environment.

### Terrain Pattern Types
1. Agricultural: Characterized by a checkerboard pattern when viewed from aircraft, due to different types of crops and vegetation on farms.
2. Urban: Features uniform rows of housing with interwoven streets and interspersed trees and shrubs.
3. Wooded: Natural, irregular features that differ from the geometric patterns found in agricultural or urban areas.
4. Barren: Uneven, irregular terrain without defined patterns; examples include desert environments.
5. Arctic: Covered with snow and ice.

### Considerations
• The goal is to avoid disturbing the existing terrain pattern as it can indicate military activity.
• Terrain features should be used strategically to enhance CCD effectiveness without introducing changes that could alert an enemy.

Prioritize Camouflage Concealment and Decoys (CCD) Operations Using METT-TC Methodology
Standard Source: FM 20 3 Camouflage Concealment and Decoys

Objective: Establish priorities for CCD operations based on mission requirements.

### Steps:
1. Analyze the Mission: The mission is always the first consideration. Ensure that CCD efforts enhance the mission without being overly elaborate and hindering its accomplishment.
2. Assess Enemy RSTA Capabilities: Conduct an intelligence analysis to identify enemy Reconnaissance, Surveillance, and Target Acquisition (RSTA) capabilities before beginning a mission. This will influence the type of camouflage materials and techniques needed.
3. Evaluate Terrain and Weather Conditions: The battlefield terrain determines what CCD techniques and materials are necessary. Different environments such as urban, mountain, forest, plains, desert, or arctic require specific CCD techniques. Refer to _Chapter 7_ for more information on terrain-specific techniques.
4. Train Troops in CCD Techniques: Friendly troops must be well trained in CCD techniques that apply to their mission, unit, and equipment. Additional training may be required if there is a change in the environment or mission. Leaders should ensure that soldiers are alert and avoid careless efforts that could disclose a unit's location.
5. Consider Time Constraints: Time is often critical. Elaborate CCD may not always be practical. Consider how long the unit will occupy an area, the time available to apply CCD countermeasures, and the time required for removal and reemployment of camouflage during relocation. Continue improving CCD measures as time allows.
6. Account for Civilian Considerations: Civilians in the Area of Operation (AO) may collect information actively or passively. Commanders must manage this capability to benefit the mission.

Objective: Select and maintain CP site locations that minimize detection and maximize concealment.

Steps:
1. Consider extended occupation needs while minimizing changes to natural terrain patterns.
2. When constructing defensive positions, minimize earth scarring as much as possible.
3. If scarred earth is unavoidable, use the following methods to conceal it:
- Cut vegetation
- Apply toned-down agents (paint)
- Use camouflage nets
4. Use existing lines of communication (LOCs) such as roads, trails, and streams whenever possible.
5. When constructing new roads or paths, make maximum use of natural concealment and existing terrain features.
6. Avoid locating a CP at a road junction, as these are high-priority targets for enemy forces and easily detectable.
7. If possible, locate a CP in an existing civilian structure to simplify hiding military activity.
8. Choose a structure that is located in an area with a sufficient number of buildings having similar EM signatures to mask the CP's location.

Notes:
• Ensure that foot paths are designated and used consistently within the CP area.
• If a unit occupies a site for more than 24 hours, periodically reroute foot paths to avoid detectable patterns.
• Conceal security and dismount points, as well as other individual emplacements.
• Make paths to the CP inconspicuous.
• Enforce proper disposal procedures for trash and spoil.
• Rigidly enforce light and noise discipline.
• Enhance the realism of a decoy CP by making it appear operational.
• Allow CCD discipline to be lax in the decoy CP, thus making it a more conspicuous target than the real CP.

Differentiate Between Blood and Air Chokes
High Priority Source: MA 1.02 USMC Fundamentals of Martial Arts
Objective: Understand the difference between blood chokes and air chokes.

Content:
• Blood Choke: Applies pressure to the carotid artery on both sides of the neck, cutting off oxygen flow to the brain. It can render an opponent...
Objective: Understand the difference between blood chokes and air chokes.

Content:
• Blood Choke: Applies pressure to the carotid artery on both sides of the neck, cutting off oxygen flow to the brain. It can render an opponent unconscious in 8–13 seconds when executed properly. This is the preferred choke for ending a fight quickly and safely.

• Air Choke: Applies pressure to the windpipe or trachea, cutting off air supply to the lungs and heart. It takes 2–3 minutes for the opponent to lose consciousness and is not recommended due to the risk of prolonged struggle and potential injury.

Safety Note: During training, ensure that students are applying blood chokes correctly and avoid air chokes to prevent unnecessary harm.
blood choke, air choke, martial arts, tactical, carotid artery
Execute a Figure-Four Variation of the Rear Choke
High Priority Source: MA 1.02 USMC Fundamentals of Martial Arts
Objective: Execute a figure-four variation to the rear choke in accordance with references.

Steps:
1. Approach the opponent from behind and take control of their body.
2. Wrap your arms around the opponent's neck, similar to the basic rear...
Objective: Execute a figure-four variation to the rear choke in accordance with references.

Steps:
1. Approach the opponent from behind and take control of their body.
2. Wrap your arms around the opponent's neck, similar to the basic rear choke technique.
3. Cross one arm over the other to form a figure-four grip on the opponent's neck.
4. Apply pressure by squeezing the carotid artery with the crossed arms.
5. Maintain control until the opponent loses consciousness or taps out.

Safety Precautions:
• Never execute a choke at full force or full speed during training because the carotid artery could collapse.
• Once a technique is applied to the point the student is uncomfortable, the student must "tap out" to indicate to his opponent to immediately release pressure or stop the technique. The student "taps out" by firmly tapping his hand several times on any part of the opponent's body that will get his attention.
• Do not hold a choke for more than five seconds in training.
• Do not apply pressure to the opponent's throat during training because the trachea and windpipe can be crushed.
figure-four choke, rear choke variation, martial arts, tactical, carotid artery

Safety Procedures: To prevent injury during training, ensure you follow these safety procedures:

1. Begin by executing the bayonet techniques in the air. Ensure bayonets are sheathed. Ensure contact is not made with an opponent when doing the target acquisition phase of “air drills”.
2. As you become more proficient, you will be allowed to execute techniques on bayonet dummies or other targets.
3. Prior to training with a rifle, conduct an "Unload, Show Clear" of the rifle to show students the weapon is not loaded.
4. Enforce the following four basic safety rules when handling a weapon:
- Treat every weapon as if it were loaded.
- Never point your weapon at anything you do not intend to shoot.
- Keep your finger straight and off the trigger until you intend to fire.
- Keep your weapon on safe until you are ready to fire.

Objective: Use off-balancing techniques to control an opponent by leveraging their momentum.

Procedure:
1. Identify the eight angles of off-balancing: Forward, Rear, Right, Left, Forward Right, Forward Left, Rear Right, and Rear Left (from your perspective).
2. Choose a technique based on the angle:
- Pulling: Grab an opponent with your hands and drive them forcefully to one of the rear quadrants or right or left.
- Pushing: Grab the opponent with your hands and drive them forcefully into one of the front quadrants or right or left.
- Bumping: Use parts of your body such as shoulders, hips, or legs to push the opponent without grabbing them.
3. Apply the technique with enough force to off-balance the opponent but not necessarily to throw them to the deck.

Notes: Off-balancing techniques rely on the momentum and power generated by the opponent, making them effective even when you are outnumbered or outmatched in strength.

Execute Uppercut
High Priority Source: MA 1.02 USMC Fundamentals of Martial Arts
Purpose: The uppercut is a powerful punch originating below the opponent's line of vision. It is executed in an upward motion traveling up the centerline of the opponent's body. It is delivered in close and usually follows a preparatory strike...
Purpose: The uppercut is a powerful punch originating below the opponent's line of vision. It is executed in an upward motion traveling up the centerline of the opponent's body. It is delivered in close and usually follows a preparatory strike that leaves the target area unprotected. When delivered to the chin or jaw, the uppercut can render an opponent unconscious, cause extensive damage to the neck, or sever the tongue.

Technique:
1. Assume the basic warrior stance.
2. Bend your arm, rotating your palm inboard. The distance your arm bends will depend on how close you are to the opponent.
3. At the same time, thrust your fist straight up toward the opponent's chin or jaw.
- Power is generated by transferring your body weight from low to high into the strike.
- Additional power can be generated by forcefully rotating your hips and shoulders toward the opponent.
4. Keep your lead hand in place to protect your head.
5. Make contact on the opponent with the first two knuckles of your fist.
6. Immediately retract your hand, resuming the basic warrior stance.
uppercut technique, martial arts punch, combat strike

Purpose: The hook is a powerful punch that is executed close in and is usually preceded by a preparatory strike.

Technique:
1. Assume the basic warrior stance.
2. Thrust your right arm in a hooking motion toward the opponent, forearm parallel with the deck and palm towards the deck, forcefully rotating your right shoulder and hip toward the opponent. Do not telegraph the punch by extending the arm too far out to the side.
3. Make contact on the opponent with the first two knuckles of your fist.
4. Continue rotating your shoulder and hip, following through with your fist through the target.
5. Immediately retract your hand, resuming the basic warrior stance.

Proper Holding Technique: When executing bayonet techniques, the rifle is held in a modified basic warrior stance. All movement begins and ends with the basic warrior stance. To hold the rifle:

1. With the right hand, grasp the pistol grip with the trigger finger kept off the trigger and included in the grip.
2. With the left hand, grasp the handguards of the rifle under-handed.
3. Lock the buttstock of the rifle against the hip with the right forearm.
4. Always execute movements with the bayonet blade within a box, shoulder-width across from your neck down to your waistline.
5. Keep the bayonet end of the rifle oriented toward the opponent.

Objective: Practice off-balancing techniques in a controlled environment to improve execution.

Procedure:
1. Have students face each other and designate one as the opponent and the other as the practitioner.
2. Instruct the practitioner to grasp the opponent's right hand with their left hand and the opponent's left shoulder with their right hand (or any other appropriate grip).
3. Practice applying off-balancing techniques at all eight angles:
- Forward, Rear, Right, Left, Forward Right, Forward Left, Rear Right, and Rear Left.
4. Ensure that students apply just enough force to demonstrate off-balancing without driving the opponent to the deck.
5. Observe when the opponent takes a step back or forward as an indication of being off-balanced and compensating for balance.

Notes: This practice helps reinforce proper technique, timing, and control during real combat scenarios.

Proper Punching Technique and Principles
Standard Source: MA 1.02 USMC Fundamentals of Martial Arts
### Principles of Effective Punching

#### Relaxation:
• Maintain muscle relaxation throughout the punch to increase speed and power.

• Relax your forearm for faster reaction times....
### Principles of Effective Punching

#### Relaxation:
• Maintain muscle relaxation throughout the punch to increase speed and power.
• Tensing up leads to fatigue and reduced effectiveness.
• Relax your forearm for faster reaction times. Clench your fist only at impact to avoid injury to your wrist and hand.

#### Weight Transfer:
• Generate power by rotating your hips and shoulders into the attack.
• Move your body mass forward or backward in a straight line.
• Drop your body weight into the opponent, transferring mass from high to low or vice versa.

#### Rapid Retraction:
• After impact, quickly return your hand and arm to the basic warrior stance.
• This protects you from counterattacks, prevents your opponent from grabbing your hand, and allows for quick follow-up strikes.

#### Avoid Telegraphing:
• Do not telegraph your punches by making visible movements (e.g., drawing back your hand, changing facial expression).
• A trained opponent can evade or counter your attack if you telegraph it.
• Staying relaxed helps reduce the likelihood of telegraphing.

### Basic Fist Formation:
1. Curl your fingers naturally into your palm and place your thumb across your index and middle fingers.
2. Do not clench your fist until movement begins to avoid increasing muscular tension in the forearm.
3. Just before impact, apply tension to your hand and forearm for maximum damage and injury prevention.
4. Make contact with the first knuckles of your index and middle fingers.
5. Ensure the first two knuckles are aligned with your wrist to prevent wrist injury.
punching technique, martial arts, combat training, self-defense, hand positioning

Execute a Lead Hand Punch
Standard Source: MA 1.02 USMC Fundamentals of Martial Arts
### How to Execute a Lead Hand Punch

1. Assume the Basic Warrior Stance: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, knees slightly bent, and hands in a ready position.

2. Snap Your Lead Hand Out: Extend your lead (forward) hand nearly fully...
### How to Execute a Lead Hand Punch

1. Assume the Basic Warrior Stance: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, knees slightly bent, and hands in a ready position.

2. Snap Your Lead Hand Out: Extend your lead (forward) hand nearly fully while rotating your palm downward (to the deck). Avoid overextending your elbow to prevent hyperextension of the joint.

3. Protect Your Head with the Rear Hand: Keep your rear hand in place to shield your face and head from counterattacks.

4. Make Contact with First Two Knuckles: Strike the target using the first two knuckles of your fist, ensuring they are aligned with your wrist for proper technique and injury prevention.

5. Immediately Retract Your Hand: Pull your lead hand back quickly to return to the basic warrior stance. This protects you from counterattacks and prepares you for follow-up strikes.

Important Notes:
• The lead hand punch is a fast, snapping strike used to stun or set up follow-up attacks.
• Aim for soft tissue areas when possible to maximize effectiveness.
• Practice this punch until it becomes instinctive and can be executed with speed and precision.
lead hand punch, martial arts technique, striking, combat, self-defense

Executing Effective Strikes in Martial Arts
Standard Source: MA 1.02 USMC Fundamentals of Martial Arts
Purpose of Strikes: The purpose of strikes is to stun the opponent or set him up for a follow-up finishing technique. Strikes are unarmed individual striking techniques performed with the arms and legs as personal weapons.

**Principles of...
Purpose of Strikes: The purpose of strikes is to stun the opponent or set him up for a follow-up finishing technique. Strikes are unarmed individual striking techniques performed with the arms and legs as personal weapons.

Principles of Execution: Regardless of the strike, there are several principles of execution that ensure its effectiveness:

1. Generating Power:
- Rotate the hips and shoulders into the attack.
- Move your body mass straight forward or backward in a straight line.
- Drop your body weight into an opponent. Body mass can be transferred into an attack from high to low or from low to high.

2. Muscular Tension:
- There should be muscular tension in the hand and forearm at the moment of impact to maximize damage to the opponent and avoid injury to your hand.
- The arms are relaxed until the moment of impact.

3. Follow-through:
- A strike should be delivered so that the weapon (e.g., hand, elbow) hits and remains on the impact site (target), and follows through the target.
- This technique will inflict maximum damage on the opponent.
- Strikes with the arms are executed with "heavy hands," i.e., the strike is executed by driving through with the strike to allow the weight of the hand to go through the target area of the body.
- Contact on an opponent should be made with the arm slightly bent; the arm extends as it moves through the target.
- Using this technique, strikes do not have to be executed at full force to be effective.

Movement: Your movement will put you in the proper position for launching an attack against your opponent and help protect yourself. Movement is initiated from the basic warrior stance and ends with resuming the basic warrior stance. Each strike can be performed with either the left or right arm depending upon:
- Your angle of attack.
- The position of the opponent.
- The available vulnerable target areas exposed on the opponent.

Target Areas of the Body: For each strike, there are target areas of the body which, when struck, maximize damage to an opponent. Strikes use gross motor skills as opposed to fine motor skills. The target areas of the body are just that: areas. Pinpoint accuracy on a specific nerve is not needed for the strike to be effective.

Safety Precautions During Training: To prevent injuries, train the practical application portion of strikes in three stages:
1. Begin by executing the strikes "in the air." Do not make contact on an opponent or a target during the initial stages of training.
- Ensure you are spaced far enough so that you will not strike each other.
- When striking in the air, avoid full extension of the arms to prevent hyper-extension of the joints. When striking an object (e.g., heavy bag), hyper-extension is not as big a concern because the object absorbs the impact.
2. In the second stage of training, pair up and acquire target areas on your opponent. At no time will contact be made.
3. As proficiency is gained, execute strikes on equipment (when available) such as an air shield, a heavy air bag, or a bayonet dummy.
- For strikes with the arms, have the opponent student block the strike with the meaty portion of his forearm by elevating his arm, with elbow bent, above his head or to his side.
4. Strikes will not be executed at full force or full speed.
strikes,martial arts,tactical execution,body movement,target areas,safety precautions

Safety Considerations for Punch Training

### Safety Guidelines for Punch Practice

### Safety Guidelines for Punch Practice

1. Pair Students Appropriately: Ensure students are paired by height and weight to prevent injury.
2. Start with Air Punches: Begin training with punches executed in the air without making contact with each other or equipment.
3. Progress to Target Areas: As proficiency improves, students should face each other but avoid physical contact, focusing on acquiring target areas.
4. Use Striking Pads: When students are proficient, practice on striking pads and ensure all contact is made only on the pad.
5. Maintain Proper Arm Positioning: Keep your arm slightly bent to avoid hyperextension of the joint during punches.
6. Start Slowly and Increase Speed Gradually: Begin with slow movements and increase speed as proficiency improves to prevent injury and build proper technique.
punch training safety, martial arts practice, combat safety, self-defense training

Urban Operations (32) -

Battle Drill 5: Enter Building/Clear Room
High Priority Source: Ranger Handbook 2006
Objective: To enter and clear a building or room in an urban environment while minimizing risk to personnel and maximizing control.

### Preparation and Planning
1. Platoon and squad leaders must consider the task and purpose they have been...
Objective: To enter and clear a building or room in an urban environment while minimizing risk to personnel and maximizing control.

### Preparation and Planning
1. Platoon and squad leaders must consider the task and purpose they have been given and the method they are to use to achieve the desired results.
2. They must operate IAW (In Accordance With) the Rules of Engagement (ROE) and be aware of the effects that platoon weapons will have on the type and composition of the buildings.
3. Before initiating entry, consider/direct employment of all organic, crew-served, and supporting weapon systems onto the objective area to suppress and neutralize the threat if mission, purpose, building composition, and ROE permit.
4. Soldiers must be equipped at all times with a properly-mounted and immediately-useable night vision device (NVD) or light source to illuminate the immediate area.
5. Leaders must include the specific use of weapons in their planning for precision operations in urban terrain. Consider using snipers or designated marksmen to apply precise fires to the objective.

### Execution
6. Clearing team members must approach the entry point quickly, quietly, and in standard order. The squad leader must ensure he is in a position to control the actions of both fire teams.
7. The members of the fire team are assigned numbers one through four: rifleman (#1), grenadier (#3), SAW operator (#4 if applicable), and team leader (#2).
8. The entire team enters the room as quickly and smoothly as possible and clears the doorway immediately. If possible, move from a covered or concealed position already in entry order.
9. If stopping is necessary to stack outside the entry point, do so only momentarily and provide cover.

### Entry Point and Sector of Fire
10. The door is the focal point for anyone in the room and known as the “fatal funnel.” Moving into the room quickly reduces vulnerability to enemy fire directed at the doorway.
11. Each team member must know their sector of fire and how it overlaps with others. Engage targets immediately upon entry, moving calmly and quickly to designated points of domination. Do not move to a point of domination first and then engage; engagements should not slow movement.

### Immediate Threats
• Immediate threats include:
- Armed personnel prepared to return fire immediately.
- Personnel blocking movement to the position of domination.
- Personnel within arm’s reach of a clearing team member.
- Personnel within 3 to 5 feet of the breach point.

### Assault Team and Overwatch
12. The squad leader designates the assault team and identifies the location of the entry point for them.
13. The squad leader positions the follow-on assault team to provide overwatch and supporting fires for the initial assault team.

### Entry Procedures
14. Assault team members use available cover and concealment, moving as close to the entry point as possible.
- If an explosive or ballistic breach is to be performed by a supporting element, the assault team remains in a covered position until the breach is made. They may provide overwatch and fire support for the breaching element if necessary.
15. All team members must signal one another that they are ready before moving to the entry point. Avoid verbal signals if stealth is a consideration to maintain the element of surprise.
16. Assault team members move quickly from the covered position to the entry point, minimizing exposure to enemy fire.

### Grenade Use
17. If required, the #2 man throws a grenade (fragmentary, concussion, or stun) into the room before entry. The use of grenades must be consistent with ROE and building structure.
- Grenades should be cooked off before being thrown if applicable to the type used.
- If stealth is not a factor, the thrower should sound off with a verbal indication (e.g., “Frag out,” “Concussion out,” “Stun out”).
- If stealth is a factor, only visual signals are given as the grenade is thrown.
battle drill, urban operations, building entry, room clearing, tactical procedure, military tactics, squad movement, immediate threat, grenade use, rules of engagement

Understand and Apply the Principles of International Law in Urban Operations
High Priority Source: FM 3 06 Urban Operations
Principles of International Law Applicable to Urban Operations:

1. Military Necessity: The principle that justifies the use of measures not forbidden by international or domestic law necessary to rapidly achieve military objectives.
2....
Principles of International Law Applicable to Urban Operations:

1. Military Necessity: The principle that justifies the use of measures not forbidden by international or domestic law necessary to rapidly achieve military objectives.
2. Discrimination (or Distinction): The principle of distinguishing between combatants and noncombatants, ensuring that only combatants are targeted.
3. Humanity: The principle of avoiding unnecessary suffering, superfluous injury, and the use of weapons or tactics that cause excessive harm to civilians.
4. Proportionality: The principle that the anticipated military advantage must be weighed against potential damage and injury to civilians, ensuring that actions are not disproportionate.

Application in Urban Operations:
• International law may affect urban operational issues such as the right of entry, base operations, use of force, and treatment of detainees.
• Adherence to these principles is essential for maintaining legitimacy and minimizing collateral damage.

Procedure:

5. Cross obstacles (walls, fences, and rooftops).

Procedure:

5. Cross obstacles (walls, fences, and rooftops).

- a. Move over walls and fences.

(1) Before crossing a wall or fence, look at and beyond it for booby traps, enemy positions, and covered or concealed positions.

(2) Move rapidly to the obstacle and roll quickly over it, keeping the lowest silhouette possible. Speed and a low silhouette deny the enemy a well aimed shot.

(3) Move rapidly to the nearest position while maintaining a low silhouette, with your weapon at the ready position (figure 071-326-0541-7).

- b. Move over rooftops.

• (1) Make a visual reconnaissance of the area and of the route to the next position.

• (2) Move rapidly across the area, maintaining a low silhouette and using all available cover and concealment.

Objective: Enter and clear a two-story building with minimal exposure to enemy fire.

Conditions: As a member of an assault force in an urban area, given a two-story building; a grappling hook attached to 50 feet of scaling rope knotted every foot; individual weapon and equipment; and hand grenades.

Steps:

2. Use the grappling hook and scaling rope to ascend or descend the building as needed, ensuring that the rope is secured properly at all times.
3. Clear the building systematically, using a team-based approach to minimize exposure to enemy fire.
4. Utilize hand grenades if necessary for clearing rooms or areas of potential threats, following proper procedures and safety protocols.
5. Maintain communication with your team throughout the operation to ensure coordination and situational awareness.
6. Secure the building after clearing it, ensuring that all hostile forces have been neutralized and that the area is safe for subsequent operations.

Warnings/Contraindications: Always be aware of potential enemy positions within the building. Use cover and concealment at all times to reduce exposure to fire.

- Ammonia: Commercial refrigerant, fertilizer, food production, petroleum, explosives, other chemicals.
- Arsine: Semiconductor industry.
- Boron Trichloride: Organic catalyst, soldering magnesium.
- Boron Trifluoride: Chemical catalyst, aluminum refining.
- Carbon Disulfide: Industrial solvent, dry-cleaning, agriculture, petroleum, electroplating.
- Chlorine: Potable water, disinfectants, metal treatment, plastics & rubber.
- Diborane: Plastics and rubber.
- Ethylene Oxide: Industrial alcohols, fumigant, industrial sterilant.
- Fluorine: Uranium processing, rocket fuel.
- Formaldehyde: Plastics, fertilizers, preservative/corrosion inhibitor, fungicide and germicide, pesticide, pharmaceuticals.
- Fuming Nitric Acid: Fertilizers, explosives, metal processing, pesticides, rocket fuel.
- Hydrogen Bromide: Chemical industry, pharmaceuticals.
- Hydrogen Chloride: Fabrics, semiconductors.
- Hydrogen Cyanide: Pesticides, other chemicals, pharmaceuticals, electroplating.
- Hydrogen Fluoride: Glass production, chemical catalyst.
- Hydrogen Sulfide: Metallurgy, agricultural disinfectant.
- Phosgene: Dyes, pharmaceuticals, herbicides & insecticides.
- Phosphorus Trichloride: Metallurgy, pesticides and germicides, gasoline additive.
- Sulfur Dioxide: Paper, food processing, ice production, disinfectant, leather processing.
- Sulfuric Acid: Fertilizers, petroleum, iron and steel production, battery electrolyte.
- Tungsten: Electronics, other chemicals.
3. Use this information to prepare for potential chemical threats in urban environments.

5. Ensure all units have access to appropriate protective equipment and decontamination procedures.

Urban Threat Tactics and Asymmetry
High Priority Source: FM 3 06 Urban Operations FM 90 10 US Army
Urban Threat Tactics:

• Use the Population to Advantage: Leverage local populations for support or as a tool against enemy forces.
• Win the Information War: Control narratives and information flow within urban areas.
• **Manipulate Key...
Urban Threat Tactics:

• Use the Population to Advantage: Leverage local populations for support or as a tool against enemy forces.
• Win the Information War: Control narratives and information flow within urban areas.
• Manipulate Key Facilities: Target critical infrastructure such as power, water, and communication hubs.
• Use All Dimensions: Engage in operations across all physical and informational dimensions of urban environments.
• Employ Urban-Oriented Weapons: Use weapons suited for confined spaces and dense populations.
• Engage Entire Enemy Force: Aim to engage the entire enemy force rather than isolated units.
• Focus Attacks on Support Areas, Isolated Groups, and Individuals: Target logistics and support structures rather than front-line forces.

Negative Effects of Urbanization:

• General Instability: Increased likelihood of unrest and conflict due to dense populations.
• Food and Water Shortage: Limited resources can lead to scarcity in urban areas.
• Disease and Pollution: Poor sanitation and overcrowding increase health risks.
• Competing Power Structures: Multiple factions may vie for control within urban environments.
urban,threat,tactics,asymmetry

Steps for Conducting Information Operations in Urban Areas:

1. Understand the Human Dimension: Recognize cultural, social, and political dynamics of the urban environment to tailor information operations effectively.
2. Perform Focused Information Operations: Use targeted messaging to influence perceptions, counter misinformation, and support military objectives.
3. Separate Noncombatants from Combatants: Identify and isolate noncombatants to reduce risk to civilians and improve operational effectiveness.
4. Restore Essential Services: Re-establish critical infrastructure such as power, water, and communication systems to stabilize the urban environment.
5. Transition Control: Shift control of information operations to local authorities or civilian agencies during the transition phase.

Considerations:
• Information operations must be conducted with sensitivity to avoid exacerbating tensions or alienating local populations.

Purpose: The dominate phase of the urban operational framework involves taking control of key areas and ensuring that military objectives are achieved.

Key Actions During the Dominate Phase:
1. Preserve critical infrastructure such as power grids, communication systems, and transportation networks to ensure continued operations and support for both military and civilian populations.
2. Conduct close combat with enemy forces in urban environments, using tactics that minimize risk to civilians and infrastructure.
3. Avoid the attrition approach, which focuses on wearing down the enemy through prolonged conflict rather than achieving decisive victories.
4. Control the essential areas of the city to maintain operational superiority and ensure long-term stability.

Considerations:
• Ensure that all actions during the dominate phase are in line with military doctrine and ethical guidelines.
• Coordinate closely with local authorities and other agencies as needed.
• Be prepared to adapt strategies based on changing conditions or new intelligence.

Implement Fire Control Principles
High Priority Source: STP 21 24 Army Warrior Leader Skills Level 2 3 and 4
Objective: Apply the principles of fire control to ensure effective and safe use of weapons.

Procedure:

Objective: Apply the principles of fire control to ensure effective and safe use of weapons.

Procedure:

1. Avoid target overkill: Conserve ammunition by not firing unnecessarily at targets that have already been neutralized or are no longer a threat.
2. Use each weapon in its intended role: Ensure that each type of weapon is used for the purpose it was designed for (e.g., machine guns for area suppression, rifles for engaging dismounted personnel).
3. Engage targets with high probability of kill: Focus fire on targets that are most likely to be neutralized effectively by the available weapons.
4. Engage long-range targets first: Prioritize targets at longer distances to reduce the risk of enemy engagement and increase the likelihood of a successful engagement.
5. Destroy targets posing the greatest threat first: Identify and eliminate the most dangerous threats immediately to protect friendly forces.

Warnings:
• Soldiers may be killed or injured when firing weapons. Minimum firing distances, backblast areas, and weapon-specific regulations must be strictly followed.
fire control principles, weapon use, target engagement, ammunition conservation, tactical priority

Conduct Area Reconnaissance
High Priority Source: Ranger Handbook 2006
Actions on the Objective, Area Reconnaissance

• The element occupies the ORP as discussed in the section on occupation of the ORP. The RTO calls in spare for occupation of ORP. The leader confirms his location on map while subordinate leaders...
Actions on the Objective, Area Reconnaissance

• The element occupies the ORP as discussed in the section on occupation of the ORP. The RTO calls in spare for occupation of ORP. The leader confirms his location on map while subordinate leaders make necessary perimeter adjustments.

• The PL organizes the platoon in one of two ways: separate recon and security elements, or combined recon and security elements.

• The PL takes subordinates leaders and key personnel on a leader’s recon to confirm the objective and plan.
- Issues a 5-point contingency plan before departure.
- Establishes a suitable release point that is beyond sight and sound of the objective if possible, but that is definitely out of sight. The RP should also have good rally point characteristics.
- Allow all personnel to become familiar with the release point and surrounding area.
- Identifies the objective and emplaces surveillance. Designates a surveillance team to keep the objective under surveillance. Issues a contingency plan to the senior man remaining with the surveillance team. The surveillance team is positioned with one man facing the objective, and one facing back in the direction of the release point.
- Takes subordinate leaders forward to pinpoint the objective, emplace surveillance, establish a limit of advance, and choose vantage points.
- Maintains commo with the platoon throughout the leader’s recon.

• The PSG maintains security and supervises priorities of work in the ORP.
- Reestablishes security at the ORP.
- Disseminates the PLs contingency plan.
- Oversees preparation of recon personnel (personnel recamouflaged, NVDs and binos prepared, weapons on safe with a round in the chamber).

• The PL and his recon party return to the ORP.
- Confirms the plan or issues a FRAGO.
- Allows subordinate leaders time to disseminate the plan.

• The patrol conducts the recon by long-range observation and surveillance if possible.
- R&S elements move to observation points that offer cover and concealment and that are outside of small-arms range.
- Establishes a series of observation posts (OP) if information cannot be gathered from one location.
- Gathers all PIR using the SALUTE format.

• If necessary, the patrol conducts its recon by short-range observation and surveillance.
- Moves to an OP near the objective.
- Passes close enough to the objective to gain information.
- Gathers all PIR using the SALUTE format.

• R&S teams move using a technique such as the cloverleaf method to move to successive OP’s. In this method, R&S teams avoid paralleling the objective site, maintain extreme stealth, do not cross the limit of advance, and maximize the use of available cover and concealment.

• During the conduct of the recon, each R&S team will return to the release point when any of the following occurs:
- They have gathered all their PIR.
- They have reached the limit of advance.
- The allocated time to conduct the recon has elapsed.
- Contact has been made.

• At the release point, the leader will analyze what information has been gathered and determine if he has met the PIR requirements.

• If the leader determines that he has not gathered sufficient information to meet the PIR requirements, or if the information he and the subordinate leader gathered differs drastically, he may have to send R&S teams back to the objective site. In this case, R&S teams will alternate areas of responsibilities. For example, if one team reconnoitered from the 6 – 3 – 12, then that team will now recon from the 6 – 9 – 12.

• The R&S element returns undetected to the ORP by the specified time.
- Disseminates information to all patrol members through key leaders at the ORP, or moves to a position at least one terrain feature or one kilometer away to disseminate. To disseminate, the leader has the RTO prepare three sketches of the objective site based on the leader's sketch and provides the copies to the subordinate leaders to assist in dissemination.
- Reports any information requirements and/or any information requiring immediate attention to higher headquarters, and departs for the designated area.

• If contact is made, move to the release point. The recon element tries to break contact and return to the ORP, secure rucksacks, and quickly move out of the area. Once they have moved a safe distance away, the leader will inform higher HQ of the situation and take further instructions from them.
- While emplacing surveillance, the recon element withdraws through the release point to the ORP, and follows the same procedures as above.
- While conducting the reconnaissance, the compromised element returns a sufficient volume of fire to allow them to break contact. Surveillance can fire an AT-4 at the largest weapon on the objective. All elements will pull off the objective and move to the release point. The senior man will quickly account for all personnel and return to the ORP. Once in the ORP, follow the procedures previously described.
area reconnaissance,objective site,SALUTE format,release point,observation posts,limit of advance,cloverleaf method,PIR requirements,AT-4

Conduct Area Reconnaissance Using Surveillance or Vantage-Point Method
High Priority Source: STP 21 24 Warrior Leader Skills Level 2 3 4
### Procedure: Conduct Area Reconnaissance Using Surveillance or Vantage-Point Method

#### Objective:
Obtain information about a specific location and the area immediately around it (e.g., road junctions, hills, bridges, enemy...
### Procedure: Conduct Area Reconnaissance Using Surveillance or Vantage-Point Method

#### Objective:
Obtain information about a specific location and the area immediately around it (e.g., road junctions, hills, bridges, enemy positions).

#### Steps:
1. Receive Mission: Once given an area reconnaissance mission, move the platoon to the appointed area in the shortest amount of time.
- This normally involves traveling along existing roads using the appropriate movement techniques.
- During this movement to an area, the platoon reports and bypasses enemy opposition unless ordered to do otherwise.

2. Establish Objective Rallying Point (ORP):
- When the platoon reaches its area, it halts and sets up an objective rallying point (ORP).

3. Reconnoiter the Objective:
- The objective can be reconnoitered in one of two ways:
- Option 1: When the terrain permits the security element to move to a position to overwatch the reconnaissance element, the leader may decide to have small reconnaissance teams move to each surveillance point or vantage point around the objective instead of having the entire element move as a unit from point to point.
- After the objective has been reconnoitered, the elements return to the ORP and information is issued.
- The patrol then returns to friendly lines.
- Option 2: When the terrain does not allow the platoon to secure the objective area, the platoon leaves a security element at the ORP and uses reconnaissance and security (R&S) teams to reconnoiter the objective.
- These teams move to different surveillance points or vantage points, from which they reconnoiter the objective.
- Once the objective has been reconnoitered, the R&S team returns to the ORP, shares the information, and returns to friendly lines.

4. Sterilize Reconnaissance Site:
- The reconnaissance site should be sterilized before withdrawal.
- Withdrawal from the area must be as skillful, patient, and precise as the movement into it.

5. Provide Security for the Force:
- The reconnaissance element(s) with this mission must provide the commander with sufficient warning of the location and movement of enemy forces to permit the parent force to take evasive action or, when this is not possible, to provide covering fires that permit withdrawal of the reconnaissance element.
- Only if warnings are timely and information is accurate does the commander have the time and space to react.
- It is also the only way that, if the reconnaissance element is detected, the commander can arrange to give it sufficient overwatching suppressive fires or time to evade and withdraw safely.

6. Transmit Information:
- Information received about the target may be transmitted back to the appropriate headquarters by electronic means as it is observed.
- Or, the reconnaissance personnel may withdraw from the target and disseminate information by other means.

7. Designate Objective Location:
- Designate the location of the objective by either grid coordinates or a map overlay with a boundary line drawn around the area.

8. Use Deception Techniques:
- Conduct deceptive measures during infiltration and exfiltration to avoid detection.

9. Apply Stealth, Camouflage, and Concealment Techniques:
- Apply stealth, camouflage, and concealment techniques along with noise and light discipline to avoid detection.

10. Conduct Pre-Mission Inspection and Rehearsal:
- Conduct a pre-mission inspection and rehearsal to ensure all personnel are prepared for the mission.

11. Use Correct Size Command and Control Group:
- Use the correct size command and control group for the mission.

12. Apply Appropriate Movement Techniques:
- Use the correct movement techniques during the mission.

13. Apply Correct Security Techniques:
- Use the correct security techniques during the mission.

#### Evaluation Preparation:
• At the test site, provide all equipment and material given in the task conditions statement.
• Tell the Soldier to organize and conduct an area reconnaissance using the surveillance or vantage-point method.
• Obtain and report any information about the terrain and enemy within the specified area.
• Tell the Soldier to complete the mission within the time specified by the commander.
• You will act as the battalion intelligence officer (S2) to provide answers to any questions the Soldier may ask.

#### Performance Measures:
|Performance Measure|GO|NO GO|
|---|---|---|
|1. Established a plan of action based on the mission and the enemy situation.|——|——|
|2. Conducted a reconnaissance.|——|——|
|3. Conducted deceptive measures during infiltration and exfiltration.|——|——|
|4. Used the smallest unit required to conduct the reconnaissance.|——|——|
|5. Applied stealth, camouflage, and concealment techniques along with noise and light discipline to avoid detection.|——|——|
|6. Conducted pre-mission inspection and rehearsal.|——|——|
|7. Used the correct size command and control group for the mission.|——|——|
|8. Used the correct movement techniques during the mission.|——|——|
|9. Used the correct security techniques during the mission.|——|——|
area reconnaissance, surveillance method, vantage-point method, objective rallying point, security of the force, stealth techniques, camouflage, concealment, movement techniques, tactical reconnaissance

• It is also the only way that, if the reconnaissance element is detected, the commander can arrange to give it sufficient overwatching suppressive fires or time to evade and withdraw safely.

Control the Route Reconnaissance

Ensure that:

1. Reconnaissance commences from the flanks or rear when reconnoitering areas along the route are not likely to be defended by enemy detachments (such as bridge approaches, defiles, or built-up areas).
2. Detailed observation precedes actual reconnaissance.
3. Approach routes are checked for mines, booby traps, and signs of ambush.

Additional Steps:

• When time is available, dismounted personnel are sent forward first, covered by the remaining elements of the unit. The number of dismounted personnel sent forward depends on the size of the objective and on the available approaches, cover, and concealment. If the dismounted patrols find that the near edge of the area is clear, the remainder of the unit moves quickly forward. The dismounted patrols then continue the reconnaissance and overwatch. The remainder of the unit closely follows the dismounted patrols.

• When conducting a mounted reconnaissance, part of the unit remains mounted and moves forward cautiously but rapidly, overwatched by the remaining mounted elements. If the near edge of the area is clear, the overwatching elements moved forward quickly and the advance continues.

Plan the Reconnaissance

Step 1: Receive the order.

Step 2: Issue a warning order.

Step 3: Gather information and prepare an operation order based on METT-TC factors: mission, enemy, terrain and weather, troops and support available, time available, civil considerations.

Step 4: Ensure that the plan is as detailed as possible and includes:

1. Exact information to obtain, the time to report the information, where to report the information, where to seek the information, action to take on enemy contact, and when to execute the mission.

2. Essential details include:
- Pertinent information on the enemy, friendly troops, and the area of operations.
- Proposed plans of higher commands, including anticipated traffic flow along the route and types of vehicles to be employed.
- When, where, and how to report information.
- Time of departure.
- Appropriate control measures.
- Action to take after completing the mission.
- Special equipment requirements.

3. Terrain considerations of existing routes and their physical characteristics:
- Gradients of slope and the radius of curvature.
- Bridges.
- Vehicular fording, ferrying, and swimming sites.
- Tunnels, under passes, and similar obstructions to traffic flow.
- Artificial obstacles (such as areas of chemical, biological, and radiological contamination, roadblocks, craters, and minefields).
- Rock falls and slide areas.
- Drainage.
- Other natural or manmade features (such as wooded and built-up areas) that may affect movement.

Engage Targets with an M249 Machine Gun Using an AN/PAS-13 Thermal Weapon Sight
High Priority Source: STP 21 1 Warrior Skills Level 1
### Procedure: Engage Targets with an M249 Machine Gun Using an AN/PAS-13 Thermal Weapon Sight

Conditions: Given an M249 machine gun with a mounted and zeroed AN/PAS-13 thermal weapon sight (TWS), linked 5.56-mm ammunition, threat targets, and...
### Procedure: Engage Targets with an M249 Machine Gun Using an AN/PAS-13 Thermal Weapon Sight

Conditions: Given an M249 machine gun with a mounted and zeroed AN/PAS-13 thermal weapon sight (TWS), linked 5.56-mm ammunition, threat targets, and a requirement to engage such targets.

Standards: Detect and determine the range to targets. Fire the M249 machine gun and engage targets in the assigned sector of fire. Apply correct marksmanship fundamentals and target engagement techniques so that each target is hit or suppressed.

### Performance Steps:
1. Place the TWS into operation.
2. Assume an appropriate firing position based on the situation. The firing position should protect you from enemy fire and observation, yet allow you to place effective fire on targets in your sector of fire.
- Prone position, bipod-supported: Advantages: steady, easy to assume, low silhouette, and easily adapted to use of cover and support. Disadvantages: effectiveness can be limited by terrain and vegetation irregularities.
- Fighting position, bipod-supported: Advantages: best when available.
3. Identify targets in your designated sector of fire.
4. Load the weapon.
5. Acquire targets using the TWS reticle.
- Personnel: Place the target on the horizontal line and match its height with one of the vertical lines. Measurement is made from the horizontal line to the top (or bottom) of each vertical line for the range indicated. The vertical line of a crosshair reflects the height of a 5-foot man at the specified range.
- Tank: When viewed from the side, place the left edge of a tank at the left side of the horizontal line. Read the range to the tank from the scale at the right edge of the tank. When viewed from the front or rear, use one-half of the indicated range value (since width of the tank is approximately one-half of the length of the tank). The horizontal line of a crosshair reflects the width of a 10-foot tank at the specified range.
- The firing aiming point of each cross hair is the point of intersection of the vertical and horizontal lines.
6. Fire on target(s) until destroyed or until you receive an order to cease fire.

Implement Finnish 'Motti' Tactics in Subarctic Winter Warfare
High Priority Source: Canadian Military Basic Cold Weather Training
Overview: The Finnish 'motti' tactics were developed during the Russo-Finnish War (1939–40) and are particularly effective in subarctic winter conditions, especially in forested areas. These tactics exploit the environment to isolate and destroy...
Overview: The Finnish 'motti' tactics were developed during the Russo-Finnish War (1939–40) and are particularly effective in subarctic winter conditions, especially in forested areas. These tactics exploit the environment to isolate and destroy enemy forces that are unprepared for cold-weather warfare.

Phases of Motti Tactics: The motti system is divided into three phases:
1. Reconnaissance and Stopping: Continuous reconnaissance until the enemy is isolated.
2. Attack and Cutting: Surprise flanking movements and envelopments to isolate the enemy column and cut it into smaller groups.
3. Isolation and Annihilation: Maintaining isolation of the motti, cutting off communication lines, and executing attacks on flanks to prevent breakout.

Reconnaissance Phase:
• Fighting patrols attack from all directions using ambushes, hit-and-run tactics, and demolitions.
• Patrols are lightly equipped and travel on skis for speed and surprise.
• They avoid enemy security posts and hold fire until within close range of the enemy.
• Patrols move rapidly between targets after each engagement to maintain pressure on the enemy.

Attack Phase:
• Sporadic attacks in company or battalion strength are directed at limited objectives, with disengagement after the objective is achieved.
• The divisional commander controls overall operations and establishes zones of activity for regiments (brigades) and battalions.

Cutting Phase:
• Surprise flanking movements and envelopments isolate the enemy column and cut it into small groups.
• Assembly Area Selection: Assembly areas are chosen outside the radius of enemy land reconnaissance, typically 3 to 6 miles from objectives. Movement is in column with measures taken to preserve surprise.
• Advance to Attack Area: Advance is made in column along concealed routes at a controlled speed (about 1–1/2 km per hour or one mile per hour). Flank patrols secure potentially dangerous approaches into the route of the column.
• Cutting the Enemy Column: Cutting occurs within 270 metres (300 yards) of the stated location. The attacking unit halts at a concealed position 270 to 450 metres (300 to 500 yards) from the cutting point.
• Execution of Cut: Engineers are attached to the cutting troops, and obstacles such as mines are laid to deny enemy use of roads. A strong roadblock is established at each flank of the break.

Isolation Phase:
• The isolated motti is split again by attacks on flanks after the enemy exhausts itself in an effort to break out.
• Enemy lines of communication must be kept closed.
• If there are built-up fortifications, softening operations may be necessary using snipers, direct fire weapons, harassing fire, and propaganda.

Conditions for Success: The success of motti tactics depends on:
• a. Ability to move in deep snow, dense forest, and roadless terrain.
• b. Ability to live in the attack zone despite cold and snow to preserve the continuity of the battle.
• c. Ability to keep direction in dense forest, darkness, and storms/fog.
• d. Surprise.
Finnish motti tactics,cold weather warfare,subarctic winter,military strategy,forest combat,enemy isolation
Define and Mark Initial Delay Position (IDP)
Standard Source: STP 21 24 Warrior Leader Skills Level 2 3 4
Procedure for Defining and Marking an Initial Delay Position (IDP):

1. Understand the Purpose of IDP: An IDP is where a delaying action begins, trading space for time.
2. Establish Boundaries: The delay sector is defined by boundaries...
Procedure for Defining and Marking an Initial Delay Position (IDP):

1. Understand the Purpose of IDP: An IDP is where a delaying action begins, trading space for time.
2. Establish Boundaries: The delay sector is defined by boundaries that must be clearly marked on maps and in coordination with units.
3. Relate to Time-Phased Forward Edge of Battle Area (FEBA): The initial and all subsequent delay positions can be related to a time-phased FEBA for strategic planning.
4. Specify Delay Positions: Initial and successive delay positions must be specified, and PLs may be used to report the progress of the battle.
5. Hold Enemy Forward of Delay Lines: The enemy is held forward of delay lines until the specified time or until permission is granted to withdraw.
6. Mark IDP on Boundaries: Initial and successive delay positions are shown on boundaries by coordination points with a solid line between them.
7. Label IDP Appropriately: Although most IDPs are given a code name, they may have a number, letter, or a variety of code names. The letter abbreviation (IDP) can be to the flank of the coordination symbol (when at the flank, it is in parentheses) or on the line itself.
8. Indicate Time Phase: The time phase of an IDP is indicated as a date-time group having a two-digit day and a four-digit hour, both connected. The month indicator can be a three-letter type or spelled out, depending upon the desires of the commander.
9. Format Labeling Correctly: Place the letters "IDP" in parentheses between the line code name, letter, or number and the date-time group (figure 071-332-5000-22).
initial delay position,IDP,battle area,FEBA,strategic planning,military tactics

Procedure for Designating and Marking Coordinating Points:

1. Understand the Purpose of Coordinating Points: Coordinating points are designated on boundaries as specific points for coordination of fires and maneuver between adjacent units.
2. Indicate When to Use: They should be indicated whenever a boundary crosses the FEBA and should be indicated whenever the boundary crosses the covering force. They are also used where DLs and internal boundaries intersect.
3. Choose Recognizable Terrain Features: Coordinating points should be located at some terrain feature easily recognizable both on the ground and on a map.
4. Indicate General Trace of FEBA/Covering Force/DL: The location on a boundary indicates the general trace of the FEBA, covering force, or DL as visualized by the commander who designates them.
5. Mark with Appropriate Symbol: Show the symbol for a coordinating point by a circle with an "X" centered in it (figure 071-332-5000-23).
6. Label the Symbol Appropriately: Ensure that the label is clear and corresponds to the designated point.

Procedure:

1. A tactical march is conducted by platoons as part of company operations and can be either a foot march or a motor (road) march.

2. The purpose of the foot march is for troops to arrive at their destination on time and in condition to execute their tactical mission.

3. A successful foot march occurs when the unit crosses the start point and release point at the specified times outlined in the order.

4. The unit must follow the prescribed route, rate of march, and interval without deviation unless required by enemy action or orders from higher headquarters.

5. Key fundamentals for conducting a tactical march include:
- Effective control by leaders to maintain discipline and cohesion.
- Detailed planning, including all necessary logistics, security, and communication plans.
- Rehearsals of the march route and procedures before execution.

Issue and Execute a March Order for Tactical Marches
Standard Source: SH 21 76 Ranger Handbook
Procedure:

1. A march order can be issued as an OPORD (Operations Order), FRAGO (Fragmentary Order), or as an annex to either of these orders.

2. The march order must include the following:
- **Formations and order of...
Procedure:

1. A march order can be issued as an OPORD (Operations Order), FRAGO (Fragmentary Order), or as an annex to either of these orders.

2. The march order must include the following:
- Formations and order of movement: Define how units will move in formation during the march.
- Route of march: Specify the assembly area, start point, release point, rally points, checkpoints, and break/halt points along the route.
- Start point time, release point time, and rate of march: Clearly define timing and speed requirements for the operation.
- March interval for squads, teams, and individuals: Establish spacing between units to ensure control and safety during movement.

3. The order must include detailed instructions on:
- Actions on enemy contact (air and ground): Define how the unit will respond if contacted by the enemy during the march.
- Actions at halts: Outline procedures for when the unit stops or takes a break during the operation.
- Fires plan: Provide a detailed fire support plan to cover the march route and protect the unit from enemy threats.
- Water supply plan: Ensure adequate water is available for Soldiers throughout the march.
- MEDEVAC (Medical Evacuation) plan: Establish procedures for medical evacuation in case of casualties.
march order, tactical march planning, military operations, fire support plan

Plan and Execute a Tactical March Using METT-TC Analysis
Standard Source: SH 21 76 Ranger Handbook
Procedure:

1. When planning a tactical march, use the METT-TC framework to guide decision-making:
- Mission: Understand the task and purpose of the march.
- Enemy: Analyze enemy intentions, capabilities, and likely course of...
Procedure:

1. When planning a tactical march, use the METT-TC framework to guide decision-making:
- Mission: Understand the task and purpose of the march.
- Enemy: Analyze enemy intentions, capabilities, and likely course of action.
- Terrain and Weather: Consider road conditions, trafficability, visibility, and weather impact on movement.
- Troops/Equipment: Assess the condition of Soldiers, their loads, weapons, radios, and other equipment.
- Time: Determine start time, release time, rate of march, and total available time for the operation.
- Civilian Considerations: Account for movement through populated areas, refugees, and OPSEC (operational security) requirements.

2. Based on METT-TC analysis, determine the appropriate task organization:
- Security: Include advance and trail teams to protect the flanks of the march.
- Main Body: Composed of two remaining line squads and a weapons squad for support.
- Headquarters: Provide command and control functions during the march.

3. Establish clear control measures such as checkpoints, rally points, dispersion distances, communication plans, and other necessary coordination tools.
mett-TC analysis, tactical march planning, military operations, task organization
Establish Start Point and Release Point for Tactical Marches

Procedure:

1. The start point and release point are established by higher headquarters or as specified in the order.

2. Use checkpoints to report progress, maintain orientation, and ensure all units stay on course.

3. Define rally or rendezvous points for use when elements become separated during movement.

4. Identify location of leaders, where they can best control their elements during the march.

5. Establish a communications plan (commo plan) that includes:
- Locations of radios and other communication equipment.
- Frequencies, call signs, and operational frequencies (OPSKEDs) for coordination.

6. Implement a dispersion plan between Soldiers to avoid congestion and maintain safety:
- During the day: 3 to 5 meters between individuals.
- At night: 1 to 3 meters between individuals.

Procedure:

• Step 1: Inspect the chamber.

Options:

• (1) If no round is in the chamber:
- (a) Reload and try to fire.
- (b) If the gun fires, you have corrected the stoppage.
- (c) If the weapon fails to fire, apply immediate action for a second time.

• (d) If immediate action fails, continue to the next step.

• (e) Disassemble and inspect the weapon.

• (f) Clean, lubricate, and replace damaged or missing parts, as needed.

• (2) If a round is in the chamber:
- (a) Close the cover and try to fire.
- (b) If the weapon fires, you have corrected the stoppage.
- (c) If the weapon fails to fire, ensure the cocking handle is forward and the weapon is on safe.

Steps to Disarm a Weapon Safely:

1. Place the safety switch on the safe (S) position. This is critical to prevent accidental discharge.
2. Charge the weapon. Ensure that the weapon is fully charged in preparation for disarming.
3. Return the charger handles to the forward position and rotate only one charger handle up. This action ensures proper alignment for removal of the round or spent case.
4. Remove the live round or spent case from the bolt:
- Insert the tip of a cleaning rod through the right handrail as close to the bolt face as possible (refer to figure 071-030-0006-1 for visual guidance).
- Lift up on the cleaning rod to force the live round or case off the bolt face and out the bottom of the gun. Be sure to catch the live round or spent case as it falls out.
5. Remove the linked rounds from the feeder:
- Open the top cover.
- Check for rounds in the feeder. If any rounds are found, perform the following actions (refer to figure 071-030-0006-2 for visual guidance).
disarming weapon, safety switch, charger handle, cleaning rod, live round removal, spent case removal
Load the MK19 Machine Gun
High Priority Source: STP 21 1 Warrior Skills Level 1
Procedure for Loading the MK19 Machine Gun:

1. Ensure the Weapon is Safe:

Procedure for Loading the MK19 Machine Gun:

1. Ensure the Weapon is Safe:
- Make sure the chamber is empty, the bolt is forward, and the charger handles are in the lock position.
- Ensure the safety switch is in the safe (S) position.

2. Insert the First Round:
a. Open the top cover and insert the first round through the feed throat and into the feeder, link opening first.
b. Push or slide the round across the first set of feeder pawls; make sure the round is straight and firmly seated against the bolt.
c. Index the feed slide assembly to the left and close the top cover.

3. Charge the Weapon:
a. Grasp the charger handles palms down.
b. Press the charger handle locks and rotate charger handles down.
c. Pull the charger handles sharply to the rear until the bolt seated.
d. Push the charger handles forward and rotate them up into the lock position.

4. Load the First Round:
a. Place the safety switch on the fire (F) position and press the trigger.
b. Rotate the charger handles down and pull them sharply to the rear until the bolt seated.
c. Place the safety switch on the safe (S) position.
d. Push the charger forward and rotate the charger handles up into the locked position.
e. Leave the safety switch in the safe (S) position until ready to fire.
load,mk19,loading,procedure,weapon,safety,charger handles,bolt,chamber

WARNING: If the transport safety pin cannot be reinserted, do not move the weapon. Notify the noncommissioned officer in charge (NCOIC).

Steps:
1. While cradling the launcher with the left arm, reinsert the transport safety pin.
- _Note_: In a training situation only, after inserting the transport safety pin, wait 2 minutes. Keep the launcher pointed toward the target area.
2. Carefully lay the launcher on the ground with the muzzle pointed toward the target area.
3. Immediately use another launcher to engage the target.

Performance Measures for Misfire:
• Shouted "MISFIRE".
• Released the red safety catch.
• Recocked the cocking lever.
• Tried to refire after checking the backblast area.
• Repeated performance measures 1 through 4 when the launcher failed to fire.
• Returned the red safety lever to the SAFE (uncocked) position.
• Removed the launcher from the shoulder while keeping the muzzle pointed at the target area.
• Replaced the transport safety pin.
• Placed the launcher on the ground with the muzzle pointed toward the target area.

Procedure:

To field zero the weapon on a 300-meter target:

1. Assume the correct bipod-supported prone position or fighting position.
2. Set up on a live-fire range with appropriate equipment and materials.
3. Fire at a 300-meter target using no more than 12 rounds to achieve proper zeroing.
4. Adjust the weapon's sights based on bullet impact points until accuracy is achieved.

Notes:
• This task should be evaluated in accordance with FM 3-22.68.
• Ensure range safety protocols are followed as per installation regulations.

Prepare the M136 Launcher for Firing
High Priority Source: STP 21 1 Army Warrior Skills Level 1 Soldiers Manual of Common Tasks
Procedure:

1. Remove the launcher from the carrying position and cradle it with the left arm.

2. While cradling the launcher, pull the transport safety pin with the right hand and release it.
- Ensure the transport safety pin is...
Procedure:

1. Remove the launcher from the carrying position and cradle it with the left arm.

2. While cradling the launcher, pull the transport safety pin with the right hand and release it.
- Ensure the transport safety pin is attached to the launcher by its lanyard.
- If the launcher has no lanyard, place the transport safety pin in your pocket.
- If the launcher remains unfired, reinsert the transport safety pin.

3. Unsnap and unfold the shoulder stop.

4. Place the launcher on the right shoulder.

5. Release the front sight by pressing down on the sight cover and sliding it to the rear.
- Release the rear sight by pressing down on the cover and sliding it forward.
- Sliding the covers off allows the sights to pop up.

6. Check the backblast area.

7. Cock the launcher by unfolding the cocking lever with the right hand.
- Place the thumb of the right hand under the cocking lever.
- Grip the front of the firing mechanism for support.
- Push the cocking lever forward to the right.
- Let the cocking lever slide back.

8. Adjust the rear sight for the required range.
- When closing the sight cover, set the sight on a range of 200 meters.
- If the range to the target is more than 200 meters but less than 250 meters, no sight adjustment is required.
- To adjust the rear sight range setting to more than 200 meters, turn the range knob clockwise (toward the muzzle).
- To decrease the range, turn the range knob counterclockwise (toward the gunner).
- There is a click at each 50-meter increment; this sound aids you during limited visibility.

Warnings:
• Make sure personnel wear earplugs.
• Point the weapon toward the target.
• Clear the backblast area.

- Once you have zeroed the weapon, record the elevation setting.

Procedure for Zeroing an M16A1 Rifle:

Conditions:

• One of the following situations exists:

Procedure for Zeroing an M16A1 Rifle:

Conditions:
• On a 25-meter range.
• Given an M16A1 rifle, 18 rounds of 5.56-mm ammunition, a 250-meter zero target, and sandbags for support.
• One of the following situations exists:
- You receive a rifle that you have never fired.
- Your rifle is returned after repair.
- You think something may have changed the battle sight zero.

Standards:
• Battle sight zero the rifle so that five out of six rounds, in two consecutive shot groups, strike within the 4-centimeter circle on the target, using 18 rounds or less.
• Bullets that break the line of the 4-centimeter circle are accepted.

Steps:
1. Set up the rifle with sandbags for support.
2. Load the M16A1 rifle with 5.56-mm ammunition.
3. Aim at the 250-meter zero target on a 25-meter range.
4. Fire two consecutive shot groups of three rounds each, ensuring proper sight alignment and trigger control.
5. Evaluate the impact points of the shots on the target.
6. Adjust the battle sight zero as needed to ensure that five out of six rounds fall within the 4-centimeter circle on the target.
7. Repeat the process if necessary until the standard is met.
