Steps:
1. The **bridge team...
Purpose: To dismantle a rope bridge using the dry method after all but two troops have crossed.

Materials Required:
• Transport knot
• Fixed loop
• Carabiner
• Rappel seat or harness
• Three-man pull team

Steps:
1. The bridge team commander (BTC) should have anchored his tightening system with the transport knot.
2. The BTC back-stacks all of the slack coming out of the transport knot and ties a fixed loop, placing a carabiner into the fixed loop.
3. The next to last man to cross attaches the carabiner to his rappel seat or harness and moves across the bridge using the Tyrolean traverse method.
4. The BTC removes all knots from the system, leaving the far side anchored while the rope passes around the near side anchor.
5. A three-man pull team, assembled on the far side, takes the end brought across by the next to last man and pulls the rope tight again, holding it in place.
6. The BTC attaches himself to the rope bridge and moves across using the same method as the next to last man.
7. Once across, the BTC breaks down the far side anchor, removes all knots, and pulls the rope across for final dismantling.

Notes:
• Ensure that all personnel are properly trained in the Tyrolean traverse method before attempting this procedure.
• The dry method is preferred when conditions allow for safe removal of the system without submersion.
dismantle rope bridge, dry method, transport knot, Tyrolean traverse, fixed loop
Retrieving the One Rope Bridge
Standard Source: US Marine Corps Wilderness Medicine
Procedure for Retrieving a One Rope Bridge

Steps:
1. Before the bridge NCO sends the last Marine to cross, they must make the bridge retrievable.
2. Break down the mechanical advantage, ensuring the braking knot is set before doing so....
Procedure for Retrieving a One Rope Bridge

Steps:
1. Before the bridge NCO sends the last Marine to cross, they must make the bridge retrievable.
2. Break down the mechanical advantage, ensuring the braking knot is set before doing so. Continue breaking down the system until the bridging line is attached only to the brake knot.
3. Take the rope around to the back of the anchor and tie a slip figure 8. With the loop of the slip 8, attach it to the bridging line just in back of the braking knot with an 85.
4. Pull the running end coming out of the slip 8 until it tightens and bites on the rope. Once the rope bites, tie a thumb knot behind the slip 8 as close to the slip figure 8 as possible.
5. The bridge NCO, with the help of another Marine, will now untie the swammi wrap until all of the tension is on the bridging line.
6. Bring up the safety line and attach it to the end of the bridging line with an overhand knot.
7. The bridge NCO and the other Marine will now cross the bridge.
8. After both Marines have crossed, bring up the safety line from downstream.
9. Take off the tree wrap. Once the tree wrap is off, remove all knots and carabiners.
10. Pull the safety line to retrieve the bridge.

Note: It is possible that the bridge may lose tension after breaking it down. The packs of the last two Marines across can be sent over with other Marines prior to the slip figure being tied.
one rope bridge, retrieving bridge, mechanical advantage, braking knot, slip figure 8, thumb knot, swammi wrap, safety line, tree wrap, tactical rope techniques

Establish and Maintain Tactical Radio Nets in Northern Operations
High Priority Source: Canadian Military Basic Cold Weather Training
Procedure:

1. Prioritize command radio nets:
- Establish command radio nets first and ensure their maintenance throughout the tactical operation.

2. Set up rebroadcast or relay stations:
- When a unit moves out of ground range of...
Procedure:

1. Prioritize command radio nets:
- Establish command radio nets first and ensure their maintenance throughout the tactical operation.

2. Set up rebroadcast or relay stations:
- When a unit moves out of ground range of its base, establish rebroadcast or relay stations to maintain communication; otherwise, rely on sky wave propagation.

3. Request additional communication support when needed:
- If distances are too long for available equipment, request higher headquarters to provide communication support.

4. Include alternative means in the signal plan:
- Always include messenger services or other non-radio alternatives in case of communication failure.

5. Account for environmental effects on radio nets:
- Environmental conditions (e.g., atmospheric changes) can affect all levels of radio communications.
- Initiate and follow loss-of-contact drills to ensure preparedness.

6. Establish air-ground nets:
- Air-ground communication is critical in northern operations due to reliance on aircraft for airmobile operations, logistical support, observation, and messenger missions.
radio nets,tactical operations,northern conditions,air-ground communication,loss-of-contact drills
Select and Use a Means of Communication for Transmitting Information
High Priority Source: STP 21 1 Warrior Skills Level 1
Procedure:

1. Select a means of communication based on the situation:
- Radio: Fast and mobile but less secure.
- Wire: More secure than radio, but requires more time, personnel, and equipment to install and is subject to...
Procedure:

1. Select a means of communication based on the situation:
- Radio: Fast and mobile but less secure.
- Wire: More secure than radio, but requires more time, personnel, and equipment to install and is subject to wiretapping.
- Cable: Secure but limited by terrain and enemy action.
- Messenger: Very secure but slower and limited by weather, terrain, and enemy action.

2. Consider the communications means available to you and the information's potential significance to your mission.

3. Transmit the message to the receiving authority:
- If using a messenger, provide explicit reporting instructions and a clear, complete, and concise written message.

- If you encounter jamming or interference on your radio net, within 10 minutes of the incident, transmit a meaconing, intrusion, jamming, and interference (MIJI) report, preferably via messenger, wire, or cable to your net control station. Your signal operating instructions (SOI) contain the MIJI format.

Cross Barbed Wire Obstacles Safely
High Priority Source: STP 21 1 Army Warrior Skills Level 1 Soldiers Manual of Common Tasks
Procedure for Crossing Barbed Wire Obstacles Safely

### Steps:

1. Check for booby traps or early warning devices:
- Look carefully for any signs of booby traps or early warning devices attached to the barbed wire.

2. **Use a grappling...
Procedure for Crossing Barbed Wire Obstacles Safely

### Steps:

1. Check for booby traps or early warning devices:
- Look carefully for any signs of booby traps or early warning devices attached to the barbed wire.

2. Use a grappling hook with rope to set off potential booby traps:
- Throw a grappling hook with a length of rope over the barbed wire.
- Pull the rope to trigger any booby traps or early warning devices before crossing.

3. Protect yourself while crossing using mats or chicken wire:
- Throw wood, grass mats, or chicken wire over the barbed wire to protect your body from the barbs.
- Cross carefully because such a mat or net forms an unstable path.

4. Cross under barbed wire:
- Slide head first on your back under the bottom strands of the barbed wire.
- Push yourself forward with your shoulders and heels, carrying your weapon lengthwise on your body.
- Hold the barbed wire with one hand while moving to prevent it from catching on your clothing or equipment.
- Let the barbed wire slide along the weapon to avoid entanglement.

5. Cut through barbed wire if necessary:
- Leave the top wire in place to reduce the chance of detection by the enemy.
- Wrap cloth around the barbed wire between your hands for protection.
- Cut partly through the barbed wire, then bend it back and forth quietly until it separates.
- Cut only the lower strands to avoid alerting the enemy.
barbed wire, obstacle crossing, booby traps, early warning devices, tactical movement

Procedure for Crossing Exposed Danger Areas Safely

### Steps:

1. Select a crossing point:
- Choose a point at or near a bend in the road, trail, or stream.
- If possible, select a bend that has cover and concealment on both sides to reduce exposure.

2. Approach carefully:
- Crawl up to the edge of the open area to avoid detection.

3. Observe the other side before crossing:
- Carefully observe the other side of the danger area for potential threats or obstacles.

4. Cross rapidly but quietly:
- Move quickly across the exposed area while remaining as quiet as possible to avoid drawing attention.

5. Take cover on the other side:
- Once you reach the other side, take immediate cover behind any available natural or manmade concealment.

6. Check your surroundings:
- After crossing, check the area around you for signs of enemy presence or additional threats.

Room Clearing (9) -

Clearing a Room with an Assault Team
High Priority Source: SH 21 76 Ranger Handbook
Procedure:

1. On the signal to go, or after the grenade detonates, the assault team moves through the entry point and quickly takes up positions inside the room that allow it to completely dominate the room and eliminate the threat.
2. Unless...
Procedure:

1. On the signal to go, or after the grenade detonates, the assault team moves through the entry point and quickly takes up positions inside the room that allow it to completely dominate the room and eliminate the threat.
2. Unless restricted or impeded, team members stop movement only after they have cleared the door and reached their designated point of domination.
3. All team members are responsible for identifying possible loopholes and mouseholes in the ceiling, walls, and floor.

Note: Where enemy forces may be concentrated and the presence of noncombatants is highly unlikely, the assault team can precede their entry by throwing a fragmentation or concussion grenade (structure dependent) into the room, followed by bursts of automatic small-arms fire by the # 1 man as he enters. Carefully consider the ROE and building composition before employing this method.

Additional Steps:
• The # 1 and # 2 men are initially concerned with the area directly to their front, then along the wall on either side of the door or entry point. This area is in their path of movement, and it is their primary sector of fire. Their alternate sector of fire is from the wall they are moving toward, back to the opposite far corner.
• The # 3 and # 4 men start at the center of the wall opposite their point of entry and clear to the left if moving toward the left, or to the right if moving toward the right. They stop short of their respective team member (either the # 1 man or the # 2 man).
• Team members move toward their points of domination, engaging all threat or hostile targets in sequence in their sector. Team members must exercise fire control and discriminate between hostile and noncombatant room occupants. The most practical way to do this is to identify whether or not the target has a weapon in his or her hands. Shooting is done without stopping, using reflexive shooting techniques. Because the Soldiers are moving and shooting at the same time, they must move using the careful hurry.
• The first man (rifleman) enters the room and eliminates the immediate threat. He has the option of going left or right, normally moving along the path of least resistance to one of two corners. When using a doorway as the point of entry, the team uses the path of least resistance, which they determine initially based on the way the door opens. If the door opens inward, the first man plans to move away from the hinges. If the door opens outward, he plans to move toward the hinged side. Upon entering, his direction is influenced by the size of the room, the enemy situation, and furniture or other obstacles that hinder or channel his movement.
• The direction each man moves in should not be preplanned unless the exact room layout is known. Each man should go in a direction opposite the man in front of him. Every team member must know the sectors and duties of each position.
• As the first man goes through the entry point, he can usually see into the far corner of the room. He eliminates any immediate threat and continues to move along the wall if possible and to the first corner, where he assumes a position of domination facing into the room.

Note: Team members must always stay within 1 meter of the wall. If a team member finds his progress blocked by some object that will force him more than 1 meter from the wall, he must either step over it (if able) or stop where he is and clear the rest of his sector from where he is. If this action creates dead space in the room, the team leader directs which clearing actions to take once other members of the team have reached their points of domination.

• The second man (normally the team leader), entering almost simultaneously with the first, moves in the opposite direction, following the wall. The second man must clear the entry point, clear the immediate threat area, clear his corner, and move to a dominating position on his side of the room. The second man must also immediately determine if he is entering a center door or corner door and act accordingly.
• The third man (normally the grenadier) simply goes opposite of the second man inside the room, moves at least 1 meter from the entry point, and takes a position that dominates his sector.
• The fourth man (normally the SAW gunner) moves opposite of the third man, clears the doorway by at least 1 meter, and moves to a position that dominates his sector.

Note: If the path of least resistance takes the first man to the left, then all points of domination are the mirror image of those shown in the diagrams.
• Points of domination should not be in front of doors or windows so team members are not silhouetted to the outside of the room. No movement should mask the fire of any of the other team members.
clearing, room, assault team, tactical procedures, military operations
Clearing a Room with an Assault Team Using Fragmentation or Concussion Grenades

Procedure:

1. Assess the situation: Leaders must determine if using fragmentation or concussion grenades is effective compared to the risk of harm to friendly troops, especially in structures that may be compromised by previous explosive engagements.
2. Signal to proceed: On the signal to go, or after a grenade detonates, the assault team moves through the entry point and quickly takes up positions inside the room that allow them to completely dominate it and eliminate threats.
3. Stop only at designated points: Team members stop movement only after they have cleared the door and reached their designated point of domination.
4. Identify loopholes: All team members are responsible for identifying possible loopholes and mouseholes in the ceiling, walls, and floor.
5. Grenade use (if applicable): In situations where enemy forces may be concentrated and noncombatants are unlikely, the assault team can precede entry by throwing a fragmentation or concussion grenade into the room, followed by bursts of automatic small-arms fire from the #1 man as he enters.
6. Consider ROE and building composition: Carefully consider rules of engagement (ROE) and building composition before employing this method.

- No immediate threat, speed is critical: 1 to 3 men visually search each room

4. Short room signal: If the # 1 or # 2 man discovers that the room is very small, he can yell, “ _Short room_ ” or “ _Short_ ,” which tells the # 3 or # 4 man (whoever following the # 1 or # 2 man) to stay outside the room.

Weapon Malfunction Handling in Room Clearance
High Priority Source: Ranger Handbook 2006
Procedure:

1. Immediate decision: If at any point a team member experiences a weapon malfunction in the presence of enemy combatants, he has to make an immediate decision.
2. Enemy not in immediate danger distance: If the enemy is...
Procedure:

1. Immediate decision: If at any point a team member experiences a weapon malfunction in the presence of enemy combatants, he has to make an immediate decision.
2. Enemy not in immediate danger distance: If the enemy is outside immediate danger distance from the Soldier, then the Soldier should drop to one knee, which indicates that he has experienced a weapon malfunction and prevents fratricide by ensuring that the next Soldier’s fields of fire are clear. Once on a knee, the Soldier must remain there until the team leader directs him to stand up.
3. Correcting malfunction: If the kneeling Soldier corrects his weapon malfunction, he can continue to engage targets from his kneeling position.
4. Enemy in immediate danger distance: If, however, the enemy Soldier is so close that he presents an immediate threat, and if dropping to a knee would expose the US Soldier to immediate harm, then the US Soldier must try to subdue or disable the enemy Soldier. He can strike the enemy with the muzzle of his weapon or a bayonet to the face, throat, or chest. Or, he could grapple with the enemy soldier and take him to the ground immediately to clear the other team members’ fields of fire.
5. Assistance from others: Once they have cleared their sectors and eliminated any other threats in the room, the other members of the clearing team assist.
weapon malfunction, room clearance, tactical procedure

Conduct Mountain Scouting Game
Reference Source: Boy Scout Handbook 1911
Mountain Scouting is a game played by groups in mountainous areas. The procedure involves:

1. Preparation: At daybreak, three hares are sent out to hide themselves around the mountains.
2. Search Party: After breakfast, a group of...
Mountain Scouting is a game played by groups in mountainous areas. The procedure involves:

1. Preparation: At daybreak, three hares are sent out to hide themselves around the mountains.
2. Search Party: After breakfast, a group of hounds (Scouts) sets out to find the hidden hares before a specified time, such as 4 o'clock P.M.
3. Finding Hares: If a Scout finds a hare, even with field-glasses, it counts only if they can definitively identify who was spotted.
4. Boundaries: Certain limits of ground must be established. Anyone found beyond these boundaries is disqualified from the game.
mountain scouting,game,hunt,field glasses,bounds

Knight Errantry is a Scout activity that involves helping others and reporting on good deeds. The procedure includes:

1. Scout Deployment: Scouts go out singly, in pairs, or as a patrol.
2. Urban Assistance: In towns, Scouts seek out women or children in need of help and return to report what they have done, on their honor.
3. Rural Assistance: In the countryside, Scouts visit farms or cottages and offer to perform odd jobs for nothing.
4. Race Variation: This activity can be turned into a competition called a "Good Turn" race, where Scouts compete to complete good deeds efficiently.

Unprepared Plays is a method to develop imagination and expression through spontaneous acting. The procedure involves:

1. Plot Assignment: Provide the players with a short, simple play plot.
2. Role Distribution: Assign each player their role, along with an outline of what they need to do and say.
3. Spontaneous Acting: Allow players to act out the play using their own words and imagination as they go along.
4. Simpler Exercise: Before attempting a full play, start with simpler exercises where two or three players engage in a conversation on given topics leading up to a specific point, using their creativity.

How to Play Badger-Pulling
Reference Source: Boy Scout Handbook 1911
Badger-Pulling is a contest where the two contestants, on hands and knees, face each other.

A strong belt or strap is buckled into one great loop that passes round the head of each: that is, crosses his nape. Half-way between them is a dead...
Badger-Pulling is a contest where the two contestants, on hands and knees, face each other.

A strong belt or strap is buckled into one great loop that passes round the head of each: that is, crosses his nape. Half-way between them is a dead line. The one who pulls the other over this line is winner.

The contestant can at any time end the bout by lowering his head so the strap slips off; but this counts one against him.

Game is best out of five, seven, eleven, or thirteen points.

How to Play Cock-Fighting
Reference Source: Boy Scout Handbook 1911
Cock-Fighting is a game where two stout sticks, each two feet long (broomsticks will do), are used. Pad each of these on the end with a ball of rag. These are the spurs. Make an eight-foot ring.

The two rivals are on their hunkers, each with a...
Cock-Fighting is a game where two stout sticks, each two feet long (broomsticks will do), are used. Pad each of these on the end with a ball of rag. These are the spurs. Make an eight-foot ring.

The two rivals are on their hunkers, each with a stick through behind his knees, his hands clasped in front of the knees, and the arms under the ends of the spurs.

Now they close; each aiming to upset the other, to make him lose his spurs, or to put him out of the ring, any of which ends that round and scores one for the victor. If both fall, or lose a spur, or go out together, it is a draw. Battle is for seven, eleven, or thirteen rounds.

Feather Football or Feather Blow is an in-door, wet-weather game.

The players hold a blanket on the knees or on the table. A soft feather is put in the middle. As many may play as can get near. They may be in sides, two or four or each for himself. At the signal, "Go!" each tries to blow the feather off the blanket at the enemy's side, and so count one for himself.

A game is usually best out of seven, eleven, or thirteen.

Hand-Wrestling is a jiujitsu game introduced by Dr. L. H. Gulick. The two contestants stand right toe to right toe, each right hand clasped, left feet braced, left hand free. At the word, "Go!" each tries to unbalance the other: that is, make him lift or move one of his feet. A lift or a shift ends the round.

Battles are for best out of five, seven, eleven, or thirteen rounds.

Poison is an ancient game where a circle about three feet across is drawn on the ground. The players, holding hands, make a ring around this, and try to make one of the number step into the poison circle. He can evade it by side-stepping, by jumping over, or by dragging another fellow into it.

First to make the misstep is "it" for the time or for next game.

Games are for seven, eleven, or thirteen points.

Knots Rope (8) -

Proper Knot Tying for Suture Closure
Standard Source: Medical Survival Wound Closure Manual
Procedure:

1. Understand the importance of knot security:
- Each knot placed for tissue approximation or vessel ligation must be tied with precision and hold under proper tension.
- Knots must be secure to prevent slippage, especially...
Procedure:

1. Understand the importance of knot security:
- Each knot placed for tissue approximation or vessel ligation must be tied with precision and hold under proper tension.
- Knots must be secure to prevent slippage, especially in high-stress areas.

2. Select appropriate suture material:
- Multifilament sutures are generally easier to handle and tie due to their higher coefficient of friction, which helps the knots remain as tied.
- Monofilament sutures have a lower coefficient of friction and may require specific knotting techniques to prevent loosening after tying. These materials also possess memory, meaning they tend to return to a pre-set shape unless properly handled.

3. Use the simplest knot for the material:
- The completed knot must be firm, with slipping virtually impossible.
- The simplest and most effective knot is typically preferred over more complex ones.

4. Minimize knot size and tissue reaction:
- Knots should be as small as possible to reduce foreign body or tissue reaction, especially when using absorbable sutures.
- Ends of the suture should be cut as short as possible after tying.

5. Avoid friction between strands during tying:
- Friction (or 'sawing') between strands can weaken the integrity of the suture and compromise knot security.
- Use smooth, controlled motions when tying to avoid unnecessary stress on the material.

6. Consider suture delivery systems:
- Systems like the RELAY* suture delivery system are designed to minimize package memory, ensuring that sutures lie flat and tie effectively after being delivered.
knot tying,sutures,tissue approximation,vessel ligation,knot security,monofilament,multifilament,friction,package memory

Avoid Tying a Granny Knot

The granny knot is an undesirable knot with no useful purpose. It is often mistakenly tied when someone intends to tie a square knot.

1. The granny knot is larger and less strong than the square knot.
2. It is tied by going left or right, then repeating the same direction (e.g., left over right again), or beginning with right over left and continuing in that direction for both overhand knots.
granny knot, incorrect knots, rope mistakes, farm knots
Tie a Bowline Knot
Reference Source: Tying Farm Knots
Tie a Bowline Knot

The bowline knot is the preferred knot when tying a rope around any part of an animal’s body because it won’t slip and tighten around the animal, and it is relatively easy to untie.

1. Create a loop in the rope where the...
Tie a Bowline Knot

The bowline knot is the preferred knot when tying a rope around any part of an animal’s body because it won’t slip and tighten around the animal, and it is relatively easy to untie.

1. Create a loop in the rope where the knot is to be tied. The loop should point toward the free end, with the working part behind it.
2. Insert the free end of the rope through the loop from the back.
3. Go around the working part of the rope, then back through the loop and tighten.
4. To help remember how to tie this knot: “The rabbit jumps out of the hole, runs around the front and down behind the tree and jumps back in the hole.”
5. With a little practice, it can be tied quickly.
bowline knot, animal restraint, farm knots, rope tying

Tie a Honda Knot

The honda knot is one overhand knot inserted into another. It creates a nonslip loop, similar to the bowline knot.

1. Start by tying an overhand knot in the rope.
2. Insert the free end of the rope through the loop formed by the first overhand knot.
3. Pull tight to complete the knot.
4. This knot is used to form a small loop for the end of a lariat to pass through or to tie a rope around an animal’s neck due to its nonslip property.
honda knot, nonslip loop, farm knots, rope tying

Tie a Quick Release Knot

The quick release knot is frequently used when tying a haltered animal to a post or fence. It can be released very quickly should the need arise, although it may tighten up to the point where the bow is hard to pull out.

1. Tie the knot as you would for a standard loop or hitch.
2. After tying the knot, insert the free end through the bow to prevent the animal from releasing itself.
3. This ensures that the knot remains secure even if the animal tries to move.

Tie a Ring Knot

The ring knot is used to fasten a ring to a rope or can be quickly formed and dropped over or tied to a post.

1. Make a bight in the rope, grasping the two strands with one hand.
2. Pull the bight over your hand, forming a double loop.
3. This double loop can then be dropped over a post or tied securely.

Tie a Square Knot

Tie a Square Knot

A square knot is two overhand knots tied one after the other. The sequence must be correct:

1. Right over left, then left over right as you tie the overhand knots.

Tie a Square Knot

A square knot is two overhand knots tied one after the other. The sequence must be correct:

1. Right over left, then left over right as you tie the overhand knots.
2. Alternatively, left over right, then right over left.
3. The completed knot should have a square appearance.
4. This knot is strong and small, used to tie the ends of two ropes together.
5. It is commonly used when splicing two balls of twine together in a baler.
6. Under tension, a square knot will tighten and may be difficult to untie.
square knot, tying knots, rope knots, farm knots, overhand knots

Reference Source: Tying Farm Knots
Tie a Surgeon’s Knot

The surgeon’s knot is a variation of the square knot with an advantage: the first overhand knot holds while the second is being tied.

1. Start by making the first overhand knot, but wrap the rope around 2 or 3 times...
Tie a Surgeon’s Knot

The surgeon’s knot is a variation of the square knot with an advantage: the first overhand knot holds while the second is being tied.

1. Start by making the first overhand knot, but wrap the rope around 2 or 3 times instead of once to create additional friction and hold.
2. Continue by tying the second overhand knot in the usual way (right over left, then left over right, or vice versa).
3. This knot is used when the rope is under tension as you are trying to tie it.
4. Common uses include retying a bale, tying an overstuffed package, or during suturing.

Procedure:

1. Avoid dropping the carabiner onto hard surfaces to prevent hairline fractures.
2. Keep the carabiner off the bare ground to avoid dirt and grit entering working parts.
3. If the carabiner has fallen from a significant height, it should be retired immediately.
4. After use, remove all dirt, moisture, and grime from the carabiner.
5. Lubricate the carabiner with tri-flow graphite and wipe off excess with a clean cloth.

Note: The weakest part of a carabiner is the gate. If engraving is needed, it should be applied to the gate, not the load-bearing side.

Procedure for Replacing a Canister on an M42 Protective Mask

Steps:
1. Remove the canister carrier cover by pressing in and rotating it counterclockwise.
2. Remove the canister by unscrewing it counterclockwise from the hose and removing it from the canister carrier.
3. Check connectors and mating surfaces of the new canister, the facepiece, and areas between these surfaces for dirt or debris that could allow contaminated air into the facepiece.
4. Check expiration date on the new canister to ensure it has not expired.
5. Insert the canister into the canister carrier.
6. Ensure gasket is in place on the canister connection before connecting the canister to the hose.
7. Attach the canister to the hose:
a. Position the hose on the canister.
b. Tighten the canister by screwing it clockwise into the hose while holding the hose securely.
8. Attach the canister carrier cover to the carrier:
a. Position the canister carrier cover on the canister carrier.
b. Press in on the canister carrier cover while rotating it clockwise.

1. Ensure the gate snaps shut with no friction, and there is no gap between the locking pin and locking notch.
2. Check that there is no excessive side-to-side movement of the gate.
3. Confirm that the pivot pin is tight and not loose or damaged.

Movement Techniques (8) -

Implement Movement Techniques Based on METT-TC Analysis
High Priority Source: SH 21 76 Ranger Handbook
Objective: Ensure effective and secure unit movement by selecting the appropriate technique based on METT-TC analysis.

Procedure:
1. Understand the three basic movement techniques:
- Traveling: Used when speed is not a priority,...
Objective: Ensure effective and secure unit movement by selecting the appropriate technique based on METT-TC analysis.

Procedure:
1. Understand the three basic movement techniques:
- Traveling: Used when speed is not a priority, but security and dispersion are important.
- Traveling overwatch: Combines movement with overwatch by elements to provide security during transit.
- Bounding overwatch: Alternates between bounding and overwatch positions for maximum security and control.
2. Select the appropriate technique based on METT-TC factors:
- Consider the likelihood of enemy contact, terrain, speed requirements, and overall mission objectives.
3. Maintain unit cohesion and dispersion:
- Ensure that all Soldiers can see their fire team leader at all times.
- The platoon leader must be able to see his lead squad leader.
4. Use control measures during movement:
- Implement head counts, rally points, or phase lines as needed for control and accountability.
5. Maintain 360-degree security at all times:
- During movement, maintain full 100% alertness and 360-degree security.
- During halts, maintain a minimum of 75% security.
6. Minimize enemy contact impact:
- If contact is made with the enemy, it should be made by the smallest element possible to avoid full engagement.
7. Use stealth and dispersion for avoidance:
- Use cover and concealment to avoid detection.
- Move during limited visibility (e.g., night) when possible to maximize technological advantages like night vision devices.
movement technique,METT-TC analysis,traveling overwatch,bounding overwatch,tactical security,dispersion
Apply Movement Techniques Based on Enemy Contact Likelihood and Speed Requirements
High Priority Source: Ranger Handbook 2006
Objective: Traverse terrain effectively using the appropriate movement technique based on enemy contact likelihood and speed requirements.

Procedure:
1. Select one of the following movement techniques based on METT-TC analysis:
-...
Objective: Traverse terrain effectively using the appropriate movement technique based on enemy contact likelihood and speed requirements.

Procedure:
1. Select one of the following movement techniques based on METT-TC analysis:
- Traveling: Used when speed is not a priority, and stealth or dispersion are required for security.
- Traveling Overwatch: Combines movement with overwatch by designated elements to provide security while moving.
- Bounding Overwatch: Alternates between bounding (moving forward) and overwatch (providing cover fire) to maintain security and speed.
2. Consider the following factors when selecting a technique:
- Control: Ensure leaders can effectively manage the unit.
- Dispersion: Maintain appropriate spacing for security and observation of flanks.
- Speed: Adjust movement pace based on mission requirements.
- Security: Prioritize techniques that minimize exposure to enemy contact.
3. Leaders must remain within 200 meters of their assigned route unless METT-TC dictates otherwise.
4. Maintain 360-degree security at all times during movement and a minimum of 75% security during halts.
5. If enemy contact occurs, ensure it is made with the smallest element possible to minimize casualties and maintain unit cohesion.

Notes:
• Movement techniques are not fixed formations but refer to spacing between units based on METT-TC.
• Leaders use hand-and-arm signals for control; radios should be used only when necessary.
movement technique, traveling, overwatch, security, METT-TC, leadership
Bounding Overwatch Technique
High Priority Source: SH 21 76 Ranger Handbook
Purpose: Used when enemy contact is likely or when crossing a danger area.

Procedure:
1. Maintain a distance of about 20 meters between individuals.
2. The squad or platoon has two elements:
- Bounding element: Moves forward...
Purpose: Used when enemy contact is likely or when crossing a danger area.

Procedure:
1. Maintain a distance of about 20 meters between individuals.
2. The squad or platoon has two elements:
- Bounding element: Moves forward along the route.
- Overwatch element: Occupies an overwatch position that can cover the route of the bounding element by fire.
3. Each bound must be within supporting range of the overwatch element.
4. Types of bounding:
- Successive bounding: One squad moves to a position, then the overwatching squad moves to a position generally in line with the first squad.
- Alternating bounding: One squad moves into position, then the overwatching squad moves to a position in front of the first squad.
5. The length of a bound depends on:
- Terrain
- Visibility
- Control
6. Before a bound, the leader must give instructions to subordinates including:
- Direction of the enemy (if known)
- Position of overwatch elements
- Next overwatch position
- Route of the bounding element
- What to do after the bounding element reaches the next position
- How the elements receive follow-on orders

Characteristics:
• Maximum control.
• Maximum dispersion.
• Minimum speed.
• Maximum security.
bounding overwatch technique, enemy contact likely, danger area, squad movement

Crawling on the Stomach Technique
Standard Source: Canadian Military Fieldcraft
Procedure for Crawling on the Stomach:

Procedure for Crawling on the Stomach:

1. Positioning: Lie down on your stomach.
2. Check the Ground: Use your right hand to ensure the ground in front of you is free from branches, dry leaves, and tripwires.
3. Support Yourself: Lift yourself up on your forearms and the balls of your feet.
4. Move Forward: Push yourself forward slowly and carefully.
5. Return to Position: Lower yourself back down to the ground.
6. Weapon Handling: Keep your weapon in your left hand while crawling.

Notes:

Kitten Crawl: A low-profile crawling technique for moving behind cover:

1. Assume a position on hands and knees, keeping your body as close to the ground as possible.
2. If silence is required, choose a safe place without twigs or debris where you can place your hands.
3. Alternatively, let one leg trail behind while using only one knee for support.
4. Keep your heels, head, and elbows down at all times.
5. Maintain observation of the surroundings during movement.
6. Hold your weapon with either hand on the pistol grip or small of the butt, and the other hand at the forestock.
7. Alternatively, grasp the weapon by the front of the sling with one hand, with the rifle resting on the other arm, muzzle forward.

Traveling Overwatch Technique
Standard Source: SH 21 76 Ranger Handbook

Purpose: The basic movement technique used when enemy contact is possible.

Procedure:
1. Maintain a distance of about 20 meters between individuals and 50 meters between teams.
2. In platoon traveling overwatch:
- The lead squad must be far enough ahead to detect or engage any enemy before the enemy observes or fires on the main body (normally 50 to 100 meters, depending on terrain, vegetation, and light/weather conditions).
- It must remain close enough to be supported by the platoon’s small arms fire.
3. In a column formation:
- Only the lead squad should use traveling overwatch unless greater dispersion is desired (in which case all squads may use it).
4. In other formations:
- All squads use traveling overwatch unless the platoon leader specifies otherwise.

Characteristics:
• Good control.
• Good dispersion.
• Good speed.
• Good security forward.
traveling overwatch technique, enemy contact possible, platoon movement, squad distance

Objective: Minimize detection during short stops by using concealment techniques.

Procedure:
1. Quickly disperse vehicles under tree crowns or other natural cover along the sides of the road during brief stops.
2. Enforce strict CCD (Camouflage, Concealment, and Deception) discipline to avoid exposure.
3. Monitor for glare from vehicle windshields, headlights, or reflectors and correct it immediately if detected.
4. Control troop movement on roads or open areas to reduce visibility.
5. Conduct recon to identify suitable areas for long halts that allow sufficient CCD and dispersion.
6. Predetermine vehicle placement and develop a circulation plan for the quartering party to guide vehicles into concealed locations.
7. Prioritize moving vehicles off the road as quickly as possible, even if initial dispersion is not optimal.
8. Use camouflage nets and natural vegetation to enhance concealment of vehicles and dug-in positions.

Notes:
• Brief stops should be executed with minimal exposure to enemy observation.
• Vehicle placement during long halts must ensure adequate concealment.

Operations Order (OPORD) Format and Issuance
High Priority Source: SH 21 76 Ranger Handbook
### Operations Order (OPORD) Format and Issuance

An operations order (OPORD) is a directive issued by a leader to his subordinates in order to effect the coordinated execution of a specific operation. A five-paragraph format is used to organize the...
### Operations Order (OPORD) Format and Issuance

An operations order (OPORD) is a directive issued by a leader to his subordinates in order to effect the coordinated execution of a specific operation. A five-paragraph format is used to organize the briefing, to ensure completeness, and to help subordinate leaders understand and follow the order. Use a terrain model or sketch along with a map to explain the order. When possible, such as in the defense, give the order while observing the objective.

The platoon/squad leader briefs his OPORD orally off notes that follow the five-paragraph format. Before the issuance of the OPORD, the leader ensures that the following resources are in place: pencil, pen, paper; RHB; map; protractor; leader’s monitor. Then he calls roll and says "_Please hold all questions till the end._" Figure 2-4 shows an example OPORD format. Figure 2-5 shows an OPORD shell.

Combat Procedures (8) -

Break Contact Procedure for Squad/Platoon Under Enemy Fire
Critical Source: SH 21 76 Ranger Handbook
Procedure:

1. The platoon/squad leader directs fire support for the disengagement by:
- Directing one squad/fire team in contact to support the disengagement of the remainder of the unit.
- Considering the use of indirect fires for...
Procedure:

1. The platoon/squad leader directs fire support for the disengagement by:
- Directing one squad/fire team in contact to support the disengagement of the remainder of the unit.
- Considering the use of indirect fires for breaking contact.
- Clearing the location, task, purpose, and method of conducting the fire mission with the platoon FO.

2. The platoon/squad leader orders a distance and direction, a terrain feature, or last ORP (Orienting Reference Point) for the movement of the first squad/fire team. In conjunction with the platoon FO, the leader maintains accurate battle tracking of all friendly elements to facilitate quick clearance of fires.

3. The base of fire squad/team continues to suppress the enemy. The platoon/squad leader directs the platoon FO to execute the fire mission, if needed.

4. The moving squad/team assumes the overwatch position. The squad/team should use M203 grenade launchers, throw fragmentation and concussion grenades, and use smoke grenades to mask movement. The platoon/squad leader directs the platoon FO to execute a smoke mission to screen friendly elements' movement, if needed.

5. The moving squad/team takes up the designated position and engages the enemy position.

6. The platoon leader directs the base-of-fire element to move to its next location. Based on the terrain and the volume and accuracy of the enemy’s fire, the moving fire team or squad may need to use fire and movement techniques.

7. The platoon/squad continues to bound away from the enemy until:
- It breaks contact. It must continue to suppress the enemy as it does this.
- It passes through a higher-level SBF (Squad Base Fire) position.
- Its squad/fire teams are in the assigned position to conduct the next mission.

8. The leader should consider changing his unit's direction of movement once contact is broken. This will reduce the ability of the enemy to place effective indirect fires on the unit.

9. If the platoon/squad becomes disrupted, Soldiers stay together and move to the last designated rally point.

10. The platoon/squad leaders account for Soldiers, report, reorganize as necessary, and continue the mission. With the platoon FO, the platoon/squad develops a quick fire plan to support the hasty defense or new route of march.
break contact, enemy fire, tactical movement, suppression, smoke mission, overwatch position, disengagement, SBF position, rally point

Critical Source: SH 21 76 Ranger Handbook

When encountering an ambush within hand-grenade range:

1. Immediate Fire Return: Soldiers in the kill zone return fire immediately, depending on terrain conditions.

Procedure:

When encountering an ambush within hand-grenade range:

1. Immediate Fire Return: Soldiers in the kill zone return fire immediately, depending on terrain conditions.

- If cover is not available:
- Assume a prone position without order or signal.
- Throw concussion or fragmentation and smoke grenades.

- If cover is available:
- Seek the nearest covered position.
- Assume a prone position.
- Throw fragmentation or concussion and smoke grenades.

2. Post-Grenade Actions:
- After the explosion of concussion or fragmentation grenades, soldiers in the kill zone return fire and assault through the ambush position using fire and movement techniques.

3. Supporting Soldiers' Actions:
- Soldiers not in the kill zone identify enemy positions and shift fire as personnel in the kill zone begin to assault.

4. Continuation of Assault:
- Soldiers in the kill zone continue the assault to eliminate the ambush or until contact is broken.

5. Consolidation and Reorganization:
- The platoon/squad conducts consolidation and reorganization after the assault.
ambush, near ambush, grenade, fire return, tactical response, combat drill
React to Indirect Fire (Battle Drill 8)
Critical Source: SH 21 76 Ranger Handbook
Procedure:

1. Any Soldier announces, _Incoming_.
2. If the platoon/squad is moving:
a. The platoon/squad leader gives direction and distance for the platoon/squad to move to a rally point by ordering direction and distance, for example,...
Procedure:

1. Any Soldier announces, _Incoming_.
2. If the platoon/squad is moving:
a. The platoon/squad leader gives direction and distance for the platoon/squad to move to a rally point by ordering direction and distance, for example, _Four o’clock, three hundred meters_.
b. Platoon/squad members move rapidly along the direction and distance to the rally point.
c. At the rally point, the leader immediately accounts for personnel and equipment, and forms the platoon/squad for a move to an alternate position.
d. The senior leader submits a SITREP (Situation Report) to higher headquarters.
3. If the platoon/squad is halted (not dug in) or is preparing to move because they hear incoming artillery:
a. The platoon/squad leader gives direction and distance for the platoon/squad to move to a rally point by ordering direction and distance, for example, _Four o’clock, three hundred meters_.
b. Platoon/squad members secure all mission-essential equipment and ammunition and move rapidly along the direction and distance to the rally point.
c. At the rally point, the leader immediately accounts for personnel and equipment, and forms the platoon/squad for a move to an alternate position.
d. The senior leader submits a SITREP (Situation Report) to higher headquarters.

Note: If platoon/squad members are in defensive (dug in) positions, then members will remain in those positions if appropriate. Senior leader submits SITREP.

Handling Weapon Malfunctions in Combat Situations
Critical Source: SH 21 76 Ranger Handbook
Procedure:

1. If a team member experiences a weapon malfunction in the presence of enemy combatants, he has to make an immediate decision.
2. If the enemy is outside immediate danger distance from the Soldier, then the Soldier should drop to...
Procedure:

1. If a team member experiences a weapon malfunction in the presence of enemy combatants, he has to make an immediate decision.
2. If the enemy is outside immediate danger distance from the Soldier, then the Soldier should drop to one knee, which indicates that he has experienced a weapon malfunction and prevents fratricide by ensuring that the next Soldier’s fields of fire are clear. Once on a knee, the Soldier must remain there until the team leader directs him to stand up.
3. If the kneeling Soldier corrects his weapon malfunction, he can continue to engage targets from his kneeling position.
4. If, however, the enemy Soldier is so close that he presents an immediate threat, and if dropping to a knee would expose the US Soldier to immediate harm, then the US Soldier must try to subdue or disable the enemy Soldier.
5. The US Soldier can strike the enemy with the muzzle of his weapon or a bayonet to the face, throat, or chest. Or, he could grapple with the enemy soldier and take him to the ground immediately to clear the other team members’ fields of fire.
6. Once they have cleared their sectors and eliminated any other threats in the room, the other members of the clearing team assist.

Immediate Action for Weapon Malfunction in Close-Quarters Combat
High Priority Source: STP 21 1 Warrior Skills Level 1
When your weapon malfunctions during close-quarters combat, follow these steps:

1. Take a knee to perform immediate action, unless you are in a doorway or staircase.
2. If possible, seek cover in such situations.
3. If needed, **stand up to...
When your weapon malfunctions during close-quarters combat, follow these steps:

1. Take a knee to perform immediate action, unless you are in a doorway or staircase.
2. If possible, seek cover in such situations.
3. If needed, stand up to engage targets, but do so carefully.
4. Avoid impeding the movement of other team members.
5. Continue to engage from one knee to save precious seconds.
6. When other team members see a Soldier take a knee stance, they must automatically clear his/her sector of fire.
7. Before rising, warn the clearing team members that you are about to move, and only rise after they acknowledge this warning.
8. This reduces the chance of fratricide among team members.
9. Another technique is to remain in place until after the engagement, when another team member comes and signals you to arise.
weapon malfunction, close-quarters combat, immediate action, tactical procedures, fratricide prevention

Procedure for Performing Individual Movement

1. Assess the terrain and environment to determine the most efficient movement technique.
2. Use a low profile stance when moving through open areas or under enemy observation.
3. Move in a staggered formation with team members to avoid detection and maintain cover.
4. Utilize natural cover and concealment to reduce visibility during movement.
5. Maintain silence and control of body movements, especially during stealth operations.
6. Adjust movement speed based on the tactical situation, slowing down when necessary for observation or avoiding threats.
individual movement, tactical movement, stealth techniques

Objective: Choose the appropriate movement technique based on terrain and situation.

Steps:
1. Select the high crawl when:
- The route provides cover and concealment.
- Poor visibility reduces enemy observation.
- Speed is required, but the terrain and vegetation are suitable only for the low crawl.
2. Select the low crawl when:
- The route provides cover or concealment less than 1 foot high.
- Visibility provides the enemy with good observation.
- Speed is not required.
3. Select the rush when:
- You must cross open areas.
- Time is critical.
high crawl, low crawl, rush movement, tactical technique selection
Low Crawl Technique
Standard Source: STP 21 1 Warrior Skills Level 1
Procedure for Low Crawl:

1. Positioning the Body:

2. Weapon Handling:
- Hold your weapon by...
Procedure for Low Crawl:

1. Positioning the Body:
- Keep your body as flat as possible to the ground.
- Ensure your knees are well behind your buttocks, keeping your buttocks low.

2. Weapon Handling:
- Hold your weapon by grasping the sling at the upper sling swivel.
- Let the handguard rest on your forearm and allow the butt of the weapon to drag on the ground. This helps keep the muzzle off the ground.

3. Movement Technique:
- Move forward by alternately advancing your right elbow and left knee, then your left elbow and right knee.
- Use a push-pull movement:
- Push both arms forward while pulling your right leg forward.
- Pull with both arms while pushing with your right leg.
- Continue this push-pull movement until you reach your next position.
- Change your pushing leg frequently to avoid fatigue.
low crawl, movement technique, tactical positioning, weapon handling
Rush Movement Technique

1. Starting Position:
- Move from your firing position by rolling or crawling.
- Start from the prone position.

2. Head and Body Positioning:

Procedure for Rush Movement:

1. Starting Position:
- Move from your firing position by rolling or crawling.
- Start from the prone position.

2. Head and Body Positioning:
- Slowly raise your head and select your next position.
- Lower your head while drawing your arms into your body, with elbows down, and pulling your right leg forward.

3. Rising to Feet:
- Raise your body in one movement by straightening your arms.
- Spring to your feet, stepping off with either foot.

4. Running to Next Position:
- Run to the next position, keeping the distance short to avoid accurate enemy fire.
- Stay up for no longer than 3 to 5 seconds to prevent being tracked by automatic fire.

5. Landing Technique:
- Plant both feet just before hitting the ground.
- Fall forward by sliding your right hand down to the heel of the butt of your weapon.
rush movement, tactical positioning, enemy fire avoidance, landing technique

Objective: Identify terrain features that provide cover, concealment, or temporary positions for movement.

Steps:
1. Search the terrain to your front for the following features:
- A gully, ravine, ditch, or wall at a slight angle to your direction of movement.
Note: These features provide cover and concealment when using the low or high crawl.
- Hedgerows or a line of thick vegetation.
Note: These features provide concealment only during the low or high crawl.
- Large trees, rocks, stumps, fallen timber, rubble, vehicle hulks, folds, or creases in the ground.
Note: These features provide cover and concealment for use as temporary positions. Use the rush if the area between them has no concealment.
- High grass or weeds.
Note: These features provide only partial concealment. You can use the rush because using the high or low crawl could move vegetation and reveal your location.
terrain search, cover concealment, movement features, tactical positioning

### Adjusting Formation Intervals

The distances between Soldiers in the formation should be adjusted based on terrain, visibility, and control factors. The following guidelines apply:

• Normal interval: About 10 meters during daylight.
• Increase interval when operating in open terrain to allow for better visibility and maneuverability.
• Decrease interval when underbrush, darkness, smoke, or dense fog limits visibility.
• Resume normal interval as soon as conditions improve.

### Implementation Steps
1. Assess the current environment (terrain, weather, visibility).
2. Adjust intervals accordingly: increase in open terrain, decrease in low-visibility conditions.
3. Maintain visual contact with the team leader and follow their instructions or signals.
4. Ensure that all members of the formation are aware of changes in spacing and adjust their movement accordingly.

### Notes
• Formation flexibility is key to adapting to changing battlefield conditions.
• Always prioritize safety and communication within the team.
adjust formation intervals, visibility conditions, open terrain, low visibility, military spacing
Command Echelon Left Formation with Support Squad in Lateral Support (Skill Level 4)

Procedure:

1. Ensure that the 1st squad leader commands, "Follow me," and the squad executes an echelon left (or right).
2. Ensure that the 2d and 3d squad leaders command, "Stand fast."
3. Ensure that as the 1st squad clears the column, the 3d squad moves to extend the echelon formed by the 1st squad.
4. After the echelon has formed, the squad leader for the 2d squad commands, "Odd-numbered Soldiers, follow me," and the assistant squad leader commands, "Even-numbered Soldiers, follow me."
5. The odd-numbered Soldiers move out to the left (or right) and form a column behind the last Soldier in the 3d squad.
6. The even-numbered Soldiers move out to the left (or right) and form a column behind the first Soldier in the 1st squad.
echelon formation,lateral support,military command,skill level 4

### Fire Team File Formation

### Fire Team File Formation

This formation is used when the fire team is not using a wedge or diamond formation. It has the following characteristics:

• Provides maximum control over the team.
• Provides minimum frontage, making it suitable for close terrain or vegetation.
• Facilitates speed of movement.
• Is less flexible than the wedge or diamond.
• Provides immediate fires to flanks, but masks most Soldiers' fires to the front and rear.

### Implementation Steps
1. Arrange the fire team in a single file, with each Soldier following directly behind the one ahead.
2. Ensure that all members maintain visual contact with the team leader.
3. Adjust spacing based on terrain, visibility, and control factors (e.g., increase interval in open terrain or decrease when visibility is limited).
4. Maintain communication with the team leader for coordination during movement or engagement.

### Notes
• This formation is ideal for moving through tight spaces or dense vegetation.
• It allows for quick changes in direction but reduces flexibility compared to other formations.
fire team file, military formation, tight terrain movement, maximum control, minimum frontage

### Procedure: Move as a Member of a Fire Team

Conditions: In a designated position (other than team leader) in a moving fire team.
Standards: React immediately to the fire team leader's example and perform the same actions as the fire team leader does in the designated position within the formation.

Performance Steps:
1. Understand fire team formations, which include:
- Wedge (figure 071-326-0501-1): The basic fire team formation that is easy to control, flexible, allows immediate fires in all directions, and offers all-round local security.
- Modified Wedge (figure 071-326-0501-2): Used when rough terrain, poor visibility, or other factors reduce control of the wedge formation. The sides are closed up to almost a single file for better control in reduced visibility or rough terrain. It offers less flank security than a wedge but more than a file and masks fires initially to the front and rear for the majority of the team.
- Diamond (figure 071-326-0501-3): Not described in detail here, but used as an alternative formation depending on mission requirements.
- File (figure 071-326-0501-4): A linear formation that provides minimal flank security and is typically used for movement over long distances or through narrow passages.

Form Platoon Wedge with Support Squad in Lateral Support
Standard Source: STP 21 24 Warrior Leader Skills Level 2 3 4
Procedure:

1. Give the command, "Platoon wedge, 2d squad in lateral support, move." The 1st and 3d squads execute the wedge, while the 2d squad stands fast.

2. Ensure that after the wedge has been formed, the squad leader for the 2d squad...
Procedure:

1. Give the command, "Platoon wedge, 2d squad in lateral support, move." The 1st and 3d squads execute the wedge, while the 2d squad stands fast.

2. Ensure that after the wedge has been formed, the squad leader for the 2d squad commands, "Odd-numbered Soldiers, follow me," and the assistant squad leader commands, "Even-numbered Soldiers, follow me."

3. The odd-numbered Soldiers move out to the left and form a column behind the last Soldier in the 3d squad.

4. The even-numbered Soldiers move out to the right and form a column behind the last Soldier in the 1st squad.

5. Give the command, "2d squad, lateral support, move," to move the 2d squad from general support to lateral support.

6. Give the command, "2d squad, extend the wedge, move," to have the 2d squad join the wedge from either general support or lateral support.

7. The 2d squad leader and assistant squad leader command, "Follow me," and move out to the left and right, respectively, to extend the wedge on the 1st and 3d squads.
platoon wedge, lateral support, military formation, squad movement

Procedure:

1. Assemble the company into an echelon right (or left) formation, but in a mass formation, which is a more compact and concentrated arrangement.
2. Position one platoon in lateral support, placed to the side of the main echelon for immediate tactical support.
3. Place one platoon in general support, positioned further back or on the flanks to provide broader, more strategic support as needed.

Note: This formation is used offensively to turn crowds in either open or built-up areas and to move crowds away from buildings, fences, or walls.

Procedure for Adjusting Fire:

2. Steps:
- If the initial burst misses the target, rapidly select a new aiming point the same distance from the center of impact of the initial burst, but in the opposite direction.

1. Definition: This technique combines traversing and searching fire to distribute fire in both width and depth by successive changes in direction and elevation.

- For minor changes in direction: Shift the shoulders to the right or left and choose successive aiming points throughout the width of the target area.
- For major changes in direction: Move the elbows and align the body to remain directly behind the gun.

### Procedure: Fire Around a Building or Wall Using the Right-Handed Firing Technique

Objective: To fire around the right corner of a building or wall while minimizing exposure to return fire.

Steps:
1. Position yourself behind cover, ensuring that you are concealed from enemy view.
2. Use the right-handed firing technique, which allows for better concealment when firing around the right corner of a structure (see figure 071-326-0557-2).
3. Ensure your body is positioned so that only the rifle's barrel and sights are visible from the enemy’s perspective.
4. Fire accurately while maintaining a low profile to avoid exposure.

Notes:
• This technique is especially useful in urban combat scenarios where cover is limited.
• Always seek covered firing positions to reduce your risk of being hit by return fire.
firing position, right-handed technique, building corner, concealment, urban combat

Steps:

2. Use terrain features or structures such as walls to provide additional concealment.
3. Fire around the wall, not over it (see figure 071-326-0557-3).
4. Ensure your body is positioned so that only the rifle's barrel and sights are visible from the enemy’s perspective.
5. Fire accurately while maintaining a low profile to avoid exposure.

Notes:
• Firing around a wall provides better concealment than firing over it.
• Always seek covered firing positions to reduce your risk of being hit by return fire.

### Procedure: Use the Prone Firing Technique When Possible

Objective: To fire from a prone position to minimize exposure and improve accuracy.

Steps:
1. Find a flat, stable surface on which you can lie prone (face down) without risk of injury.
2. Position your body so that it is fully covered by terrain features or debris for concealment.
3. Place your rifle in the firing position with both hands gripping the weapon securely.
4. Ensure that only the rifle’s barrel and sights are visible from the enemy’s perspective.
5. Fire accurately while maintaining a low profile to avoid exposure.

Notes:
• The prone position is ideal for long-range fire and provides maximum concealment.
• Always ensure your firing position is stable before taking a shot.

a. Tripod Firing:
• Use prone, sitting, or kneeling positions depending on the...
Step 1: Assume a suitable firing position based on the situation, ensuring it allows you to observe and engage targets while minimizing exposure to enemy fire.

a. Tripod Firing:
• Use prone, sitting, or kneeling positions depending on the situation.
• Standing may be used if firing from a prepared position.

b. Bipod Firing:
• The best positions are the prone-supported position and bipod-supported fighting position.
• Assume these positions when possible for effective fire delivery.

1. Shoulder Firing Position:
• Use this during movement or in the final stages of an assault if no other position is available.

2. Underarm Firing Position:
• Use this when closing with the enemy, requiring a heavy volume of fire and rapid movement.

3. Hip Firing Position:
• Use this when a heavy volume of fire is required but rapid movement is not necessary.

Lashing a Toboggan Load for Transport

1. Use two men, if possible, one on each side.
2. Starting from the back end or where the handle hinges on the toboggan, load it as follows:
- On Bottom of Toboggan:
- 2 billy cans
- 1 lamp lying flat and crosswise
- 1 can of gas (upright)
- 3 stoves (upright), 2 M1950, 1 C1B1
- 1 pressure cooker
- Board for stove stand: 2' by 1' by 1/4"
- 2 axes arctic (normally on top in forest country)
- 2 snow kits (normally on top in tundra)
- Spare Parts Box
- 2 flashlights (may be carried by personnel)
- Spare batteries for flashlights
- Flare projector 10 gauge (may be carried)
- Flare for projector: 5 red, 5 green (may be carried)
- Mantles
- Generators (lamps, C1B1, M1950)
- Wrench: 8" adjustable
- Pliers: slip joint
- Screwdriver: 8" flat tip
- First aid kit
- Protractor (may be carried)
- Pace counter reciprocating hand held (may be carried)
- Compass (may be carried)
- Pump leathers (M1950 and C1B1)
- Spare burner cap for the lamp
- Spare filler plugs (C1B1 & lamp)
- 1 pr snowshoe bindings
- 5 candles
3. Tuck in the nylon cover, making sure it covers all the load.
4. Lash the load in crisscross fashion, passing each end of the cord from side to side.
5. When each side is finished, pass two ends around the rear hook and tie them tightly with a slip knot.
6. If there is enough cord left over, pass the ends back to the front hook and tie again.

Towing a Toboggan by Vehicle Using the Whippletree Method

1. Place 2, 3, or 4 toboggans abreast, with the handle folded and tied down.
2. Across the hinge portion of the handles, lash a log, using two lashings per handle, one on each edge.
3. Lash the toboggan handles together or, if the toboggans are equipped with hooks, fasten them.
4. Lash each end of a tow rope to a whippletree near the ends of the log.
5. Tie an overhand thumb knot in the centre of the tow rope and place the small loop thus formed in the towing hitch of the vehicle.

Transportation Planning for Collective-Protection Systems
Standard Source: FM 3 4 NBC Protection
Transportation Planning for Collective-Protection Systems

1. Determine whether to transport collective-protection systems (e.g., M51 or SCPE) based on the tactical situation and threat assessment.
- If there is no indication of chemical...
Transportation Planning for Collective-Protection Systems

1. Determine whether to transport collective-protection systems (e.g., M51 or SCPE) based on the tactical situation and threat assessment.
- If there is no indication of chemical agent use, or if the tactical situation is unsuitable for collective protection, the maneuver commander may decide not to transport these assets into battle.
- If the threat actively employs chemical agents or the tactical situation supports collective protection, the commander may choose to accept the transportation burden for the advantage of a readily available shelter system.
2. When deciding against transporting shelter assets in maneuver units based on IPB (Intelligence Preparation of the Battlefield), retain these assets in the unit trains area ready for use.
- This allows a quick response to changes in the tactical situation.

- One man secures the cords of his harness to the front tow ring by means of a bowline.
- The other man attaches the two ends of his towing cords to the two rings on the first man's web waist-band. The cords should be adjusted to allow for a straight pull.

Care and Maintenance of a Toboggan
Standard Source: Canadian Military Basic Cold Weather Training

Before a move, the toboggan must be carefully checked. The points to note are the same as for the one-man toboggan. Also check to see that:

1. Tow rings are intact.
2. **The handle-bar is free to move and...
Care and Maintenance of a Toboggan

Before a move, the toboggan must be carefully checked. The points to note are the same as for the one-man toboggan. Also check to see that:

1. Tow rings are intact.
2. The handle-bar is free to move and undamaged.
3. Hauling a toboggan can be tiring work unless you are fit. Men detailed to pull toboggans should be changed as often as circumstances permit.
4. In deep snow, it is less tiring if the haulers follow a packed trail.
5. Ensure that the web band of the towing harness is fitted to their waist, riding at hip bone level. If it slips too far down, it will be very tiring on their legs.
6. The brass hooks on the cargo pack become very brittle in very cold weather and will snap easily if pried or forced. Once they have been adjusted, they should be treated with care when the toboggan is unloaded.
7. Emergency replacements can be made from nails or wire (see Figure 2-9A).

Hauling a Two-Man Toboggan

• The two-man toboggan can be hauled by:
- Two men in single file, approximately seven to eight feet apart (preferable in deep snow and wooded area), or
- Two men abreast, preferable in open areas.

• A third man normally operates at the rear of the toboggan, using the handle-bar. This man assists by:
1. Keeping a cheek on the load and lashing.
2. Preventing the toboggan from overtaking the haulers on a down grade.
3. Pushing in hard going.
4. Preventing the toboggan from tipping when traversing a steep slope.
5. Controlling the toboggan on rough snow or ice.

Objective: Assume a stable kneeling firing position with proper cover and support.

Steps:
1. Use available cover for support, such as a low wall, rocks, or a vehicle that you can fire over.
2. Place your firing knee on the ground. Put your left knee down to fire left-handed, or your right knee down to fire right-handed.
3. Bend your other knee and place the foot on your nonfiring side flat on the ground, pointing toward the target. Extend your arms over available cover and use it for support.
4. Lock the wrist and elbow of your firing arm.
5. Wrap your nonfiring hand around your firing fist or wrist to support your firing arm.

Notes:
• This position could silhouette you, making you a better target.
• When possible, fire around the sides of walls, rocks, or vehicles instead of over them.

Objective: Assume a stable standing-with-support firing position using available cover for support.

Steps:
1. Use available cover for support, such as standing behind a tree or wall.
2. Stand behind a barricade with your firing side in line with the edge of the barricade.
3. Place the palm of your nonfiring hand at eye level on the edge of the barricade, and extend your thumb past the edge.
4. Lock the elbow of your firing arm and rest your forearm on the extended thumb of your nonfiring hand.
5. Move the foot on your nonfiring side forward until your toe touches the bottom of the barricade.

Notes:
• This position provides stability and concealment when using available cover.
• Ensure that your firing arm is properly supported for accuracy.

Combat Training (7) -

Advanced Hand-to-Hand Combat Techniques
High Priority Source: FM 3 25 150 Combatives
Objective: To teach advanced hand-to-hand combat techniques for soldiers.

Procedure:
1. Close-Quarters Combat: Practice close-quarters combat techniques such as grappling, joint locks, and strikes using the hands, elbows, knees, and...
Objective: To teach advanced hand-to-hand combat techniques for soldiers.

Procedure:
1. Close-Quarters Combat: Practice close-quarters combat techniques such as grappling, joint locks, and strikes using the hands, elbows, knees, and feet.
2. Defensive Techniques: Learn to defend against grabs, holds, and strikes by using body positioning, counterstrikes, and disengagement tactics.
3. Offensive Techniques: Develop offensive moves including punches, kicks, elbow strikes, and knee strikes aimed at vulnerable areas such as the eyes, throat, and groin.
4. Escape from Holds: Practice techniques to escape from various holds and submissions by using leverage, body movement, and counterattacks.
5. Use of Environment: Learn how to use the environment to your advantage, such as using objects for striking or creating barriers for defense.
6. Drills and Repetition: Regularly practice these advanced techniques through drills to build muscle memory and reflexes.

Warnings/Contraindications: Always use proper safety precautions when practicing hand-to-hand combat. Ensure that no one is within striking distance during training exercises.
hand-to-hand combat, close-quarters combat, defensive techniques, offensive techniques, escape from holds, use of environment
Basic Rifle-Bayonet Fighting Techniques
High Priority Source: FM 3 25 150 Combatives
Objective: To teach the fundamentals of rifle-bayonet fighting.

Procedure:
1. Stance and Footwork: Assume a stable stance with feet shoulder-width apart, knees slightly bent, and weight evenly distributed. Move using controlled steps to...
Objective: To teach the fundamentals of rifle-bayonet fighting.

Procedure:
1. Stance and Footwork: Assume a stable stance with feet shoulder-width apart, knees slightly bent, and weight evenly distributed. Move using controlled steps to maintain balance and readiness.
2. Grip and Stance: Hold the rifle with both hands, ensuring a firm but not overly tight grip. Keep the bayonet aligned with the rifle barrel for optimal striking power.
3. Basic Thrusts: Practice forward thrusts targeting the opponent's torso or head. Maintain a straight arm during the thrust to maximize force and accuracy.
4. Parrying Techniques: Learn to parry incoming strikes by using the rifle as a defensive tool. Use the rifle's barrel or stock to block or redirect an attacker's weapon.
5. Counterattacks: After successfully parrying, immediately follow up with a counterattack using thrusts or controlled slashes.
6. Distance Management: Maintain proper distance from the opponent to avoid being struck while ensuring effective striking range.
7. Drills and Repetition: Regularly practice these techniques through drills to build muscle memory and reflexes.

Warnings/Contraindications: Always use proper safety precautions when practicing with a bayonet. Ensure that no one is within striking distance during training exercises.
rifle-bayonet fighting, hand-to-hand combat, stance, footwork, grip, thrusts, parrying, counterattacks, distance management
Instinctive Rifle-Bayonet Fighting Instruction

Objective: To train soldiers in instinctive rifle-bayonet fighting techniques.

Procedure:
1. Instinct Development: Train soldiers to react instinctively to threats without relying on conscious thought, using repetitive drills and...
Objective: To train soldiers in instinctive rifle-bayonet fighting techniques.

Procedure:
1. Instinct Development: Train soldiers to react instinctively to threats without relying on conscious thought, using repetitive drills and simulations.
2. Scenario-Based Training: Use realistic scenarios such as ambushes, close-quarters combat, and enemy encounters to simulate real-world conditions.
3. Instructor Guidance: Instructors should provide clear guidance and feedback during training sessions to ensure proper technique and safety.
4. Progressive Difficulty: Start with basic drills and gradually increase the difficulty level to challenge soldiers and improve their skills.
5. Evaluation and Feedback: Regularly evaluate soldiers' performance and provide constructive feedback to help them improve.
6. Mental Preparation: Teach soldiers how to stay calm under pressure and make quick decisions during combat situations.

Warnings/Contraindications: Always use proper safety precautions when practicing rifle-bayonet fighting. Ensure that no one is within striking distance during training exercises.
instinctive rifle-bayonet fighting, scenario-based training, instructor guidance, progressive difficulty, evaluation and feedback, mental preparation
Understand the Purpose and Importance of Warrior Tasks and Battle Drills (WTBD)

Procedure:

Purpose: To understand the importance of Warrior Tasks and Battle Drills (WTBD) in enhancing Soldier readiness for combat.

Procedure:
1. Recognize that Warrior Tasks are individual Soldier skills critical to survival on the battlefield, such as weapons training, tactical communications, urban operations, and first aid.
2. Understand that Battle Drills are group skills designed to teach units how to react and survive in common combat situations, such as reacting to an ambush, chemical attack, or evacuating injured personnel from a vehicle.
3. Learn that WTBD increase the relevance of training to current combat requirements and enhance the rigor in training.
4. Understand that the driving force behind changes in training is lessons learned from real-world operations.
5. Recognize that while standards remain constant, commanders must be aware that the enemy adapts quickly, requiring Soldiers to train more rapidly to meet evolving operational environments.

Objective: Prevent injury during weapons of opportunity training.

Procedure:
1. Avoid full-speed or full-contact practice until proficiency is achieved.
2. Train in three stages:
(1) Execute techniques in the air, without making contact with an opponent or target during initial stages.
(2) Practice strikes against equipment such as a bayonet dummy, heavy bag, or locally produced target.
(3) Allow pairing up for blocking and striking practice only after students are proficient; ensure no full-speed or full-force execution occurs at this stage.
3. Start slowly with techniques and gradually increase speed as proficiency improves.

### Convoy Techniques

### Convoy Techniques

The following convoy techniques are essential for operational success:

#### Convoy Warning Order
• Provide a basic overview of the mission, route, and security plan to all units involved.

#### Convoy Brief
• Conduct a detailed briefing with all personnel on truck assignments, routes, checkpoints, and contingency plans.

#### React to Ambush (Near/Far)
• Near Ambush: Immediately take cover, return fire if possible, and follow the platoon leader’s orders for breaking contact or moving to a secure location.
• Far Ambush: Continue movement while maintaining situational awareness; prepare for potential engagement based on threat level.

#### Convoy Forced to Stop (Methods 1 and 2)
• Method 1: Secure the area, report the situation, and wait for further instructions from higher command.
• Method 2: If forced to stop due to a threat or mechanical failure, establish a perimeter and prepare for potential enemy contact.

#### Break Contact
• Execute a coordinated maneuver to disengage from an ambush or hostile engagement, ensuring all vehicles and personnel move to a secure location.

#### Recovery/CASEVAC Operations
• Coordinate with recovery teams to extract damaged vehicles or injured personnel.
• Ensure CASEVAC (Casualty Evacuation) procedures are followed for medical support and evacuation of the wounded.
convoy techniques,ambush reaction,break contact,recovery operations,cas evac,forced stop,security plan
