Combat Sports Rules (4) -

Define Methods of Victory in Combat Sports
Standard Source: FM 3 25 150 Combatives
Methods of Victory:

(1) Knockout (KO): If one fighter goes down from the impact of a blow (not from a push, slip, or throw), the referee will send the fighter who struck the blow to a neutral corner and begin a 10 count. If the downed...
Methods of Victory:

(1) Knockout (KO): If one fighter goes down from the impact of a blow (not from a push, slip, or throw), the referee will send the fighter who struck the blow to a neutral corner and begin a 10 count. If the downed fighter cannot return to his feet before 10 is reached, a knockout is awarded.

(2) Technical Knockout (TKO): A TKO is registered when the referee deems that one fighter cannot defend himself and is in danger of receiving excessive damage if the match continues. In this case, the referee will award the other fighter a TKO victory.

(3) Tap Out: A fighter may give up at any time during the match by tapping out. This is done by slapping their open palm several times (a minimum of twice) on the mat. The referee acknowledges a victory for the opponent and ends the match immediately.

(4) Verbal Submission: A fighter may give up at any time during the match by saying “stop” loud enough for the referee to hear. The referee will stop the fight and award the victory to the other fighter.

(5) Choke Out: When a choke has been applied, the referee will watch for any sign of unconsciousness, including failure to respond to verbal questions, and immediately stop the match, awarding the victory to the fighter who applied the choke.

(6) Referee Stoppage: The referee will consider both combatants’ safety at all times. He may stop the match if he thinks that a fighter’s safety is in danger or an injury is imminent. This is especially important when a joint lock is being applied and the “locked” fighter refuses to tap out or verbally submit. The referee will award the victory to the appropriate fighter.

(7) Judges’ Decision: The match will be judged by three judges. When a match goes to the time limit, the judges will make a decision based on the following point system:

• Standing Superiority: The fighter who shows superior skills on his feet will be awarded one point and the opponent no points. In the case of equal display of standing skills, both fighters will be awarded one point.
• Takedown Superiority: The fighter who shows superiority in takedowns will be awarded one point and the opponent no points. In the case of equal display of takedown skills, both fighters will be awarded one point.
• Ground Superiority: The fighter who shows superiority in ground fighting will be awarded one point and the opponent no points. In the case that neither fighter displays superiority during ground fighting, both fighters will be awarded one point.
• Total Superiority: The fighter who controls most of the action during the match will be awarded two points. In the case that neither fighter controls most of the action, both fighters will be awarded no points.

The points will be totaled and the fighter with the most points will be judged as the winner by each individual judge. The judges will turn in their scorecard with their name on it at the end of the match. The referee will award a decision based on the decision of the judges as follows:
• Unanimous Decision: All three judges awarded victory to the same fighter.
• Majority Decision: Two judges award a victory to the same fighter and the third judge scores the fight a draw, or one judge awards a victory to one fighter and the other two score the fight a draw.
• Split Decision: Two judges award a decision to the same fighter and the third judge awards a decision to the other fighter.
• Draw: All three judges score the match a draw or one judge scores the fight a draw and the other two judges are split.

• When the combatants are on the ground and neither is attempting to gain an advantage position or submission, the referee will start a 30-second count.

Due to the inherent dangers of rappelling, special care must be taken to ensure a safe and successful descent.

Operation of the Rappel Point

Due to the inherent dangers of rappelling, special care must be taken to ensure a safe and successful descent.

Communication: Climbers at the top of a rappel point must be able to communicate with those at the bottom. During a tactical rappel, radios, hand signals, and rope signals are considered. For training situations use the commands shown in Table 7-1:

|COMMAND|GIVEN BY|MEANING|
|---|---|---|
|LANE NUMBER<br>,<br>ON RAPPEL|Rappeller|I am ready to begin<br>rappelling.|
|LANE NUMBER<br>,<br>ON BELAY|Belayer|I am on belay and you<br>may begin your<br>rappel.|
|LANE NUMBER<br>,<br>OFF RAPPEL|Rappeller|I have completed the<br>rappel, cleared the<br>rappel lane, and am<br>off the rope.|
|LANE NUMBER<br>,<br>OFF BELAY|Belayer|I am off belay.|

Notes: 1. In a training environment, the lane number must be understood.
2. In a tactical situation, a series of tugs on the rope may be substituted for the oral commands to maintain noise discipline. The number of tugs used to indicate each command is IAW the unit SOP.

Establishing an Indirect Belay
High Priority Source: FM 3 97 61 Military Mountaineering
Indirect Belay is the most commonly used type of belay and involves using a belay device attached to the belayer’s harness. This method provides dynamic shock or weight absorption by the belayer if the climber falls or weights the rope, reducing...
Indirect Belay is the most commonly used type of belay and involves using a belay device attached to the belayer’s harness. This method provides dynamic shock or weight absorption by the belayer if the climber falls or weights the rope, reducing direct force on the anchor and preventing severe shock load to the anchor.

Steps to Establish an Indirect Belay:
1. Attach a Belay Device to the Belayer’s Harness: Ensure that the belay device is properly secured to the harness using a locking carabiner or other appropriate attachment method.
2. Thread the Rope Through the Belay Device: Pass the rope through the belay device, ensuring it is correctly positioned for effective braking and control.
3. Monitor the Climber’s Movement: The belayer should maintain constant awareness of the climber's position and be prepared to apply the brake if necessary.

Advantages of an Indirect Belay:
• Provides dynamic shock or weight absorption by the belayer, reducing force on the anchor.
• Prevents severe shock load to the anchor in case of a fall.
• Offers greater flexibility for the belayer during the belaying process.

Disadvantages of an Indirect Belay:
• Requires proper use of a belay device and harness attachment.
• May be less stable than a direct belay in certain rescue scenarios.
indirect belay, belay device, harness, shock absorption, anchor load
Install Fixed Rope with Intermediate Anchors
High Priority Source: FM 3 97 61 Military Mountaineering
Installation of a fixed rope with intermediate anchors:

1. Preparation:
- Two experienced climbers prepare for a roped climb.
- The leader carries a typical rack with enough hardware to place an adequate number of intermediate anchor...
Installation of a fixed rope with intermediate anchors:

1. Preparation:
- Two experienced climbers prepare for a roped climb.
- The leader carries a typical rack with enough hardware to place an adequate number of intermediate anchor points.
- The second sets up a standard belay.
- Select a route that has the following characteristics:
- Most suitable location, ease of negotiation, avoids obstacles.
- Availability of anchors (natural and artificial).
- Area is safe from falling rock or ice.
- Tactical considerations are met.
- A rope routed between knee and chest height (waist high preferred).
- Rope crossovers should be avoided.

2. Leader Climbs and Places Anchors:
- The leader climbs the route, placing anchors at all points where a change of direction occurs.
- He routes the climbing rope as in a typical roped climb, using any available natural anchors.
- Sling attachments should be kept as short and snug as possible to ensure that a load on the fixed rope below the anchor is placed only on that anchor. This will prevent one section from affecting another section.

3. Leader Anchors Rope at End of Pitch:
- When the leader reaches the end of the pitch, he temporarily anchors the rope using a sling if there is any chance of slipping and falling.
- He takes up any excess slack and attaches the rope to the anchor.
- Enough slack must be left in the rope so the second can tie the knots necessary to fix the rope.

4. Second Climber Sets Up Fixed Rope:
- The second unties from the rope and anchors it at the bottom.
- He attaches himself to the rope with a sling using a friction knot to create a self-belay.
- The self-belay will protect the second as he climbs and fixes the rope to the intermediate anchor points.

5. Fixing Rope at Anchor Points:
- When the second reaches an anchor point, he unclips the climbing rope so he can advance the self-belay beyond the anchor point.
- He takes the slack out of the section below the anchor point and ensures that the fixed rope will be approximately knee to chest level as climbers negotiate the installation.
- He attaches the rope using an anchor knot (for example, middle-of-the-rope clove hitch, double figure-eight).

6. Adjusting Long Runners:
- If a long runner is used at any anchor point, the second should adjust the section below it so the runner is oriented in the direction where the load or pull on the anchor will come from.

7. Adjusting Slack Between Anchor Points:
- Sections are normally adjusted fairly snug between anchor points.
- A slack section may be necessary to move around obstacles in the route or large bulges in the terrain.
- If clove hitches are used, adjusting the clove hitches at each end of the section can leave any amount of slack.

8. Using Utility Ropes for Adjustments:
- A middle-of-the-rope Prusik safetied with a figure eight may be used when utility ropes are available. These are used to adjust the rope height (either higher or lower).

9. Anchoring Etriers as Footholds:
- The second could anchor etriers to be used as footholds if needed.

10. Completing Installation:
- When the second reaches the end of the pitch, the rope is removed from the top anchor and the remaining slack is removed from the last section.
- The rope is reattached to the anchor.
- If additional fixed rope is required, the procedure is repeated using another rope. The second will tie the ropes together before anchoring the next section, creating one continuous fixed rope.
fixed rope, intermediate anchors, mountaineering, military climbing, anchor placement, rope installation

- Ensure the installation runs in a straight line between two anchors.
- Use natural pockets to place the base of the A-frame poles if possible.

2. Prepare Equipment:
- Two sturdy poles, at least 3 inches in diameter and 9 to 12 feet long.
- Three to five 14-foot sling ropes (depending on pole size).

3. Construct the A-Frame:
- Place two poles with their butt ends flush and mark the apex on both poles.

4. Tie Clove Hitch:
- Tie a clove hitch around the left pole 3 inches above the apex marking, leaving about 18 inches of rope free on top of the hitch.
- Ensure the rope end points down as it is tied.

5. Wrap Horizontally:
- Wrap the sling rope horizontally around both poles six to eight times, starting from the clove hitch and wrapping downward.
- If needed, join another sling rope with a square knot secured by overhand knots on the outside of one pole.
- Make at least two additional wraps below the joining knot.

6. Wrap Vertically:
- On the last horizontal wrap (not tied to the clove hitch), pass the rope between the poles below the wraps and make four to six tight vertical wraps around the horizontal wraps.
- Ensure the wraps are as flat as possible next to each other, in the same direction as the 18-inch tail on top of the clove hitch.

7. Insert Carabiner:
- Insert a carabiner into the last two vertical wraps.

8. Secure with Square Knot:
- On the last vertical wrap, pass the rope between the poles above the horizontal wraps and tie it off with a square knot in the section coming from the clove hitch.
- Secure with overhand knots tied in the tails.

9. Use Spreader Rope:
- Use a spreader rope to prevent collapse at the apex.
- If ground is soft, dig legs about 6 inches and tie a sling rope between them using a round turn with two half hitches around each leg.
- Remove all slack in the rope between the legs.

10. Secure on Hard Surface:
- Tie end-of-the-rope clove hitches with locking portions facing to the rear (direction of kick).
- Tie tails off at a 45-degree angle using round turn and two half hitches to a secondary anchor point.
- Ensure spreader rope is no more than 6 inches above ground level.

11. Anchor Traverse Ropes:
- One person rappels down the pitch and secures two installation (traverse) ropes to the far anchor with an anchor knot.
- Place a transport tightening system in each installation rope at the near (upper) anchor.
- Run the installation ropes through or around the anchor in opposite directions and tie off.

12. Position A-Frame:
- Ensure both traverse ropes run over the apex of the A-frame, which splits the angle between the near (upper) and far (lower) anchors.
- Anchor legs firmly with pitons or other means if necessary.

13. Tighten Installation Ropes:
- Use either a transport tightening system or z-pulley tightening system to tighten installation ropes.

14. Anchor A-Frame to Traverse Rope:
- Tie a clove hitch at the center of a sling rope and place it over one pole above the apex.
- Move down to the apex so that the locking bar is on the inside of the A-frame.
- Secure each end of the sling rope to one of the tightened static lines with two Prusik knots—one forward and one to the rear of the A-frame on the same static line rope.

15. Position A-Frame Correctly:
- Ensure angles created by the A-frame bisecting the installation rope are approximately equal on both sides for downward pressure, not lateral force.
- Place in a straight line between upper and lower anchor points.

16. Prepare Carrying Rope:
- Join ends of a 14-foot sling rope with a square knot and two overhand knots.
- Displace the knot one-third down the loop and tie an overhand knot both above and below the square knot, forming two small loops and one large loop.

17. Attach Carrying Rope to Traverse Ropes:
- Use carabiners (or a pulley) with gates reversed and opening in opposite directions to attach the carrying rope to traverse ropes.
- Attach a belay rope to the center loop of the carrying rope using a fixed loop or locking carabiner on the side opposite the joining knot.

18. Attach Load:
- Insert second carabiner into wraps of A-frame for belay rope attachment.
- Tie a six-wrap middle-of-the-rope Prusik knot to both static ropes near the far side off-loading point (acts as stopper knot).
- Attach load by running long loop of carrying rope through load or soldier’s harness and attaching bottom loop to traverse rope carabiner.

Note: Descent must be belayed slowly and controlled. Soldiers should hold onto the carrying rope, keep feet high, and use a mechanical belay if necessary. A relay man may be needed if the belayer cannot view the entire descent route.
A-frame installation, suspension traverse, mountaineering, rope techniques, military procedures

Mountaineering Rappelling (4) -

First Rappeller Down Responsibilities
Standard Source: FM 3 97 61 Military Mountaineering
Duties of the First Rappeller Down:

1. Select a smooth route for the rope that is clear of sharp rocks.
2. Conduct a self-belay using a self-belay attached to the rappel seat, which is hooked to the rappel rope with a friction knot.
3. Clear...
Duties of the First Rappeller Down:

1. Select a smooth route for the rope that is clear of sharp rocks.
2. Conduct a self-belay using a self-belay attached to the rappel seat, which is hooked to the rappel rope with a friction knot.
3. Clear the route by placing loose rocks far enough back on ledges to be out of the way, which the rope may dislodge.
4. Ensure the rope reaches the bottom or is at a place from which additional rappels can be made.
5. Ensure that the rope will run freely around the rappel point when pulled from below.
6. Clear the rappel lane by straightening all twists and tangles from the ropes.
7. Belay subsequent rappellers down the rope or monitor subsequent belayers.
8. Take charge of personnel as they arrive at the bottom (off-loading platform).
first rappeller, responsibilities, military mountaineering
Rappel Procedures and Body Positioning
Standard Source: FM 3 97 61 Military Mountaineering
Proper Rappel Descent Technique:

• Soldiers wear gloves for all types of rappels to protect their hands from rope burns.
• Descend in a smooth, controlled manner.
• The body forms an L-shape: feet shoulder-width apart, legs straight, and...
Proper Rappel Descent Technique:

• Soldiers wear gloves for all types of rappels to protect their hands from rope burns.
• Descend in a smooth, controlled manner.
• The body forms an L-shape: feet shoulder-width apart, legs straight, and buttocks parallel to the ground. When carrying equipment or additional weight, use a modified L-shape with the legs slightly lower than the buttocks to compensate for the extra weight.
• Keep the back straight and look over the brake shoulder.
• Extend the guide hand on the rope with the elbow extended and locked. The rope slides freely through the guide hand. Use the guide hand to adjust equipment and assist balance during descent.
• Grasp the rope firmly with the brake hand and place it in the brake position. Releasing tension on the rope and moving the brake hand regulates the rate of descent.
• Never let go of the ropes with the brake hand until the rappel is complete.
rappel technique, body positioning, military mountaineering

Procedure for Rappeller Clearing the Ropes:

• Each rappeller down clears the ropes and shouts, “Off rappel,” (if the tactical situation permits).
• After the rope is cleared and the rappeller is off rappel, he acts as the belayer for the next rappeller.

Inspection Skis Movement
Reference Source: FM 31 70 Basic Cold Weather Manual
Procedure for Inspection Skis (From Order Skis):

1. Start at the position of *Order Skis*. The command is INSPECTION SKIS.
2. At the command SKIS, perform the following:
- Use the left hand to unstrap the skis and place the loose...
Procedure for Inspection Skis (From Order Skis):

1. Start at the position of *Order Skis*. The command is INSPECTION SKIS.
2. At the command SKIS, perform the following:
- Use the left hand to unstrap the skis and place the loose strap in the pocket.
- Separate the skis and assume the position of attention, holding one ski in each hand between the toe and heel section of the bindings.
- Ensure that the running surfaces are facing forward and the tip of each ski is aligned with and approximately 8 cm (3”) outside the toe of the corresponding boot.
- Place the ski poles in the snow beside the left foot.
3. After the inspecting officer has examined the running surfaces, rotate the skis 180° to display the top surface.
4. Once the inspection is complete, refasten the skis and resume the position of *Order Skis*.

Procedure for Open and Close Ranks (Based on FM 22-5 with Adjustments):

1. Front rank takes 4 steps forward.
2. Second rank takes 2 steps forward.
3. Third rank stands fast (remains in place).
4. Fourth rank takes 4 steps backward.

*Note: This is a general formation adjustment, and each rank takes double the distance compared to FM 22-5.*

Right Shoulder Skis Movement
Reference Source: FM 31 70 Basic Cold Weather Manual
Procedure for Right Shoulder Skis (Four Count Movement):

1. Start at the position of *Order Skis*. The command is RIGHT SHOULDER SKIS.
2. At the command SKIS, perform the following:
- Lift the skis vertically until the upper right...
Procedure for Right Shoulder Skis (Four Count Movement):

1. Start at the position of *Order Skis*. The command is RIGHT SHOULDER SKIS.
2. At the command SKIS, perform the following:
- Lift the skis vertically until the upper right arm is horizontal.
- Simultaneously, use the left hand to grasp the skis over the front edges and approximately 30 cm (1’) below the front of the toe section of the binding.
- Keep the ski poles on the left wrist during this movement.
3. (TWO) Move the right hand down and grasp the skis over the front edges, midway between the ski tips and the front of the toe section of the binding.
4. (THREE) Lower the skis so that the balance point rests on the shoulder, with the skis at an angle of approximately 45° to the horizontal, and the right elbow close to the side.
5. (FOUR) Cut the left arm smartly back to the side and resume grip on the ski poles.

A platoon/squad that requires foot movement through a friendly forward unit must coordinate with that unit’s commander for safe and orderly passage. 7. Possible enemy ambush sites.
8. Latest enemy activity.
9. Detailed information on friendly positions such as crew-served weapons, FPF.
10. Fire and barrier plan:
- a. Support the unit can furnish: How long and what can they do? (1) Fire support. (2) Litter teams. (3) Navigational signals and aids. (4) Guides. (5) Communications. (6) Reaction units. (7) Other.
- b. Call signs and frequencies.
- c. Pyrotechnic plan.
- d. Challenge and password, running password, number combination.

Unit Operations (4) -

Plan Unit Move for Deployment
High Priority Source: STP 21 24 Warrior Leader Skills Level 2 3 4
### Plan Unit Move for Deployment

Conditions: You are given a command directive to plan for your unit to conduct a move to port of embarkation to deploy in support of an Army or Joint operations plan (OPLAN). You have access to the unit...
### Plan Unit Move for Deployment

Conditions: You are given a command directive to plan for your unit to conduct a move to port of embarkation to deploy in support of an Army or Joint operations plan (OPLAN). You have access to the unit standing operating procedure (SOP), and all unit movement directives.

Standards: Plan a unit movement using the necessary references (vehicle -10s) and equipment to deliver vehicles and equipment at the port of debarkation (POD) with no loss of vehicles, equipment, or personnel.

### Performance Steps:

1. Identify what needs to be moved
- Personnel
- Equipment
- Supplies
2. Identify the equipment to be moved
- What needs to accompany troops—Yellow (to accompany troops) TAT.
- What is needed immediately upon arrival—Red TAT.
- What does not have to accompany troops—NTAT (all other equipment required for the unit to perform its mission).
3. Identify what needs to be moved by air
- Advance party personnel
- Main body personnel
- Baggage TAT
- Equipment
4. Identify hazardous, sensitive, and classified equipment/material
- Determine appropriate packaging, labeling, segregating, and placarding for movement.
- Identify TAT ammunition quantities.
- Identify vehicles (3/4 tank full sea/air).
- Identify individual weapons (remain with the Soldier; bolt may be removed).
- Identify crew-served weapons (palletized or carried in the baggage compartment).
5. Identify bulk cargo
- Develop a packing list for all consolidated cargo loaded in vehicles, containers, and 463L pallets.
- Determine packing list distribution.
- Determine blocking, bracing, packing, crating, and tiedown (BBPCT) requirements.
6. Develop vehicle load plans
- Plan for cross-country payload capacity.
- Reduce vehicles according to the mode of transportation and type of movement.
- Test planned loads.
- Weigh and record planned loads.
- Identify transportation requirements exceeding the unit's organic lift capability.
7. Translate what needs to be moved into transportation terms using TC ACCIS/TC-AIMS II
- Use TC ACCIS to translate the automated unit equipment list/deployment equipment list (AUEL/DEL).
- Use TC AIMS II to translate the organization equipment list (OEL)/unit deployment list (UDL).
8. Determine how the personnel and equipment will move to the aerial/seaport of debarkation (APOD/SPOD)
- Roadable vehicles
- Tracked vehicles
- Rotary wing aircraft
9. Prepare the unit movement plan
- Determine administrative, logistical, and coordinating requirements for the plan such as transportation for drivers from the APOD/SPOE and back to the unit and for petroleum, oil and lubricants (POL).
10. Maintain the movement plan
- Keep the AUEL/OEL current with changes in unit equipment, personnel, and supplies.

### Evaluation Preparation:
• Evaluate this task during a field training exercise or a unit training exercise.
• Brief Soldier: Inform the Soldier that the evaluation is measured on the ability to perform all the functions listed.

Conduct Small Boat Annex Planning
Standard Source: Ranger Handbook 2006

Objective: Plan and execute small boat operations considering enemy, friendly forces, terrain, and weather conditions.

### Steps:
1. Assess the Situation
- Identify enemy forces, including their weather-related factors (tide, surf, wind) and terrain features (river width, depth, water temperature, current, vegetation).
- Determine friendly forces providing support.
- Note any attachments or detachments.
- Plan the organization for movement.

2. Define the Mission
- Clearly state the objective and purpose of the operation.

3. Execute the Operation
- Develop a concept of operation, including:
- Maneuver: Movement strategy and tactics.
- Fires: Use of weapons and fire support.
- Assign tasks to combat units, such as:
- Security measures.
- Tie-down teams responsible for:
- Loading equipment.
- Securing equipment.
- Designate coxswains and boat commanders.
- Select navigators and observers.
- Provide coordinating instructions, including:
- Formations and order of movement.
- Route and alternate route.
- Method of navigation (e.g., GPS, landmarks).
- Actions on enemy contact (response plan).
- Designate rally points for regrouping.
- Plan for embarkation and debarkation.
- Conduct rehearsals to ensure readiness.
- Establish a time schedule for all phases of the operation.

4. Service Support
- Develop a ration plan for sustenance during operations.
- Ensure availability of weapons and ammunition.
- Distribute uniforms and equipment, including:
- Method of distribution of paddles and life jackets.
- Plan for disposition of boats, paddles, and life jackets upon debarkation.

5. Command and Signal
- Define the location of patrol leader and assistant patrol leader.
- Establish signals used between boats and within boats, including code words for communication.
small boat operations, tactical planning, enemy forces, terrain analysis, navigation, security, signal communication

### Arming the M18A1 Claymore Mine

Steps:
1. Slide the slotted end of the shipping plug priming adapter onto the firing wire of the blasting cap between the crimped connections and the blasting cap.
2. Pull the excess wire through the slotted end of the adapter until the top of the blasting cap is firmly seated in the bottom portion of the shipping plug priming adapter (figure 071-325-4425-11).
3. Screw the adapter, with the blasting cap, into the detonator well.
4. Ensure that the face of the mine marked 'front toward enemy' and the arrows on the mine point in the direction of the enemy.
5. Recheck the aim of the mine.

### Procedure: Fire the M249 Machine Gun Using Correct Sight Picture and Trigger Manipulation Techniques

#### Conditions:
• Given an M249 machine gun and linked 5.56-mm ammunition.

#### Standards:
• Apply correct M249 machine gun target engagement techniques and hit each target in your assigned sector of fire.

### Steps:
1. Fire the weapon using the correct sight picture (figure 071-010-0006-6).
- Sight alignment: Center the front sight post in the peep sight (A, figure 071-010-0006-6).
- Focus of the eye: Place your eye directly on line with the center of the rear sight. Focus on the tip of the front sight post.
- Sight picture: Center the target over the front sight post (B, figure 071-010-0006-6). If firing on a 10-meter range target, use the sight picture in C, figure 071-010-0006-6.

2. Fire the weapon in three-round bursts at the rate of fire appropriate for the target size.
- Use correct trigger manipulation techniques: Pull the trigger straight to the rear and release it.

Note: Figure 071-010-0006-6 is referenced but omitted; it describes the sight picture for firing with an M249 machine gun.

Tell the Soldier to assume a bipod-supported prone position or the bipod-supported fighting position. Tell him/her that you are evaluating his/her ability to place effective fire on targets using the AN/PEQ-2A-equipped M240B machine gun.

Performance Measures:

- 2. Assumed a suitable firing position.

Load and Fire on Targets Using Appropriate Engagement Techniques
High Priority Source: STP 21 1 Army Warrior Skills Level 1 Soldiers Manual of Common Tasks
### Procedure: Load and Fire on Targets Using Appropriate Engagement Techniques

Steps:

### Procedure: Load and Fire on Targets Using Appropriate Engagement Techniques

Steps:

1. Load the weapon: Ensure your rifle is properly loaded with ammunition.
2. Use appropriate aiming techniques:
- For a stationary target, use reference points or sighting points to aim accurately.
- For a target moving towards you, engage it as you would a stationary target.
- For a target moving laterally, use the new single lead technique by placing the trailing edge of the front sight post at the center of the target. This method causes the lead to increase automatically as the range increases.
3. Engage multiple targets:
- First fire at the target presenting the greatest danger (usually the closest), then rapidly proceed to the next target.
4. Use quick-fire technique when there is no time to properly aim, such as in urban terrain or heavy bush:
- Use the standing position.
- Use the raised stock well, looking 2 or 3 inches above the sights on a plane level with the barrel.
- Look at the target, not at the sights.
5. Fire on targets until they are destroyed or you receive an order to cease fire.
engagement techniques, quick-fire, aiming, target engagement
Use Correct Application of Fire to Engage Specific Targets
High Priority Source: STP 21 1 Army Warrior Skills Level 1 Soldiers Manual of Common Tasks
### Use the correct application of fire to engage specific targets

#### Point target
Engage point targets with fixed fire using a single aiming point (figure 071-030-0004-7).

#### Linear target
Initially aim just outside of either flank or fire....
### Use the correct application of fire to engage specific targets

#### Point target
Engage point targets with fixed fire using a single aiming point (figure 071-030-0004-7).

#### Linear target
Initially aim just outside of either flank or fire. Traverse fire back and forth from flank to flank, covering the entire target area (figure 071-030-0004-8).

#### Linear target with depth
Initially aim at the near flank with range set to the midpoint of the target unless another portion of the target is more critical or presents a greater threat. Fire on the near flank, then traverse and search back and forth, covering the entire target (figure 071-030-0004-9).

#### Deep target
Initially aim at the end of the target closest to the gun, unless another portion of the target is more critical or presents a greater threat (auto rifleman). Fire and search up the far end and back again repeatedly (figure 071-030-0004-10).

#### Area target
Initially aim at the midpoint of the target area. Traverse and search to either flank, then traverse and search to the opposite flank (figure 071-030-0004-11).

Apply Correct Engagement Technique Based on Target Types
High Priority Source: STP 21 1 Army Warrior Skills Level 1 Soldiers Manual of Common Tasks
### Apply Correct Engagement Technique Based on Target Types

There are four types of engagement techniques based on target types:

1. Fixed Fire: This type of fire is delivered against a point target when the depth and width of the beaten zone...
### Apply Correct Engagement Technique Based on Target Types

There are four types of engagement techniques based on target types:

1. Fixed Fire: This type of fire is delivered against a point target when the depth and width of the beaten zone will cover the target. Only one aiming point is necessary to cover the target with fire.

2. Traversing Fire: This type of fire is distributed in width by successive changes in direction, which means moving the muzzle of the weapon to the left or right to distribute fire laterally. To make minor changes in direction, shift the shoulders to the right or left to select successive aiming points throughout the width of the target area. For major changes, move the elbows and align the body to remain directly behind the gun.

3. Searching Fire: This type of fire is distributed in depth by successive changes in elevation, which means moving the muzzle of the weapon up or down to distribute fire in depth. Select successive aiming points in depth throughout the target area. To make changes in elevation, move elbows closer together to lower the muzzle or farther apart to raise the muzzle.

4. Traversing and Searching Fire: This type of fire is distributed in width and depth by successive changes in direction and elevation. Combining traversing fire and searching fire provides good coverage of the target. Adjustments are made in the same manner as described for traversing fire and searching fire, which means moving the muzzle of the weapon to the left or right to distribute fire laterally. To make minor changes in direction, shift the shoulders to the right or left to select successive aiming points throughout the width of the target area. For major changes, move the elbows and align the body to remain directly behind the gun.
fixed fire,traversing fire,searching fire,engagement techniques,tactical shooting

Purpose: Recover human remains safely and according to protocol.

Steps:
1. Check the human remains for booby-traps and unexploded ordnance.
2. Establish tentative identification of the remains by reviewing identification media found on the human remains.
3. Interview anyone in the area that can visually identify the human remains and record information on DD Form 565 or a blank piece of paper.
4. Place personal effects and identification media found on the human remains in a personal effects bag or sealed container and place the personal effects bag or sealed container securely on the remains.
5. Record the believed-to-be (BTB) name of the deceased and other pertinent information regarding the recovery site on DD Form 567 or a blank piece of paper.

Steps:

1. Search during daylight hours only.
2. Conduct the search with other team members.
3. Question local inhabitants to gain information relevant to the loss using DD Form 1074 or a blank piece of paper.
4. Search open areas at double-arm intervals and heavily vegetated areas at single-arm or close intervals.
5. Mark the location of the human remains with a stake and cloth streamer.
6. Search a 100-meter area in each direction around the human remains in an attempt to locate additional human remains.

### Procedure: Perform Vehicle Signals

Steps:
1. Move to the left: Signal to direct a vehicle to move left.
2. Move to the right: Signal to direct a vehicle to move right.
3. Move forward: Signal to direct a vehicle to move forward.
4. Attention: Signal to get the attention of personnel or vehicles.
5. I am ready, or Ready to move, are you ready?: Signal to indicate readiness for movement and confirm readiness from others.
6. Mount: Signal to direct personnel to mount a vehicle.
7. Disregard previous command, or as you were: Signal to cancel a previous command and return to the last action.
8. I do not understand: Signal to indicate that a command was not understood.
9. Start engine or prepare to move: Signal to start an engine or prepare for movement.
10. Halt or stop: Signal to halt or stop a vehicle.
11. Increase speed: Signal to increase the speed of a vehicle.
12. Advance or move out, open up: Signal to advance or move forward and disperse.
13. Close up: Signal to close the distance between vehicles.
14. Right or left turn: Signal to direct a vehicle to make a right or left turn.
15. Slow down: Signal to slow down a vehicle.
16. Move in reverse: Signal to move a vehicle in reverse.
17. Close distance between vehicles and stop: Signal to close the distance between vehicles and bring them to a halt.
18. Stop engines: Signal to shut off vehicle engines.
19. Dismount: Signal to direct personnel to dismount from a vehicle.
20. Neutral steer, stop: Signal to neutralize steering and stop a vehicle.
21. Button up or unbutton: Signal to button up or unbutton (e.g., for protection against NBC threats).
22. Message acknowledged: Signal to acknowledge receipt of a message or command.

Details:
• These signals are used in military operations to coordinate vehicle movements and ensure operational readiness.
• Visual aids (figures 071-326-0608-13 through 071-326-0608-36) illustrate the correct posture and hand movements for each signal.
vehicle signals, move left, move right, halt, stop, increase speed, close up, neutral steer
Perform Vehicle Signals for Military Communication

Procedure:

1. Perform the following vehicle signals:
- Move to the left: Signal indicating that vehicles should move or turn left.
- Move to the right: Signal indicating that vehicles should move or turn right.
- Move forward: Signal indicating that vehicles should proceed in a forward direction.
- Attention: Signal used to direct attention or halt movement momentarily.
- I am ready, or Ready to move, are you ready?: Signal used to confirm readiness before proceeding with an action or movement.
- Mount: Signal directing personnel to mount vehicles.
- Disregard previous command, or as you were: Signal indicating that a prior command should be ignored and the unit should return to its previous state.
- I do not understand: Signal used when a signal is not understood or cannot be executed.
- Start engine or prepare to move: Signal directing vehicle operators to start engines or prepare for movement.
- Halt or stop: Signal indicating that vehicles should stop immediately.
- Increase speed: Signal directing vehicles to accelerate.
- Advance or move out, open up: Signal directing a formation to advance and spread out.
- Close up: Signal directing a formation to close ranks or formations.
- Right or left turn: Signal indicating that vehicles should make a right or left turn.
- Slow down: Signal directing vehicles to reduce speed.
- Move in reverse: Signal directing vehicles to move backward.
- Close distance between vehicles and stop: Signal directing vehicles to close the gap between them and then stop.
- Stop engines: Signal directing vehicle operators to shut off engines.
- Dismount: Signal directing personnel to dismount from vehicles.
- Neutral steer, stop: Signal directing vehicles to neutralize steering and come to a complete stop.
- Button up or unbutton: Signal used in armored vehicles to direct the closing or opening of hatches or armor.
- Message acknowledged: Signal confirming that a message has been received and understood.

Details:
• These signals are used during military operations involving vehicles to coordinate movement, readiness, and communication among units.
• Visual aids such as figures 071-326-0608-13 through figure 071-326-0608-36 provide visual representations of each signal.
• Proper execution of these signals is critical for effective communication and coordination in the field.

Procedure for Two-Man Lift Support

(1) Position the climber with both feet on the support, facing the wall. The climber's palms should be flat against the building, and their feet should be about 2 feet out from the building with heels raised.

(2) Two Soldiers stand on either side of the climber, facing each other. They bend forward and cup their hands.

(3) Each Soldier grasps a heel of the climber. With a quick upward motion, they lift the climber and guide them into the entrance.

Map Reading And Situation Analysis (4) -

Draw and Mark Tactical Boundaries on Maps
Standard Source: STP 21 24 Warrior Leader Skills Level 2 3 4
Procedure for Drawing and Marking Tactical Boundaries on Maps:

1. Identify Key Terrain Features: Draw boundaries along terrain features that are easily recognizable on the ground.
2. Position Boundaries Strategically: Ensure that key...
Procedure for Drawing and Marking Tactical Boundaries on Maps:

1. Identify Key Terrain Features: Draw boundaries along terrain features that are easily recognizable on the ground.
2. Position Boundaries Strategically: Ensure that key terrain features, avenues of approach, and rivers completely include the unit if possible.
3. Use Solid Lines for Current or Effective Boundaries: Show boundaries with a solid line if they are currently in effect or if the OPORD will affect them.
4. Use Broken Lines for Future or Proposed Boundaries: Represent future or proposed boundaries using a broken line and label them to indicate their effective time, as appropriate (see figure 071-332-5000-2).
5. Mark Boundaries with Symbols: Place a symbol on the boundary to show the size and designation of the highest units that share the boundary.
6. Show Units of Unequal Size: Completely show the symbols of the higher unit and the designation of the lower unit to indicate its size (see figure 071-332-5000-3).
7. Indicate Task Organization Overlays or Sketches: Identify overlays or sketches accompanying written or oral orders that specify task organization.
8. Label Unit Boundaries Correctly:
- Indicate numerical unit designation on battalion boundaries.
- When the battalion is organized into a task force, precede the numerical designation with the letters 'TF.'
- Identify a unit symbol as a task force by placing the TF symbol over the unit size designation (||).
- Label company boundaries with the appropriate letter unless the company is organized into a team. In that case, label the boundary with the abbreviation TM plus the letter designation or a code name.
9. Use Designations for Clarity:
- On other boundaries, only include the unit designation needed for clarity.
- Add branch designations only when necessary for clarity.
10. Spell Out Smaller Unit Designations: When unequal-sized units share a boundary, spell out the designation of the smaller unit.
boundaries,map symbols,tactical operations,unit designation,task force,labeling,map reading

Captured Enemy Materiel Handling (4) -

Handle Captured Communication-Electronics (C-E) Equipment and Documents
Critical Source: STP 21 24 Warrior Leader Skills Level 2 3 4
Procedure:

When handling C-E equipment or documents marked TECHDOC:

1. Coordinate closely with the communications staff.
2. Treat all CEDs containing communications or cryptographic information as secret material.
3. **Tag and...
Procedure:

When handling C-E equipment or documents marked TECHDOC:

1. Coordinate closely with the communications staff.
2. Treat all CEDs containing communications or cryptographic information as secret material.
3. Tag and evacuate through secure channels without delay.
4. Ensure that any associated TECHDOC sheet is included in the evacuation process.
5. If no preprinted tags are available, use a field expedient method, including:
- Date and time of capture
- Capturing unit and designation
- Circumstances of capture
- Identity of the CED or CEE captured
- Location where the document was captured (including six- or eight-digit grid coordinate)
6. Never write on the document itself.
7. Place the tag in a waterproof bag, and attach it to the CEM so that it will not come off.
8. Ensure that all markings present at the time of capture are preserved, and that items are tagged without damaging or destroying documents or equipment.
secure handling, C-E equipment, TECHDOC, field expedient tagging
Select Disposition Procedures for Captured Enemy Materiel (CEM)
Critical Source: STP 21 24 Warrior Leader Skills Level 2 3 4
Procedure:

1. Identify all time-sensitive CEM to be evacuated to the S2 (intelligence officer). The S2 will screen for intelligence or technical value and then evacuate to the rear for examination and exploitation.
2. All enemy documents...
Procedure:

1. Identify all time-sensitive CEM to be evacuated to the S2 (intelligence officer). The S2 will screen for intelligence or technical value and then evacuate to the rear for examination and exploitation.
2. All enemy documents captured on the battlefield are sent immediately to the first intelligence staff officer in the chain.
3. The S2/G-2 routes all enemy documents to the nearest interrogation element for tactical exploitation.
4. Interrogators screen the documents for immediate information and forward them to higher command, as required.
5. Evacuate CEM with any technical documents found that relate to its design or operation.
6. When materiel cannot be evacuated:
- Attach a sheet marked TECHDOC to the item.
- Include on the sheet:
- The precise location, time, and circumstances of capture.
- A detailed description of the materiel.
- Photographs of the equipment, evacuated with the document.
- Photographs of the materiel, placing an object of known size (e.g., a ruler) near the item to provide a size reference.
7. Protect equipment that is too large to evacuate by assigning detail guards until further instructions are received.
8. Keep all photos with the TECHDOC and evacuate them through your chain of command to the S2.
disposition, evacuation, CEM handling, TECHDOC

Proper identification through insignia is crucial for militia members.

Overview:

Selecting the right headgear is important for both practicality and identification.

Recommended Headgear Options:
1. Boonie Hat: The best all-around choice, offering shade, weather protection, and comfort without overheating. Available in woodland, tiger-stripe, desert, and other patterns.
2. Military Soft Cap: Provides eye shading and can be folded with ear flaps for cold weather protection.
3. Watch Cap: Ideal for nighttime use but may become too warm in summer.

Avoid Inappropriate Headgear:
• Berets: While stylish, they offer no practical benefits such as sun or rain protection, and can overheat the head. Only wear if for appearance purposes.

Overview:

Choosing the right uniform is essential for identification and practicality in Michigan's environment.

Steps to Select a Uniform:
1. Preferred Option: Choose US Army style BDUs (battle dress uniforms) in the woodland camouflage pattern, as this is well-suited for Michigan’s forested terrain.
2. Alternative Options: Consider foreign military surplus camouflage clothing, provided you:
- Remove any foreign insignia to avoid misidentification as a foreign soldier.
- Add militia-specific patches or insignia (e.g., a subdued green 'Don't Tread On Me' patch) in highly visible locations on the uniform.
3. Avoid Inappropriate Patterns: Avoid desert, urban, or black camouflage patterns for woodland environments unless under specific conditions where they are appropriate.
4. Uniformity Considerations: While personal preference is allowed, maintaining some level of uniformity among militia members can improve group cohesion and identification.

Electro Metallurgy (3) -

Preparing and Using a Voltaic Battery
Reference Source: The Household Cyclopedia
Procedure for Preparing and Using a Voltaic Battery:

1. Definition of a Battery:
- A battery is typically composed of multiple voltaic cells connected together, though it may also refer to a single cell.
2. **Common Types of...
Procedure for Preparing and Using a Voltaic Battery:

1. Definition of a Battery:
- A battery is typically composed of multiple voltaic cells connected together, though it may also refer to a single cell.
2. Common Types of Batteries:
- Smee's, Daniell's, and nitric acid batteries are commonly used in practice.
3. Components of the Battery:
- Each battery contains two plates (zinc and another metal) and an exciting fluid.
4. Preparation of Zinc Plate:
- The zinc plate must be amalgamated by:
- Dipping it into weak sulphuric acid and rubbing with mercury.
- Alternatively, immerse the entire plate in a bath of mercury periodically during use.
5. Polarity Assignment:
- The zinc plate is the positive plate (anode), while the other plate is the negative plate (cathode).
6. Connection to External Circuit:
- A binding screw connects the zinc plate to a wire, which serves as the electrode.
7. Polarity Naming Convention:
- The pole's name is opposite to that of the plate; for example, the positive pole (anode) is attached to the negative plate, and the negative pole (cathode) is attached to the positive (zinc) plate.

Notes:
• Amalgamation ensures proper conductivity and longevity of the zinc plate in the battery.
voltaic battery,amalgamation,zinc plate,polarity,electrodes
Setting Up the Decomposing Cell for Electrolysis
Reference Source: The Household Cyclopedia
Procedure for Setting Up a Decomposing Cell (Electrolytic Cell):

1. Purpose of the Decomposing Cell:
- The decomposing cell is used to hold the electrolyte, which is the liquid being decomposed during the electroplating process.
2....
Procedure for Setting Up a Decomposing Cell (Electrolytic Cell):

1. Purpose of the Decomposing Cell:
- The decomposing cell is used to hold the electrolyte, which is the liquid being decomposed during the electroplating process.
2. Separate Vessel for Electrolyte:
- Keep the electrolyte in a separate vessel and connect it to the main battery via wires.
3. Anode Material Selection:
- Attach a piece of metal (same as that being deposited) to the anode.
4. Maintaining Solution Strength:
- The anode material is gradually consumed during the process, keeping the solution strength uniform.
5. Regulating Current Flow:
- Adjust the distance between the poles in the electrolyte to control current flow:
- Increasing the distance reduces the amount of electricity passing through.
6. Avoiding Overpowering the Current:
- Avoid using a current that is too strong, as it can cause brittle or non-adherent coatings and may produce gas bubbles from the object being plated.
7. Plating Multiple Objects Simultaneously:
- A single battery can plate multiple objects if they are suspended on copper rods connected to the poles.

Notes:
• This setup ensures even deposition of metal onto the cathode and maintains solution consistency during electroplating.
decomposing cell,electrolysis,anode,cathode,current regulation,multiple plating
Understanding Galvanoplasty (Electrotype) Process
Reference Source: The Household Cyclopedia
Procedure for Galvanoplasty or Electrotype:

1. Definition and Purpose:
- Galvanoplasty is the process of cold casting metals using electricity.
2. Applications:
- Used to multiply engravings, photographs, cover typefaces with...
Procedure for Galvanoplasty or Electrotype:

1. Definition and Purpose:
- Galvanoplasty is the process of cold casting metals using electricity.
2. Applications:
- Used to multiply engravings, photographs, cover typefaces with harder metal, and deposit metals like gold, silver, or alloys on other surfaces.
3. Principle of Operation:
- An electrical current passed through a properly prepared metallic solution causes decomposition; the metal is deposited onto any conducting body connected to the negative pole (cathode) of a voltaic cell or battery.
4. Polarity Setup:
- The zinc plate is always attached to the positive pole (anode), and the object being plated is connected to the cathode.

Notes:
• This process relies on the controlled flow of electricity through a metallic solution to deposit metal onto an object.
galvanoplasty,electrotype,cold casting,electricity,metal deposition

2. Do not outclimb the belayer, as this can create slack in the rope between the climber and belayer.

3. Avoid placing excessive pressure or weight on the belayer.

Climbing Commands and Signals for Top Rope Operations
Standard Source: US Marine Corps Wilderness Medicine
Procedure:

Voice Commands:
• “Lane #, Up Rope” – Given by the climber; indicates that the belayer needs to take in slack.
• “That’s Me” – Given by the climber; indicates that excess slack has been taken up between the climber and...
Procedure:

Voice Commands:
• “Lane #, Up Rope” – Given by the climber; indicates that the belayer needs to take in slack.
• “That’s Me” – Given by the climber; indicates that excess slack has been taken up between the climber and belayer.
• “Lane #, On Belay” – Given by the belayer; indicates that the belayer is on belay.
• “Lane #, On Climb” – Given by the climber; indicates that the climber is ready to climb.
• “Climb Climber” – Given by the belayer; indicates that the climber may begin climbing.

Rope Tugs:
• Three tugs – If given by the climber, it means the belayer needs to take in slack.
• Three tugs – If given by the belayer, it means that the belayer has taken up slack and the climber may begin climbing.
• Three tugs – If given by the climber, it indicates that the climber is now climbing.

- Two non-locking carabiners as the attachment point for the anchor.

2. Route the rope from the bottom up through the anchor and back down to the bottom.

3. Secure the climber to one end of the rope and the belayer to the other end.

Notes:
• This system is used for both direct and indirect belays.
• Ensure that the anchor is strong enough to support the weight of the climber and belayer.

Rope Crossing (3) -

Pulley Method for Crossing a One Rope Bridge
Standard Source: US Marine Corps Wilderness Medicine
Procedure:

This method is used when the one rope bridge is long, uphill, or speed is vital and the Marines crossing it have a lot of heavy personal equipment (e.g., M24OG's, radios, etc.).

1. Equipment required: One pulley, four steel...
Procedure:

This method is used when the one rope bridge is long, uphill, or speed is vital and the Marines crossing it have a lot of heavy personal equipment (e.g., M24OG's, radios, etc.).

1. Equipment required: One pulley, four steel locking carabiners, and a hauling line twice the length of the obstacle.

2. Setting up the system:
- Construct the first suspension point by attaching a pulley to the one rope bridge.
- Attach one 85 carabiner to the pulley with the gate down.
- Attach a second 85 carabiner to the first 85 with the gate facing the near side bank.
- Into this second 85, attach the hauling rope with a figure-8 loop. The figure-8 is placed halfway along the hauling rope and attached to the 85, which is then locked.
- Four feet down the line, another figure-8 on a bight is placed into the second suspension point.

3. Connection: The Marine clips his 85 into the lower 85; his equipment is clipped into the second 85. The mule team starts to pull.
pulley method, one rope bridge crossing, heavy equipment transport, tactical rope techniques
Rappel Seat Method for Crossing a One Rope Bridge
Standard Source: US Marine Corps Wilderness Medicine
Procedure:

1. The Marine ties himself into a rappel seat and inserts a large steel locking carabiner with the gate facing down and away.

2. The Marine faces the bridge with his right hand towards the near anchor to snap into the bridge. Once...
Procedure:

1. The Marine ties himself into a rappel seat and inserts a large steel locking carabiner with the gate facing down and away.

2. The Marine faces the bridge with his right hand towards the near anchor to snap into the bridge. Once the 85 is locked onto the bridge rope, a helper flips the 85 over so that the locking nut screws down. A carrier rope with a girth hitch may be added to assist the Marine in mounting the rope.

3. The Marine hangs below the bridge from his rappel seat with his head pointing in the direction of the far anchor and allows his legs to hang free.

- 4. Pulling with his arms makes progress.

- 5. This method is the safest and therefore the preferred method.

- 6. If the Marine must take a pack across, he may wear it with the waistband secured. However, the preferred method is to have another carabiner (aluminum non-locking is sufficient) attached to the pack frame at the top and attach this to the bridge behind the Marine, putting his legs through the shoulder straps and pulling the pack across with him.

- 7. One man at a time will cross, although one can load and another can unload concurrently.

- 8. Weapons will be worn across the shoulder; muzzle down with a tight sling securely attached to the weapon.
rappel seat method, one rope bridge crossing, tactical rope techniques, military survival

Selecting a Defensive Position in Cold Weather Conditions
High Priority Source: Canadian Military Basic Cold Weather Training
Objective: Choose a defensive position that maximizes the defender's advantage during cold weather conditions.

Procedure:
1. General Considerations:
- Assume a defensive role when conditions are favorable to the defender, such as...
Objective: Choose a defensive position that maximizes the defender's advantage during cold weather conditions.

Procedure:
1. General Considerations:
- Assume a defensive role when conditions are favorable to the defender, such as during break-up or freeze-up seasons, severe snowstorms, or extremely low temperatures.
- The conduct of defense under northern conditions is similar to other conditions; however, defences will be drawn closer together.

2. Siting and Location:
- Select a position that forces the enemy to attack through unfavourable terrain such as long narrow passes, deep snow, or obstacles where movement is difficult.
- In snow-covered areas (especially deep, soft snow), this will aid in constructing field defences, smother fire effects, and hinder an attacking force.
- Ensure all-around defence since attacks may come from any direction. Strong points must be sited to cover likely enemy approaches and placed into the prevailing wind.
- Locate defensive strong points on high commanding ground, as this is more valuable in winter than summer conditions. High ground forces attackers to move uphill through snow, increasing their exposure to direct fire.

3. Icing Considerations:
- If a portion of high ground is iced, it will slow down and exhaust an attacking force.
- When planning icing:
- Carefully consider the distance from the iced area to the defenders.
- If the iced area is near the defenders on a steep or smooth slope, attackers may be slowed almost completely, increasing grenade fragmentation effects.
- Iced areas can also be incorporated into registered defensive fire tasks.
- Icing increases the lethal effects of ground burst artillery or mortar fire and increases ricochets from low air bursting artillery.

4. Use of Obstructions:
- Use natural obstructions such as dense forests, thickets, fallen timber, cliffs, steep banks, rocks, and tree trunks to create obstacles for attackers.
- Enhance the effectiveness of these features by:
- Laying A/P and A/TK mines
- Setting up automatic weapons on fixed lines
- Stringing barbed or concertina wire around and through obstructions
- Placing booby traps
- Icing obstacles
- Using vehicle ice traps, artificial thaws, and artificial avalanches (of snow or rock)
defensive position, cold weather, snowstorm, terrain advantage, icing, obstructions, high ground

2. Ensure that the reinforcement is sturdy enough to withstand enemy fire and debris from explosions.
3. Place the reinforcement at least 6 inches away from the loophole to allow for proper firing clearance.
4. Secure the sandbags or materials with additional supports if necessary (e.g., tying them together or using stakes).
5. Check the reinforced area regularly for damage or wear.

Winter Operations (3) -

Conduct Winter Operations in Subarctic Environments
High Priority Source: Canadian Military Basic Cold Weather Training
Overview:

The subarctic region, characterized by dense coniferous forests, swamps, rivers, lakes, and limited road infrastructure, presents unique challenges for military operations. The following procedures outline key considerations for...
Overview:

The subarctic region, characterized by dense coniferous forests, swamps, rivers, lakes, and limited road infrastructure, presents unique challenges for military operations. The following procedures outline key considerations for conducting effective operations in this environment.

### Mobility Considerations
• In the subarctic, mobility is heavily dependent on air transport due to the lack of all-weather roads.
• Ground mobility during winter should rely on skis, snowshoes, oversnow and throughsnow vehicles. Wheeled vehicles can be used only if sufficient resources are available to keep roads open.
• Engineers will play a critical role in maintaining road access during winter operations.

### Tactical Considerations
• Both friendly and enemy forces depend heavily on air and road transport for the survival of forward troops.
• The objective is to interdict the enemy's line of communication through air and ground attacks.
• Frontal assaults in deep snow should be avoided due to reduced mobility and increased difficulty.
• Preferred tactics include envelopment, infiltration, and movement across country using skis, snowshoes, oversnow vehicles, and helicopters.

### Key Winter Challenges
• The cold, snow and ice, and frozen ground are the three major factors influencing all phases of winter operations.
• These conditions reduce equipment effectiveness, mobility, and the ability to maintain momentum.
• Human performance becomes the most critical factor in overcoming these challenges.

### Training Requirements
• Success depends on individual and sub-unit efficiency, good leadership, and high levels of physical stamina and mental conditioning.
• Training must emphasize maintaining mobility under adverse conditions, including restricted visibility and difficulty recognizing terrain features.
• Map reading and navigation skills are essential to ensure efficient movement in the field.
subarctic,winter operations,mobility,tactics,training,cold weather
Plan and Execute Winter Operations with Adjusted Procedures
High Priority Source: Canadian Military Basic Cold Weather Training
Overview:

Winter operations require adjustments to standard procedures due to the unique challenges of cold environments. The following procedure outlines key considerations for planning and executing military operations in winter...
Overview:

Winter operations require adjustments to standard procedures due to the unique challenges of cold environments. The following procedure outlines key considerations for planning and executing military operations in winter conditions.

### Tactical Principles
• Tactical principles remain consistent with those used in temperate zones, but modifications are necessary to account for environmental factors.
• Cold weather significantly impacts human performance, equipment effectiveness, mobility, and the ability to maintain momentum.
• These challenges must be addressed through comprehensive training and the application of specialized techniques.

### Human Element
• The human element becomes paramount in winter operations due to reduced equipment effectiveness and mobility restrictions.
• Personnel must be trained to a high level of physical stamina and mental conditioning to endure prolonged exposure to adverse weather conditions.
• Leaders at all levels must be carefully selected, trained, and prepared to maintain sub-unit efficiency and morale under challenging conditions.

### Training Focus
• Training should emphasize maintaining mobility in cold environments.
• Map reading and navigation skills are essential due to restricted visibility and difficulty recognizing terrain features.
• These skills ensure efficient movement and the effective use of time and effort during operations.
winter planning,winter tactics,training,cold weather,mobility

6. The break-up season is advantageous to the defender due to environmental conditions.

Patrolling (3) -

Conduct Long-Range Patrolling in Northern Cold Weather Conditions
High Priority Source: Canadian Military Basic Cold Weather Training
Procedure:

1. Increase the importance of patrolling for both intelligence gathering and security, especially when combat units are separated by large distances.
2. Reconnaissance and fighting patrols may operate for extended periods depending...
Procedure:

1. Increase the importance of patrolling for both intelligence gathering and security, especially when combat units are separated by large distances.
2. Reconnaissance and fighting patrols may operate for extended periods depending on climatic conditions and support capabilities.
3. Foot patrols should be self-sufficient for 3 to 5 days, while mobile patrols should remain operational much longer.
4. The duration of all patrols depends on the reliability of supply drops or availability of pre-arranged fuel caches.
5. Use aircraft as the most economical way to deploy long-range patrols into enemy territory.
6. Deploy patrols immediately prior to anticipated adverse weather conditions to ensure additional security at the start of the mission.
7. Ensure reliable communications for all patrols, with radio being the primary means.
8. Due to extended distances and difficulty in radio transmission in northern areas, use aerial relays or message pick-up and drop techniques as necessary.
long-range patrolling,cold weather,northern operations,self-sufficient patrols,fuel caches
Conduct Winter Patrols with Increased Precautions
High Priority Source: Canadian Military Basic Cold Weather Training
Procedure:

1. Types of Patrols:
- Conduct short range patrols similar to those in temperate climates, but equip each individual with survival gear.
- For long range patrols, plan for deep penetration over an extended period of time....
Procedure:

1. Types of Patrols:
- Conduct short range patrols similar to those in temperate climates, but equip each individual with survival gear.
- For long range patrols, plan for deep penetration over an extended period of time. Consider using light aircraft or helicopters for dropping and picking up patrols if necessary. Penetration on foot is possible given sufficient time.

2. Conduct of Patrols:
- Increase warning time to allow maximum preparation.
- Carry emergency rations and survival gear at all times.
- Plan routes meticulously using diagrammatic methods rather than written notes. Ensure each patrol member is familiar with the route, including bearings and distances for each leg. Members should be prepared to return on their own if necessary.
- When plotting routes to an objective, select a secondary objective close to the final destination. This allows the patrol to navigate securely and unencumbered by recording and navigation challenges. The secondary objective can also serve as a rendezvous point for heavy packs.
- Unless rapid transmission of information is imperative, radio sets are not required due to the short duration of most patrols.
- Use a prearranged homing device with flares to assist in returning to base. Consider methods to prevent compromise of the home position with this device.
- Reconnaissance patrols may require at least two additional members to break trail. Patrol commanders must account for this when planning operations.
winter patrol, survival gear, route planning, homing device, reconnaissance patrol

Camouflage (3) -

Camouflage Yourself and Your Individual Equipment
High Priority Source: STP 21 1 Warrior Skills Level 1
Objective: Camouflage yourself and your individual equipment to prevent detection by visual, near infrared, infrared, ultraviolet, radar, acoustic, and radio sensors.

### Conditions:
• Given load-carrying equipment (LCE), an individual weapon,...
Objective: Camouflage yourself and your individual equipment to prevent detection by visual, near infrared, infrared, ultraviolet, radar, acoustic, and radio sensors.

### Conditions:
• Given load-carrying equipment (LCE), an individual weapon, a Kevlar® helmet with camouflage cover, grass, bushes, trees, pieces of the Lightweight Camouflage Screen System (LCSS), skin paint, and charcoal and/or mud.
• Wearing a battle dress uniform (BDU).

### Standards:
• Camouflage yourself and your individual equipment to prevent detection by visual, near infrared, infrared, ultraviolet, radar, acoustic, and radio sensors.

### Performance Steps:
1. Identify critical camouflage considerations:
- a. Movement:
- Minimize movement.
- Move slowly and smoothly when movement is necessary.
- b. Shape:
- Use natural or artificial materials to breakup shapes, outlines, and equipment.
- Stay in shadows when moving, if possible.
- Disguise or distort the shape of your helmet and your body with natural or artificial materials when conducting operations close to the enemy.
- c. Light reflection:
- Cover or remove the following items to eliminate light reflection:
- Mirrors
- Eye glasses
- Watch crystals
- Plastic map cases
- Starched uniforms
- Clear plastic garbage bags
- Dust goggles worn on top of helmets
- Cigarettes and pipes
- Red-filtered flashlights (Replace all red filters on flashlights with blue-green filters)
- d. Color:
- Blend individual camouflage with the surroundings or, at a minimum, ensure that objects do not contrast with the background.
- Change camouflage, as required, when moving from one area to another.
2. Camouflage your exposed skin:
- Cover your skin oils, using paint sticks, even if you have very dark skin.
- Paint sticks cover these oils and provide blending with the background.
- Do not use oils or insect repellant to soften paint sticks. This defeats the purpose of paint sticks by making the skin shiny.
- Work in pairs when applying paint, because self-application may leave gaps, such as behind the ears.
- Use the color chart in table 052-191-1361-1 when applying paint on the face.
camouflage, survival, stealth, concealment, tactical, military, BDU, LCSS, paint sticks, light reflection, movement

Tactics and Techniques for Winter Operations
High Priority Source: FM 31 70 Basic Cold Weather Manual
Procedure:

• Place increased importance on value of reconnaissance, particularly route reconnaissance, because of widely separated units, heavily wooded areas, sparsely populated areas, and few maps.
• Use ground reconnaissance to make final...
Procedure:

• Place increased importance on value of reconnaissance, particularly route reconnaissance, because of widely separated units, heavily wooded areas, sparsely populated areas, and few maps.
• Use ground reconnaissance to make final selection of routes.
• Take advantage of ski and snowshoe mobility when snow conditions are favorable.
• Use good skiers for long-range patrols.
• Consider endurance and physical condition of troops at all times during winter operations.
• Attack front, flanks, and rear of enemy defensive position simultaneously, when possible, in order to isolate and inclose him. Minimize execution of assault in deep snow against commanding terrain.
• Use skijoring when feasible.
• Insure tactical requirements are fulfilled in conditions of extreme cold.
• Leave skis and snowshoes at assembly area or attack position only if enemy may be reached more quickly and easily without them.
• Consider frozen lakes, rivers, and streams as avenues of approach for enemy and as route of advance for friendly forces.
• Assault on foot instead of skis when it can be done effectively and rapidly. Skis are recovered and brought forward by detail from each squad.
• Do not use same tracks or route for vehicles when moving over terrain with low load bearing capability.
• Do not use wheeled trailers behind tracked vehicles in cross-country movements if other means are available.
winter tactics, cold weather operations, route reconnaissance, ski mobility
Use of Smoke Shells in Winter Conditions

Procedure:

1. Use base ejection artillery smoke shells with cannisters only where there is packed snow or ice, as they are not effective in loose snow due to burying.
2. Use white phosphorus (WP) artillery shells for the most effective smoke...
Procedure:

1. Use base ejection artillery smoke shells with cannisters only where there is packed snow or ice, as they are not effective in loose snow due to burying.
2. Use white phosphorus (WP) artillery shells for the most effective smoke generation in winter conditions, even though they may be buried in loose snow.
3. Clear snow before using smoke pots and place them on a solid platform to prevent heat from causing them to burrow into the snow.

Details:
• Smoke pots work well in low temperatures but require careful placement.
• WP shells are generally more effective than cannister-based shells in winter.

Camouflage And Concealment (3) -

Conduct Realistic CCD Training Evaluations
High Priority Source: FM 20 3 Camouflage Concealment and Decoys
Procedure for Conducting Realistic Camouflage, Concealment, and Decoys (CCD) Training Evaluations:

1. Evaluate from an Enemy's Perspective:
- Have small-unit leaders assess their unit's CCD efforts as if they were an enemy.
- Consider...
Procedure for Conducting Realistic Camouflage, Concealment, and Decoys (CCD) Training Evaluations:

1. Evaluate from an Enemy's Perspective:
- Have small-unit leaders assess their unit's CCD efforts as if they were an enemy.
- Consider the following questions:
- Could an approaching enemy detect and place aimed fire on the position?
- From what distance can an enemy detect the position?
- Which CCD principle was ignored that allowed detection?
- Which CCD technique increased the possibility of detection?

2. Use Advanced Equipment for Evaluation:
- Use binoculars, night-vision devices, or thermal imaging to show a unit how it would appear to an enemy.

3. Utilize Visual Documentation:
- Use photographs and videotapes of a unit's deployments and positions as a method of self-evaluation.

4. Incorporate Ground-Surveillance-Radar (GSR) Teams:
- Include GSR teams in training when possible.
- Educate troops on how GSR works and have them attempt to defeat it.

5. Request Aerial Imagery for Assessment:
- Request aerial multispectral (visual, IR, radar) imagery of friendly unit positions.
- This imagery shows how positions appear to enemy aerial reconnaissance.
- Obtain copies of opposing forces (OPFOR) cockpit heads-up display (HUD) or videotapes if available. These are excellent tools for determining detectability from an enemy's perspective.

6. Use Overhead Imagery:

- If participating in large-scale exercises or deployments, access such imagery through the unit's intelligence channels.

7. Incorporate OPFOR for Realism:
- Use OPFOR to make training more realistic.
- Allow supporting aviation to play an OPFOR role when possible.
- Let OPFOR participate in the after-action review (AAR) following each mission.

Establish and Operate an OP During Limited Visibility

Procedure:

1. Assess the Situation:
- The enemy may use a different, more open avenue of approach during limited visibility conditions; therefore, you might have to move the OP to another position at night.

2. **Select an Appropriate Location for the OP:
- Limited visibility OPs are usually closer to defensive positions.
- Ensure that the selected area is within small arms range of the squad or platoon-sized element.
- Choose a site that provides maximum observation of the desired area.

3. Ensure Cover and Concealment:
- Establish the OP in an area that offers cover and concealment.

4. **Set Up Communication:
- Ensure that wire or radio communication is established.
- If using a radio, ensure that the antenna is camouflaged.

5. Establish Concealed Routes:
- Create several concealed routes to and from the OP to avoid revealing its location or endangering personnel.

6. **Camouflage the OP:
- Ensure that the OP is fully camouflaged to avoid detection by enemy forces.

7. **Assign Personnel:
- Place a minimum of two personnel on the OP.

8. **Rotate Duties:
- Instruct the observer and recorder to switch duties every 20 to 30 minutes to maintain alertness and prevent fatigue.

9. **Counter Enemy Infiltration:
- Setting up a series of OPs, backed up by alert troops equipped with night vision devices and snipers, can counter enemy infiltration at night.

2. Avoid firing multiple rounds simultaneously, as this can overload radar systems and reduce their accuracy.

• Radar is highly effective at tracking single rounds but becomes less accurate when processing data on four or more simultaneous rounds.

Rope Installations (3) -

Install a Fixed Rope for Battlefield Movement
High Priority Source: FM 3 97 61 Military Mountaineering
Objective: Install a fixed rope to assist soldiers in moving over difficult terrain.

Procedure:
1. Two experienced climbers should rope up for a roped climb.
2. The leader must have the necessary equipment to rig the anchor at the top of...
Objective: Install a fixed rope to assist soldiers in moving over difficult terrain.

Procedure:
1. Two experienced climbers should rope up for a roped climb.
2. The leader must have the necessary equipment to rig the anchor at the top of the pitch.
3. If protection is being placed, the second climber will establish a belay; otherwise, he will stack and manage the rope.
4. Ensure the rope runs smoothly up the slope and does not get tangled as the climber ascends.
5. Upon reaching the end of the pitch, the leader establishes the top anchor.
6. Once the anchor is rigged, the leader takes up any remaining slack between himself and the second climber.
7. Anchor the installation rope and remain tied into the rope.
8. The second unties from his end of the rope and begins to climb.
9. If the leader placed protection, the second will clean the pitch on his way up.
fixed rope installation, battlefield movement, military mountaineering, rope climbing, anchor rigging
Utilize a Fixed Rope for Ascending Steep Terrain
High Priority Source: FM 3 97 61 Military Mountaineering
Objective: Use a fixed rope to ascend steep or difficult terrain safely.

Procedure:
1. All personnel using the fixed rope should grasp it with the palm downward.
2. Use the rope for assistance as they ascend the slope.
3. To prevent a long...
Objective: Use a fixed rope to ascend steep or difficult terrain safely.

Procedure:
1. All personnel using the fixed rope should grasp it with the palm downward.
2. Use the rope for assistance as they ascend the slope.
3. To prevent a long fall, attach yourself to the rope with a sling using a friction knot (e.g., Prusik or autoblock).
4. Slide the friction knot along the rope as you ascend.
5. If the climber slips and loses control of the rope, the friction knot will grab the rope and arrest the fall.
6. This method is referred to as a self-belay (see Figure 7-2).

Objective: Retrieve a fixed rope after it has been used for movement.

Procedure:
1. If the fixed rope is to be used on the descent, leave it in place and recover it after the last rappel.
2. If not, the last climber will tie into the rope and be belayed from above.
3. The climber can then easily free the rope if it gets caught on anything as it is taken up from the belayer.
