Mountaineering Rigging (3) -

Install an A-Frame Hauling System
High Priority Source: FM 3 97 61 Military Mountaineering
Procedure:

1. Construct and Anchor the A-Frame: If necessary, construct an A-frame and anchor it securely.
2. Prepare Installation Rope: Double one installation rope, find the middle, and lay the middle of the rope over the apex of the...
Procedure:

1. Construct and Anchor the A-Frame: If necessary, construct an A-frame and anchor it securely.
2. Prepare Installation Rope: Double one installation rope, find the middle, and lay the middle of the rope over the apex of the A-frame. Ensure a 30-centimeter (12-inch) bight hangs below the apex.
3. Secure with Clove Hitches: To maintain the 12-inch bight, tie clove hitches above the A-frame lashing on each side of the apex using the installation rope. Ensure that the locking bars of the clove hitches are on the inside and that the portion of the rope forming the bight comes out of the bottom of the clove hitch.
4. Anchor the A-Frame: Use a transport tightening system with the doubled rope, which is tied to the A-frame. Tie this off at an anchor point to the rear of the A-frame installation and adjust the angle so that it leans out over the cliff edge. The angle should be 15 to 25 degrees unloaded. The A-frame should not lean outward more than 45 degrees once loaded, as the legs can lose their position.
5. Create Hauling Line: Tie the ends of another installation rope together with a joining knot to form the hauling line. Attach this rope to the system by two carabiners with gates up and opposed or one mountain rescue pulley with a locking steel carabiner in the 12-inch bight hanging from the apex of the A-frame.
6. Add Fixed Loops: Tie fixed loops (wireman’s, directional figure-eight, or single butterfly) on opposite sides of the endless rope at the loading and unloading platforms.
7. Attach Equipment to Hauling Line: Attach equipment to the hauling line 12 inches above the joining knot by a carabiner in the fixed loop.
8. Additional Fixed Loops for Control: Additional fixed loops may be tied in the hauling line for more control over the object when moving large loads.
9. Attach Personnel: Attach personnel to the hauling line using a rappel seat or seat harness.
10. Special Handling for Objects: Mortar tubes and similar objects are attached to the line by two knots so that the tube stays parallel and as close to the hauling line as possible.
11. Create Knotted Hand Line (for Personnel Movement): Make a knotted hand line; anchor it in line with, or to, the primary anchor (round turn with a bowline); and place it over the spreader on the legs of the A-frame. Space the overhand knots in the knotted hand line 12 inches apart, with about 20 feet of rope without knots at one end for the anchor.
12. Deploy Knotted Hand Line: Throw the knotted hand line over the A-frame spreader rope and down the side of the cliff. Personnel ascending the vertical hauling line use this as a simple fixed rope.
13. Hauling Operations:
- Use as many personnel as needed to pull the load to the top by pulling on the rope opposite the load.
- If equipment and personnel are only being lowered, belay from the top using the hauling line.
- Station two climbers at the unloading platform to retrieve loads.
14. Special Handling for Equipment Only: If only equipment is being hauled up, it is not necessary to use the knotted hand line rope, but it may be necessary to use a belay rope. To move materials or troops up on one side of the hauling line, pull the other side from below.
15. Safety and Maintenance:
- Personnel using the hauling line for movement must apply all related principles of climbing.
- Always station two operators at the top of the vertical hauling line to aid men or retrieve loads when they reach the top. They will always be safetied while working near the edge.
- When in use, the A-frame should lean slightly over the edge of the cliff to prevent excessive wear on the ropes that pass over sharp rocks.
- Reduce excessive friction on the system.
- Remove all obstacles and any loose objects that could be dislodged by personnel and equipment.
A-frame, hauling system, installation rope, clove hitch, transport tightening system, fixed loops, knotted hand line, belay rope, mechanical advantage

Procedure:

Procedure:

1. Assess the Load and Environment: Evaluate the weight of the object, terrain conditions, and available manpower to determine if a simple raising system is appropriate.
2. Select Appropriate Rigging Techniques: Choose rigging techniques that increase mechanical advantage for moving heavy objects with limited manpower.
3. Set Up the System:
- Use ropes, pulleys, and carabiners to create a hauling or lifting system that reduces the effort required to move the load.
- Ensure all components are properly secured and tested before use.
4. Distribute Load Evenly: Position the rigging points so that the weight is distributed evenly across the system to prevent strain on any single component.
5. Use Mechanical Advantage: Utilize pulleys or other mechanical advantage systems (e.g., block and tackle) to reduce the force needed to lift or move the load.
6. Monitor System Performance: Continuously monitor the system during operation for signs of wear, slippage, or failure.
7. Ensure Safety:
- Always use proper safety equipment such as harnesses or belay devices when working with heavy loads.
- Station personnel at key points to assist in moving the load and ensure safe operations.
8. Retrieve Components After Use: Once the task is complete, dismantle the system and store all components for future use.

Dismantle a Vertical Hauling Line System
Standard Source: FM 3 97 61 Military Mountaineering
Procedure:

1. Retrieval of the System: The vertical hauling line is used along a main supply route. When it is no longer needed, the installing unit will return and dismantle the system.
2. Remove Equipment and Personnel: Ensure that...
Procedure:

1. Retrieval of the System: The vertical hauling line is used along a main supply route. When it is no longer needed, the installing unit will return and dismantle the system.
2. Remove Equipment and Personnel: Ensure that all equipment and personnel have been removed from the hauling line before dismantling.
3. Untie Fixed Loops: Remove any fixed loops (wireman’s, directional figure-eight, or single butterfly) tied on opposite sides of the endless rope at the loading and unloading platforms.
4. Disassemble Hauling Line: Untie the joining knot that forms the hauling line and remove it from the system.
5. Remove Carabiners and Pulleys: Detach any carabiners or mountain rescue pulleys used to attach the hauling line to the A-frame.
6. Untie Clove Hitches: Remove the clove hitches tied above the A-frame lashing on each side of the apex using the installation rope.
7. Remove Anchor Rope: Untie the transport tightening system and remove the doubled installation rope from the anchor point at the rear of the A-frame.
8. Disassemble A-Frame: If necessary, disassemble or move the A-frame from its anchored position.
9. Store Components: Securely store all components (ropes, carabiners, pulleys, etc.) for future use.

Evacuation Techniques (3) -

Secure Casualty for Buddy Rappel
Critical Source: FM 3 97 61 Military Mountaineering
Purpose: Secure an injured casualty to a rappeller’s back for a buddy rappel down a steep cliff.

Materials Required:
• A 4.2-meter sling rope
• Padding (optional)

Steps:
1. Tie Standard Rappel Seat: The carrier ties a standard...
Purpose: Secure an injured casualty to a rappeller’s back for a buddy rappel down a steep cliff.

Materials Required:
• A 4.2-meter sling rope
• Padding (optional)

Steps:
1. Tie Standard Rappel Seat: The carrier ties a standard rappel seat (brake hand of choice, depending on the injury) and rests his hands on his knees while the victim straddles his back.
2. Place Sling Rope Tail: A 45-centimeter tail of the sling is placed on the victim’s left hip (this method describes a seat-hip rappel with right-hand brake).
3. Route Remaining End Under Buttocks and Over Hip: The remaining long end of the sling rope is routed under the victim’s buttocks, passed over the victim’s and carrier’s right hip.
4. Run Diagonally Across Carrier's Chest and Shoulder: The rope is run diagonally from right to left across the carrier’s chest, over his left shoulder, and back under the victim’s left armpit.
5. Run Horizontally Across Victim's Back: The rope is then run horizontally from left to right across the victim’s back, passed under the victim’s right armpit and over the carrier’s right shoulder.
6. Run Diagonally Across Carrier's Chest and Hip: The rope is run diagonally from right to left across the carrier’s chest and back across the carrier’s and victim’s left hip.
7. Tie Ends Together with Square Knot: The two rope ends should now meet. Tie them together with a square knot and overhand knots, positioning the knot on the victim’s left hip.
8. Pad Shoulders if Necessary: The carrier’s shoulders may need to be padded to prevent cutting by the rope.

Alternate Methods:
• Use two pistol belts hooked together and draped over the carrier’s shoulders. Secure the loose ends under the victim’s buttocks.
• Use a large rucksack slit on the sides near the bottom so that the victim can step into it. The victim is belayed from the top with the carrier conducting a standard rappel.

Notes:
• A casualty secured to a carrier as described above can be rappelled down a steep cliff using a seat-hip or seat-shoulder rappel.
• If a seat-shoulder rappel is used, ensure that both the casualty’s and rappeller’s shoulders are padded where the sling rope and rappel lines cross.
• The buddy team should be belayed from above with a bowline tied around the victim’s chest under his armpits. The belay rope must run over the rappeller’s guide hand shoulder.
buddy rappel, evacuation, injured casualty, military mountaineering, rappelling techniques
Perform Rope Coil Carry
High Priority Source: FM 3 97 61 Military Mountaineering
Purpose: Transport an injured casualty using a rope coil carry in mountainous terrain.

Materials Required:

2....
Purpose: Transport an injured casualty using a rope coil carry in mountainous terrain.

Materials Required:
• A 36 1/2-meter coiled rope
• Padding (optional)

Steps:
1. Position the Casualty: Place the casualty on his back.
2. Separate Loops of Coil: Separate the loops on one end of the coil, forming two almost equal groups.
3. Secure Legs with Loops: Slide one group of loops over the casualty’s left leg and the other group over the right leg. The wraps holding the coil should be in the casualty’s crotch, with the loops on the other end extending upward toward the armpits.
4. Position Bearer Between Legs: The bearer lies on his back between the casualty’s legs and slides his arms through the loops.
5. Move Forward to Extend Coil: The bearer moves forward until the coil is extended.
6. Grasp Casualty's Arm and Roll Over: Grasping the casualty’s arm, the bearer rolls over (toward the casualty’s uninjured side), pulling the casualty onto his back.
7. Stand Up Carefully: Holding the casualty’s wrists, the bearer carefully stands, using his legs to lift up and keeping his back as straight as possible.
8. Secure with Sling Rope (Optional): A sling rope around both the casualty and bearer, tied with a joining knot at chest level, helps keep an unconscious victim upright and prevents the coils from slipping off the carrier’s chest.

Notes:
• The length of the coil and the height of the bearer must be considered. If the coils are too long and the bearer is shorter, the rope must be uncoiled and recoiled with smaller coils to prevent the casualty from hanging too low on the bearer’s back.
• A sling-rope harness can be used around the victim’s back and bearer’s chest, which frees the bearer’s hands.
rope coil carry, evacuation, injured casualty, military mountaineering
Perform Sling-Rope Carry
High Priority Source: FM 3 97 61 Military Mountaineering
Purpose: Transport an injured casualty in mountainous terrain using a sling-rope carry.

Materials Required:
• A 4.5-meter sling rope
• Padding (optional)

Steps:
1. Position the Bearer and Casualty: The bearer kneels on all fours....
Purpose: Transport an injured casualty in mountainous terrain using a sling-rope carry.

Materials Required:
• A 4.5-meter sling rope
• Padding (optional)

Steps:
1. Position the Bearer and Casualty: The bearer kneels on all fours. The assistant places the casualty face down on the bearer’s back, ensuring the casualty’s armpits are even with the bearer’s shoulders.
2. Place Sling Rope Between Shoulders: The assistant finds the middle of the sling rope and places it between the casualty’s shoulders.
3. Secure Ends Under Armpits and Over Bearer's Shoulders: The assistant runs the ends of the sling rope under the casualty’s armpits, crosses them, and runs them over the bearer’s shoulders and back under the bearer’s arms.
4. Secure Around Thighs and Tie Knot: The assistant runs the ends of the rope between the casualty’s legs, around the casualty’s thighs, and back to the front of the bearer. The rope is tied with a square knot with two overhand knots just above the bearer’s belt buckle.
5. Ensure Tightness and Padding: The rope must be tight. If available, padding should be placed where the rope passes over the bearer’s shoulders and under the casualty’s thighs.

Notes:
• This method can be used for both conscious and unconscious casualties.
• Ensure that the bearer is strong enough to carry the weight of the casualty.
sling-rope carry, evacuation, injured casualty, mountainous terrain, military mountaineering

Military Tactics Skating (3) -

Column Movement on Skis
Standard Source: FM 31 70 Basic Cold Weather Manual
Procedure for Column Movement on Skis:

1. Command: The command is given as *COLUMN RIGHT (LEFT), MARCH.*
2. Leading Man Action: At the command *MARCH*, the leading man takes a full step forward, then turns as in facing on skis, except...
Procedure for Column Movement on Skis:

1. Command: The command is given as *COLUMN RIGHT (LEFT), MARCH.*
2. Leading Man Action: At the command *MARCH*, the leading man takes a full step forward, then turns as in facing on skis, except that at each step a short slide forward is made.
3. Fourth Step: The fourth step is of full length in the new direction.
4. Succeeding Men Follow: Succeeding men follow in the trace of the leading man.
5. For COLUMN HALF RIGHT (HALF LEFT): The same procedure is followed, except that the second step is of full length in the new direction.

Notes:
• This movement is used to change direction while maintaining column formation on skis.
column movement, ski tactics, cold weather military, tactical skiing
Flanking Movement From Normal Interval on Skis
Standard Source: FM 31 70 Basic Cold Weather Manual
Procedure for Flanking Movement From Normal Interval on Skis:

1. Command: The command is given as *RIGHT (LEFT) FLANK AT INTERVAL, MARCH.*
2. Step 1 - Pivot and Slide Forward: At the command *MARCH*, the right (or left) flank man pivots...
Procedure for Flanking Movement From Normal Interval on Skis:

1. Command: The command is given as *RIGHT (LEFT) FLANK AT INTERVAL, MARCH.*
2. Step 1 - Pivot and Slide Forward: At the command *MARCH*, the right (or left) flank man pivots on the heel of his right (or left) ski 45° to the right (or left), and slides slightly forward on that ski.
3. Step 2 - Bring Opposite Ski Parallel: The left (or right) ski is brought up parallel to the right (or left) ski, allowing this ski also to slide slightly forward.
4. Repeat First Movement: Repeat the first movement (pivoting and sliding on the right or left ski).
5. Repeat Second Movement: Repeat the second movement (bringing the opposite ski parallel and sliding forward).
6. Normal Pace in New Direction: After completing these steps, take a normal pace in the new direction.
7. Synchronization with Line: As the right (or left) flank man takes his third step, the next man starts his first step. This procedure is followed by each man in line until the entire unit is marching in the new direction at ski intervals.

Notes:
• Flanking to the left is executed in the same manner, except that the left flank man starts the movement with his left foot.
• Ensure all skiers are synchronized and follow the lead of the flanking individual.
flanking movement, ski tactics, cold weather military, tactical skiing, military skiing procedures

Procedure for Marching to the Rear on Skis:

1. Command 1 - Halt: The first command is *HALT*.
2. Command 2 - About Face: After halting, the second command is *ABOUT FACE*, which is executed as described in paragraph C-23.
3. Command 3 - Forward March: Once the about face has been completed, the third command is *FORWARD MARCH*.
4. Execution of Movement: Follow the forward march command to continue movement in the new direction (toward the rear).

Notes:
• Each movement must be completed before the next command is given.
• Ensure proper synchronization between skiers during this maneuver.

Procedure for Striking with a Baton in Defensive Situations:

1. Hold the baton correctly: Grip it firmly near the middle with both hands.
2. Assess the threat level: Determine if striking is necessary and appropriate based on the situation.
3. Use controlled strikes:
- Aim for non-lethal areas such as arms, legs, or torso.
- Avoid targeting vital organs unless absolutely necessary for self-defense.
4. Apply force with precision:
- Use short, quick motions to increase accuracy and effectiveness.
- Focus on striking vulnerable spots like the temple, throat, or wrists.
5. Maintain control of the baton: Never let go during a confrontation.
6. Use follow-up strikes if needed: If the threat persists, continue using controlled strikes until the situation is under control.
7. Secure the individual: Once the threat is neutralized, use the baton to restrain or hold the person in place until backup arrives.
8. Stay alert and ready to move: Be prepared to retreat or advance as needed during the encounter.

3. Use blocking techniques:
- Raise the baton to block incoming strikes or blows.
- Use the side of the baton for better impact resistance.
4. Apply pressure to vulnerable areas: Aim for sensitive spots such as the temple, throat, or wrists when necessary.
5. Strike with controlled force:
- Target non-lethal areas if possible (e.g., arms, legs).
- Avoid striking vital organs unless absolutely necessary for self-defense.
6. Maintain control of the baton: Never let go of it during a confrontation.
7. Use the baton to restrain: If needed, use it to apply pressure or hold an individual in place until backup arrives.
8. Stay alert and ready to move: Be prepared to retreat or advance as the situation demands.
baton, defense, tactical, self-defense, security

Procedure for Using a Baton in Restraint Situations:

1. Hold the baton correctly: Grip it firmly near the middle with both hands.
2. Assess the threat level: Determine if restraint is necessary based on the situation.
3. Approach with caution: Move in slowly and avoid sudden movements that could provoke an attack.
4. Use verbal commands: Clearly state your intent to restrain, e.g., "I need to subdue you now!"
5. Apply pressure to vulnerable areas:

8. Release safely: Once the threat is neutralized, release the individual carefully and ensure their safety.

Understand the Concept of Marine Corps Leadership
Standard Source: MA 1.02 USMC Fundamentals of Martial Arts
### Understanding Marine Corps Leadership

Marine Corps leadership is a fundamental aspect of being a Marine, transcending rank and billet. Every Marine must be prepared to assume leadership responsibilities at any time, as even two Marines together...
### Understanding Marine Corps Leadership

Marine Corps leadership is a fundamental aspect of being a Marine, transcending rank and billet. Every Marine must be prepared to assume leadership responsibilities at any time, as even two Marines together will have one who is senior.

Key Points:
• Leadership Philosophy: All Marines are considered leaders, from private to commandant.
• Training Begins Early: Leadership development starts during recruit or Officer Candidate School (OCS) training through lectures, examples set by Drill Instructors and Officers, and practical application.
• Leadership Assignments: Recruits and officer candidates are assigned roles such as guides, squad leaders, and other leadership billets to introduce them to the concept of Marine Corps leadership.

Importance of Leadership:
• The primary goal is to instill in all Marines that they are warriors first, with a commitment to fight and win the Nation’s battles while maintaining professionalism.
• Objectives include mission accomplishment and troop welfare. Marines must do whatever it takes to complete missions, guided by the Core Value of commitment.

Leadership Traits and Principles:
• Leadership traits are essential for developing the character of a warrior.
• Leadership principles guide leaders on what they should be doing when applying leadership.
• Marine Corps Core Values further guide the leader in their actions and decisions.

Conclusion:
• It is not enough to simply learn about these guides; Marines must live them and apply them at all times.
marine corps leadership, leadership training, warrior ethos, core values, mission accomplishment, troop welfare, commitment

Military Conduct (3) -

Maintain Professional Boundaries to Prevent Fraternization
Standard Source: MA 1.02 USMC Fundamentals of Martial Arts
### Purpose
To maintain good order and discipline, promote mutual respect between juniors and seniors, prevent adverse impact on a junior's response to orders or the senior's exercise of command, and preserve the integrity of the chain of...
### Purpose
To maintain good order and discipline, promote mutual respect between juniors and seniors, prevent adverse impact on a junior's response to orders or the senior's exercise of command, and preserve the integrity of the chain of command.

### Key Issue
Whether a relationship has developed in which mutual respect of grade is ignored. This includes:
• Relationships that are not necessarily male-female.
• Normal social or business relationships between Marines within the following six divisions do not constitute fraternization, unless under specific instructor-student circumstances:
- General officers
- Field grade officers
- Company grade officers (including warrant officers)
- Staff noncommissioned officers
- Noncommissioned officers
- Junior enlisted Marines
• Improper relationships within the same chain of command are most obvious, but not required for fraternization to occur.

### Military Standards
The military services demand a regard for authority by juniors towards their seniors. This is enhanced by observing decorum, tradition, custom, usage, and conventions unique to the services. Failure to observe these niceties lessens respect for authority.
fraternization,military conduct,chain of command,professional boundaries,USMC regulations
Responsibility for Maintaining Professional Conduct
Standard Source: MA 1.02 USMC Fundamentals of Martial Arts
### Senior Responsibility
The responsibility for maintaining customary and traditional standards of conduct lies with the senior. The line between acceptable conduct and fraternization will not be crossed unless the senior allows it to happen.

###...
### Senior Responsibility
The responsibility for maintaining customary and traditional standards of conduct lies with the senior. The line between acceptable conduct and fraternization will not be crossed unless the senior allows it to happen.

### Leader's Role
Leaders must avoid even the perception of fraternization while preserving the traditional fraternal bond between Marines of all grades.

### Education
Educate your Marines about both the Marine Corps policy on fraternization and the reasons behind it. Ensure they understand that respect for authority is essential to unquestioned obedience in time of battle.

### Avoid Favoritism
If we expect our Marines to respect us, there can't be even the hint of favoritism. Lax attitudes toward fraternization weaken the chain of command and reduce discipline when it matters most.
leadership,military conduct,respect for authority,favoritism,USMC regulations
Understanding the Impact of Fraternization on Professionalism
Standard Source: MA 1.02 USMC Fundamentals of Martial Arts
### Daily Operations
Marines operate in various stages of the continuum of force and may face challenges to professionalism. Regardless of the situation, Marines must act professionally whether in humanitarian missions or when dealing with fellow...
### Daily Operations
Marines operate in various stages of the continuum of force and may face challenges to professionalism. Regardless of the situation, Marines must act professionally whether in humanitarian missions or when dealing with fellow Marines.

### Warrior Ethos
Fraternization is counter to the warrior ethos. Regulations against fraternization ensure that relationships between Marines are professional and productive.

### Band of Brothers
As warriors, Marines will share common experiences regardless of rank, binding them into a 'band of brothers.' Fraternization serves only to loosen or cut these ties.

Deploy for an Area Ambush

Objective: Deploy troops in two or more related point ambushes to attack an enemy force.

Steps:
1. Select multiple kill zones that are concealed and offer good fields of fire against the enemy's route.
2. Position assault elements within each kill zone, ensuring they are hidden from view but can engage the enemy effectively.
3. Place security elements around each kill zone to detect enemy movement and provide early warning.
4. Ensure coordination between ambush points so that all units can react simultaneously on the leader's signal.
5. Rehearse the ambush plan thoroughly to ensure all Soldiers understand their roles in multiple ambush points.
6. Wait for the enemy to enter the kill zones, then initiate the ambush on the leader's signal.

Notes: In an area ambush, Soldiers deploy in two or more related point ambushes.
area ambush, multiple kill zones, tactical coordination
Deploy in an L-Shaped Ambush Formation
High Priority Source: SH 21 76 Ranger Handbook
Objective: Deploy troops using an L-shaped ambush formation to attack an enemy force.

Steps:
1. Position the assault element along the long leg, parallel to the enemy's direction of movement along the kill zone.
2. **Place the support...
Objective: Deploy troops using an L-shaped ambush formation to attack an enemy force.

Steps:
1. Position the assault element along the long leg, parallel to the enemy's direction of movement along the kill zone.
2. Place the support element at one end of the short leg, forming a right angle with the assault element.
3. Ensure both elements are concealed but can provide flanking fire (long leg) and enfilading fires (short leg) against the enemy.
4. Use terrain features such as sharp bends in trails, roads, or streams to deploy this formation effectively.
5. Avoid using this formation where the short leg would have to cross a straight road or trail.
6. Rehearse the ambush plan thoroughly to ensure all Soldiers understand their roles and actions on the leader's signal.
7. Wait for the enemy to enter the kill zone, then initiate the ambush on the leader's signal.

Notes: In an L-shaped ambush, the assault element forms the long leg parallel to the enemy's direction of movement along the kill zone. The support element forms the short leg at one end of and at right angles to the assault element.
L-shaped ambush formation, flanking and enfilading fire, terrain utilization

Standard Source: STP 21 1 Warrior Skills Level 1

Steps to Evaluate Soldier Task Performance:

1. Review performance measures: Become familiar with the criteria on which you will score the Soldier.

2. Ensure equipment and clothing are available: Make sure all necessary equipment, clothing, and safety gear are present at the training site.

3. Prepare the test site: Set up the site according to the conditions section of the task summary. If there are special evaluation instructions, follow them to modify job conditions as needed.

4. Reset the site after each evaluation: After evaluating a Soldier, return the site to its original condition to ensure consistency for all Soldiers being evaluated.

5. Advise Soldiers of special guidance: Inform each Soldier of any specific guidance from the evaluation preparation section before beginning the evaluation.

6. Score based on performance measures: Use the information in the performance measures and evaluation guidance to score each Soldier. Record the date of training and task performance score (GO or NO GO) in the Soldier's training records.

7. Conduct an after-action review (if applicable): Allow participants to reflect on what happened, why it happened, and how it can be improved. Link key points to future training and make appropriate notes for inclusion into the score.

8. Determine GO or NO GO status:
- Score the Soldier GO if all performance measures are passed.
- Score the Soldier NO GO if any step is failed.
- If a Soldier fails any step, explain what was done wrong and how to correct it.

Load an MK19 Machine Gun with Linked 40-mm Grenade Ammunition
High Priority Source: STP 21 1 Army Warrior Skills Level 1 Soldiers Manual of Common Tasks
Conditions: Given a can of linked 40-mm grenade ammunition and a cleared MK19 machine gun mounted on an M3 tripod or on a vehicle. (If firing from a vehicle, the ammunition can bracket must be attached to the gun mount.)

Standards: Load...
Conditions: Given a can of linked 40-mm grenade ammunition and a cleared MK19 machine gun mounted on an M3 tripod or on a vehicle. (If firing from a vehicle, the ammunition can bracket must be attached to the gun mount.)

Standards: Load linked ammunition through the feed throat into the feeder so that when the cover is closed, the round is straight and firmly seated against the bolt and the ammunition feeds correctly.

Performance Steps:
1. Make sure the chamber is empty, the bolt is in the forward position, and the charger handles are in the up (lock) position.
2. Make sure the safety switch is in the safe (S) position.

WARNING: Do not let the top cover slam shut from the open position. Injury to personnel or damage to equipment could result.

3. Insert the first round:
- a. Open the top cover and insert the first round through the feed throat into the feeder, link opening first (figure 071-030-0005-1).
- b. Push or slide the round across the first set of feeder pawls, making sure the round is straight and firmly seated against the bolt (figure 071-030-0005-2).
- c. Index the feed slide assembly to the left and close the top cover (figure 071-030-0005-3).

4. Charge the weapon:
- a. Grasp the charger handles palms down.
- b. Press the charger handle locks and rotate the charger handles down.
- c. Pull the charger handles sharply to the rear until the bolt seats.
- d. Push the charger handles forward and rotate them up into the lock position.

5. Load the first round:
- a. Place the safety switch in the fire (F) position and press the trigger. The bolt will move forward and load the first round on the bolt face (half load).
- b. Rotate the charger handles down and pull them sharply to the rear until the bolt seats. This pulls the bolt with the loaded round into position for firing (full load).
- c. Place the safety switch in the safe (S) position.
- d. Push the chargers forward and rotate the charger handles up into the lock position. The weapon is fully loaded.
- e. Leave the safety switch on the safe (S) position until ready to fire.
MK19 machine gun,loading procedure,ammunition handling,tactical firearms

### Procedure: Mount an AN/PAQ-4-Series Aiming Light on an M4 or M4A1 Carbine

#### Conditions
Given a cleared M4 or M4A1 carbine and an AN/PAQ-4-series aiming light, and a rail grabber mount.

#### Standards
Attach and secure the AN/PAQ-4 to the M4 or M4A1 carbine without damage to equipment.

#### Steps
1. Make sure that the weapon is clear and on SAFE before proceeding.
2. Fully loosen the rail grabber mount knob on the side of the mount.
3. Turn the ON/OFF switch counterclockwise (CCW) to the #1 OFF/STORAGE position.
4. Position the aiming light on the bracket mounting rail.
5. Hand tighten the thumbscrew to secure the aiming light.

#### Evaluation Preparation
• Setup: At the test site, provide all equipment and materials given in the task condition and statement.
• Brief Soldier: Tell the Soldier to mount the AN/PAQ-4-series aiming light on an M4 or M4A1 carbine.

Procedure:

1. Preparation for Breaking Ampoules:
- Before breaking any glass ampoules (except heater ampoules), place one heater pad on each side of the sampler-detector covering the ampoule to be broken.
- These pads will prevent pieces of glass from cutting your gloves and hands.

2. Positioning the Sampler-Detector:
- Hold the sampler-detector with the test spots and the arrow pointing up.
- Crush the four center ampoules marked "3."

3. Handling Nerve-Agent Test Spots:
- Note: Nerve-agent test spots may be difficult to wet with the solution as the kit gets older.
- Work solutions into the spot carefully while pressing the protective strip over the nerve-agent test spot.

4. Adjusting the Sampler-Detector:
- Turn the sampler-detector so that the arrow points down.
- Using the heater pads, squeeze the ampoules to force the liquid through the formed channels onto the test spots.

5. Protective Thumb Placement:
- Hold the sampler-detector with the arrow pointing down, and hold your thumb on the protective strip over the middle test spot.

6. Swinging Heater Away from Blister Test Spot:
- Swing the heater away from the blister test spot.

Procedure:

1. Avoiding Hot Vapors:
- Avoid hot vapors that may burn you when crushing the heater ampoules.
- Hold the sampler-detector to one side while venting it to avoid hot vapors.

2. Do Not Use Heater Pads on Green Heater Ampoules:
- Do not use the heater pads to crush the green heater ampoules marked "4."

3. Activating Heater Ampoule Marked 4:
- Activate the first heater ampoule marked "4" by crushing one green ampoule.

4. Applying Gentle Pressure to Heater Assembly:
- Apply only a slight amount of pressure to hold down the heater assembly to avoid damaging the blister spot.

5. Avoiding Glove Contact with Sampling Spots:
- Do not touch any of the sampling spots with your glove while holding the heater assembly.

6. Using Heater Assembly Pads for Protection:
- Place one of the heater assembly pads on top of the heater assembly while holding it down on the test spot in order to provide an added level of protection.

Military Fire Support (3) -

Calculating Deviation Corrections Using the OT Factor
High Priority Source: STP 21 24 Warrior Leader Skills Level 2 3 4
Objective: Calculate deviation corrections using the observer-target (OT) factor.

Steps:
1. Measure horizontal deviation in mils, either via binocular reticle or hand measurement.
2. Estimate range to target, then divide by 1,000 to...
Objective: Calculate deviation corrections using the observer-target (OT) factor.

Steps:
1. Measure horizontal deviation in mils, either via binocular reticle or hand measurement.
2. Estimate range to target, then divide by 1,000 to calculate the OT factor:
- If OT distance is 1,000 meters or greater: round to whole number (e.g., 2,500 = 2.5 → 3).
- If OT distance is less than 1,000 meters: use decimal value (e.g., 800 = 0.8).
3. Multiply the deviation in mils by the OT factor to get correction in meters.
4. Apply corrections for both range and deviation:
- Example: If a round impacts 50 mils left at an OT distance of 2,000 meters (OT = 2), then 50 × 2 = 100 meters left.
5. Combine range and deviation corrections in the transmission to FDC (e.g., "Right 100, Drop 400, Over").
OT factor, deviation correction calculation, military fire support, range correction
Range Bracketing Guidelines for Fire Support Adjustments
High Priority Source: STP 21 24 Warrior Leader Skills Level 2 3 4
Objective: Establish a range bracket based on estimated round impact distance.

Steps:
1. Estimate the distance between the target and where the round impacted.
2. Use the following guide to establish a bracket:

Objective: Establish a range bracket based on estimated round impact distance.

Steps:
1. Estimate the distance between the target and where the round impacted.
2. Use the following guide to establish a bracket:
- If the round is more than 400 meters from the target, add or drop 800 meters.
- If the round is more than 200 but less than 400 meters from the target, add or drop 400 meters.
3. Apply these corrections to start successive bracketing procedures.
4. Continue adjusting until a 100-meter bracket is split or correct spotting is observed.
range bracketing, fire support adjustment, military tactics, correction guidelines
Successive Bracketing Procedure for Fire Support Adjustments
High Priority Source: STP 21 24 Warrior Leader Skills Level 2 3 4
Objective: Apply successive bracketing to adjust fire support rounds.

Steps:
1. Identify the first round impact and determine if it is over, short, left, or right of the target.
2. If the round is beyond the target, calculate how...
Objective: Apply successive bracketing to adjust fire support rounds.

Steps:
1. Identify the first round impact and determine if it is over, short, left, or right of the target.
2. If the round is beyond the target, calculate how far beyond (e.g., 250 meters) and drop by twice that distance (e.g., 400 meters) to start successive bracketing.
3. If the round is short of the target, add enough to get an over on the next round.
4. For example: A round impacts 50 mils left at a range of 2,100 meters (OT = 2). Deviation correction = 50 × 2 = 100 meters left. Range correction = drop by 400 meters to start bracketing.
5. Transmit corrections to FDC in the format: "Right [X], Drop [Y], Over".
6. Continue splitting the range bracket until a 100-meter bracket is split or correct spotting is observed, maintaining deviation on line.
successive bracketing, fire support adjustment, military tactics, range correction

Procedure:

1. Boundaries show the areas of tactical responsibility:
- In the offense, these are called *zones of action*.
- In the defense and retrograde, they are called *sectors of responsibility*.

2. When describing boundaries verbally:
- In the offense, describe lateral boundaries from rear to front.
- In the defense and retrograde, describe lateral boundaries from front to rear.

3. Use rear boundaries when you must precisely define the area of responsibility for forward units.
4. If no rear boundary is delineated, determine the rear limit by visualizing a rear boundary drawn generally parallel to the front, along a natural terrain feature, and connecting at the rearward limit of the unit's lateral boundaries.
5. Mark the rear boundary as shown in figure 071-332-5000-1 (not included here).
6. Ensure that the size shown along the boundary corresponds to the low unit.
7. Show the arm or branch as needed to prevent confusion.

Conduct a Spider and Fly Game
Standard Source: Boy Scout Handbook 1911
Objective: To develop observation and stealth skills.

Setup:
1. Select an area about a mile square as the 'web' and define its boundaries.
2. Set a time limit for operations (e.g., two hours).
3. Divide participants into two groups: one...
Objective: To develop observation and stealth skills.

Setup:
1. Select an area about a mile square as the 'web' and define its boundaries.
2. Set a time limit for operations (e.g., two hours).
3. Divide participants into two groups: one group is the 'spider,' and the other is the 'fly.' The spider hides, while the fly searches for them.
4. Assign an umpire to each group to oversee the game.

Procedure:
1. The spider selects a hiding spot within the defined area.
2. The fly patrol begins searching 15 minutes later and must report any discoveries to their leader.
3. If the fly does not find the spider within the time limit, the spider wins.
4. The spider records the names of any members of the fly patrol they see during the game.

Notes:
• This activity encourages teamwork, observation, and stealth.
• It can be adapted for different age groups and skill levels.

Procedure:

2. If the instructor sees a scout, they signal them to stand up as having failed.
3. After a set time, the instructor calls out 'time.' All scouts must remain where they are and the one closest to the instructor wins.

2. Observe how their visibility changes depending on background color.
3. For example:
- A boy in a gray suit is visible against dark bushes but less so against gray rocks or houses.
- A boy in a dark suit is visible in a green field but not when standing in an open doorway with shadow behind.
4. The rest of the patrol should observe and note how the scout becomes more invisible with suitable background matching.

a. When throwing the grappling hook, stand as close to the building as possible (this reduces exposure to enemy fire and reduces the throwing distance to the target). Before moving, select a point to enter a building. There are several ways to enter a building above the first floor:

• The second Soldier moves forward and places his/her foot inside of...
a. One-Soldier lift support:

• The first Soldier braces his/her back or side against the building.
• He/she then cups his/her hands together to assist the second Soldier.
• The second Soldier moves forward and places his/her foot inside of the first Soldier's cupped hands.
• The first Soldier then lifts the second Soldier up to the opening.
• Once the first Soldier reaches the point of entry, he/she enters, keeping the lowest silhouette possible (figure 071-326-0542-4).

b. Two-Soldier lift support:

• Two Soldiers face each other, holding a support such as a board or tree limb (figure 071-326-0542-5).
• A third Soldier climbs onto the support.

Ammunition Handling (2) -

Ammunition Handling in Cold Weather Conditions
Standard Source: Canadian Military Basic Cold Weather Training
Procedure:

1. Maintain temperature consistency:
- Keep ammunition at the same temperature as weapons.
- Carry ammunition in bandoliers, with additional rounds stored in the pockets of the outer parka and rucksack.

2. **Clean and...
Procedure:

1. Maintain temperature consistency:
- Keep ammunition at the same temperature as weapons.
- Carry ammunition in bandoliers, with additional rounds stored in the pockets of the outer parka and rucksack.

2. Clean and inspect regularly:
- Ensure that ammunition clips and magazines are cleaned of all oil and preservatives.
- Check frequently for any signs of damage or degradation.
- Remove ice and condensation from ammunition components to prevent malfunctions.

3. Proper storage: Store ammunition in its original container, raised off the ground, and covered with a tarpaulin to protect it from moisture and snow.

4. Marking for identification: Clearly mark ammunition containers so they can be easily located after a snowfall.

5. Propellant considerations:
- Severe cold affects the burning rate of propellent charges, which may cause weapons zeroed in temperate conditions to fire low in extreme cold due to slower combustion.
- Rocket bombs may burn unevenly in severe cold, leading to wobbling and reduced accuracy.
cold weather, ammunition storage, propellant burn rate, weapon zeroing, military, snow conditions

Arctic Operations (2) -

Arctic Operations Concept - Mobility and Air Support

Arctic Operations Concept - Mobility and Air Support

Operations in the arctic must be simple and highly mobile because of the vast distances, the low population density, and the hostile environment. The key to operations in the arctic is air...
Arctic Operations Concept - Mobility and Air Support

Operations in the arctic must be simple and highly mobile because of the vast distances, the low population density, and the hostile environment. The key to operations in the arctic is air mobility from strategic aircraft to helicopters and small fixed wing aircraft. The disadvantages in the use of most means of ground transportation are such as to give top priority both tactically and administratively to aerial movement. Aerial assaults either by air dropping or air landing men and equipment will be the norm.

- Snowshoes may be required during the final assault in deep snow conditions.

In northern operations there usually are no continuous fronts. Units may operate independently many miles apart. Installations are isolated, and communications, where they exist, are long and vulnerable to attack. Surprise is always a possibility, and security can only be guaranteed by accurate knowledge of enemy dispositions, composition, movement capabilities, and constant vigilance. The primary task of long-range patrols will be reconnaissance and raids on isolated positions and in enemy rear areas.

These patrols may form part of the harassment campaign discussed in the previous chapter or:

• a. As diversions during an attack;
• b. To prevent the movement of enemy reserves;
• c. To force further the dispersion of enemy forces;
• d. To impose a presence in contested territory; and
• e. As part of stay-behind forces in the event of a withdrawal.

Procedure for Camouflaging Vehicles:

1. Responsibility: It is the responsibility of the section to camouflage vehicles either in position or in a cache.
2. Camouflage Techniques: Use natural materials such as branches and foliage to cover or erase vehicle tracks.
3. Track Placement: Ensure that tracks are as close as possible to hedges, fences, cultivated fields, and other natural lines on the ground, and parallel to them to avoid detection from above.
4. Track Continuation: Tracks should extend beyond a position and be part of a well-planned track system.
5. Excavator Use: If an excavator is available, it can significantly reduce the time required for burying combat vehicles, support vehicles, and equipment, as well as digging trenches.

Define Strategic Level of War

The strategic level of war is the level at which a nation, often as a member of a group of nations, determines national or multinational (alliance or coalition) strategic security objectives and guidance, and develops and uses national resources to accomplish these objectives. ### Construct a Rappel Seat Using Sling Rope

Steps:
1. Find the middle of the sling rope and make a bight.

### Construct a Rappel Seat Using Sling Rope

A rappel seat is an improvised harness made from a sling rope (minimum 14 feet). Follow these steps to create it:

Steps:
1. Find the middle of the sling rope and make a bight.
2. Decide which hand will be used as the brake hand and place the bight on the opposite hip.
3. Reach around behind and grab a single strand of rope. Bring it around the waist to the front and tie two overhands on the other strand of rope, thus creating a loop around the waist.
4. Pass the two ends between the legs, ensuring they do not cross.
5. Pass the two ends up under the loop around the waist, bisecting the pocket flaps on the trousers. Pull up on the ropes, tightening the seat.
6. From rear to front, pass the two ends through the leg loops creating a half hitch on both hips.
7. Bring the longer of the two ends across the front to the non-brake hand hip and secure the two ends with a square knot safetied with overhand knots. Tuck any excess rope in the pocket below the square knot.

### Check Points:
• There are two overhand knots in the front.
• The ropes are not crossed between the legs.
• A half hitch is formed on each hip.
• Seat is secured with a square knot with overhand safeties on the non-brake hand side.
• There is a minimum 4-inch pigtail after the overhand safeties are tied.
rappel seat, sling rope, knot tying, improvised harness, mountaineering

1. **Place a bight of rope into the two anchored carabiners...
### Tie a Guarde Knot (Alpine Clutch)

The guarde knot is used for hauling systems or rescue operations and works in only one direction, cannot be reversed while under load.

Steps:
1. Place a bight of rope into the two anchored carabiners (works best with two like carabiners, preferably ovals).
2. Take a loop of rope from the non-load side and place it down into the opposite carabiner so that the rope comes out between the two carabiners.

### Check Points:
• When properly dressed, rope can only be pulled in one direction.
• The knot will not fail when placed under load.

Objective: Create dummy positions to mislead the enemy without endangering real positions.

Procedure:
1. Construct dummy positions such as tents, weapons, vehicles, and bivouac areas using available materials (e.g., snow, branches, canvas).
2. Ensure that these dummy positions are camouflaged and not obviously artificial.
3. Position dummy positions far enough from real positions to avoid endangering personnel if fire is directed at them.
4. Make dummy bivouac areas appear occupied by using small flames (e.g., gasoline or oil) to simulate stoves or idling engines.
5. Use fire or smoke in a bivouac area to create the illusion of occupation.

Details:
• Dummy positions must be part of a well-coordinated deception plan and follow tactical guidelines.
• Avoid creating obvious signs that could reveal the presence of dummy positions.

Tactical use of ice demolitions includes:

1. Protection from attacks: Used to protect against frontal or flanking enemy attacks.
2. Charge placement strategy:
- Place one or more sets of charges close to the friendly shore.
- Place additional charges farther out in the direction of the enemy (see figure 6-36).
3. Trapping technique: Allow the enemy to advance past the first set of charges and detonate both at the same time, trapping them on an ice floe.
4. Application against armor: Same method can be used to trap enemy armor or detonate charges directly under advancing tanks.
5. Observation and security: Ice demolitions must be kept under observation and secured by friendly fire.

Firebase Construction (2) -

Constructing an Artillery Firebase - Phase I: Combat Assault and Initial Clearing
High Priority Source: FM 5 103 Survivability
Objective: Secure the firebase site and clear an area large enough to accommodate CH-47 and CH-54 helicopters if the site is inaccessible by ground vehicle.

Steps:
1. Secure the Site: Conduct a combat assault on the firebase site to...
Objective: Secure the firebase site and clear an area large enough to accommodate CH-47 and CH-54 helicopters if the site is inaccessible by ground vehicle.

Steps:
1. Secure the Site: Conduct a combat assault on the firebase site to establish initial control.
2. Clear Area for Helicopter Access: Clear an area sufficient for helicopter operations, especially if the site is not accessible by ground vehicles.
3. Assess Terrain Conditions: If the site is free of trees and undergrowth, or if these obstacles were removed by artillery and tactical air fire preparation, proceed immediately to Phase II after the initial combat assault.
4. Clear Foliage and Trees: If the site is covered with foliage and trees, security forces and combat engineers must descend into the site from hovering helicopters.
5. Initial Clearing: Use demolitions and chain saws to clear the site of obstacles. Depending on the density of the foliage, this phase may take up to 3 hours.

Notes:
• The time required for Phase I depends heavily on terrain conditions.
• Dedicated engineer support is essential for all phases of firebase construction.
artillery firebase, phase I, combat assault, initial clearing, terrain assessment, foliage removal
Constructing an Artillery Firebase - Phase II: Immediate Construction
High Priority Source: FM 5 103 Survivability
Objective: Begin immediate construction of the firebase to establish a tenable tactical position by nightfall on the first day.

Steps:
1. Deploy Airmobile Dozers: Two light airmobile dozers are lifted to the site and used to clear brush...
Objective: Begin immediate construction of the firebase to establish a tenable tactical position by nightfall on the first day.

Steps:
1. Deploy Airmobile Dozers: Two light airmobile dozers are lifted to the site and used to clear brush and stumps, expanding the perimeter and clearing howitzer positions.
2. Expand Perimeter with Engineers: Combat engineers continue to expand the perimeter using chain saws, demolitions, and bangalore torpedoes.
3. Deploy Heavy Airmobile Dozer (if applicable): If enough area is available, a heavy airmobile dozer is committed to clear a logistics storage area and sling-out pad, then expand the perimeter and fields of fire.
4. Excavate Protective Positions: Backhoes are used to excavate protective positions for the infantry TOC, artillery FDC, and perimeter fighting positions as soon as the perimeter trace is established.
5. Coordinate Efforts: Coordinate efforts among infantry, artillery, and engineer forces to ensure a tenable tactical position by nightfall on the first day.
6. Prepare Site Plan and Priorities: Prepare and constantly update a coordinated site plan and list of priorities for transportation and construction. These are established by the tactical commander in coordination with the project engineer.
7. Focus on Defensive Construction: As soon as a perimeter trace is set up and the site can accept logistics and artillery lifts, direct maximum effort toward defending the firebase.
8. Push Back Undergrowth: Combat engineers and heavy dozers continue to push back undergrowth to ensure adequate fields of fire.
9. Construct Parapet: The two light airmobile dozers construct a 5 to 8 foot thick parapet around the perimeter to protect against direct fire.
10. Build Perimeter Fighting Positions: Infantry troops construct perimeter fighting positions at sites previously excavated by backhoes, with assistance from combat engineers.
11. Install Tactical Wire: With the help of combat engineers, infantry troops begin placing the first band of tactical wire, usually triple standard concertina.
12. Construct Ammunition Storage Positions: Artillery troops not immediately committed to fire missions prepare ammunition storage protective positions and parapets around each howitzer.

Notes:
• Immediate construction is a coordinated effort among infantry, artillery, and engineer forces.
• A site plan and list of priorities must be prepared and updated continuously.
artillery firebase, phase II, immediate construction, perimeter expansion, parapet construction, tactical wire installation

Unarmed Combat (2) -

Unarmed Combat Defense Against Knife Attacks
Standard Source: FMFRP 12 80 USMC Kill or Get Killed
Procedure for Defending Against a Knife Attack with Unarmed Techniques:

1. Assess the threat immediately: Recognize that an individual is armed with a knife.
2. Create distance if possible: Move away from the attacker to reduce the risk...
Procedure for Defending Against a Knife Attack with Unarmed Techniques:

1. Assess the threat immediately: Recognize that an individual is armed with a knife.
2. Create distance if possible: Move away from the attacker to reduce the risk of injury.
3. Use verbal commands: Clearly state your intent to de-escalate the situation, e.g., "I don't want to hurt you!"
4. Defensive stance: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, knees slightly bent, and body weight shifted forward for stability.
5. Block incoming strikes:
- Use arms or hands to block the knife if necessary.
- Avoid using bare hands directly; use clothing or other objects as a barrier if available.
6. Use evasive movements: Step back or move sideways to avoid being struck by the blade.
7. Apply pressure to vulnerable areas:
- Target sensitive spots such as the eyes, throat, or wrists with strikes or grabs.
8. Maintain control of the situation: If possible, use techniques like grappling or joint locks to subdue the attacker until backup arrives.
knife defense, unarmed combat, tactical, self-defense, security

4. Defensive stance: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, knees slightly bent, and body weight shifted forward for stability.
5. Apply strikes to vulnerable areas:
- Target sensitive spots such as the eyes, throat, or wrists with controlled blows.
6. Use grappling techniques: If necessary, use holds or joint locks to subdue the attacker.

8. Secure the individual: Once the threat is neutralized, use techniques like holding or restraining until backup arrives.

Procedure: Construct a Hasty Fighting Position

Conditions: Given load-carrying equipment (LCE) with bayonet, scabbard, entrenching tool, poncho, and M16A1 rifle; a specific location and sector of fire; and logs to construct overhead cover.

Standards: 1. Construct a hasty fighting position that gives frontal cover from enemy direct fire and allows you to fire to the front and oblique.
2. Construct a one-Soldier fighting position wide enough for you and your equipment, armpit deep, with frontal and overhead cover at least 18 inches deep, with grenade sumps, and with a floor sloped toward the sumps. Ensure that the position allows you to place fire on your assigned sector.

Steps:
1. Select a hasty fighting position that—
- Is behind whatever cover is available.
- Provides frontal protection.
- Allows you to shoot to the front and at an oblique angle.
- Is in a small depression or a hole at least 18 inches deep.
2. In whatever time you have, improve your position by digging or scraping out a prone shelter that gives you some protection (figure 071-3265703-1).

Notes:
• The term 'hasty position' does not preclude digging.
• This procedure is intended for immediate use in combat situations where time is limited.
hasty fighting position, combat survival, military construction

Rifle and Shotgun Retention Technique - Under-Handed Grab
High Priority Source: MA 1.02 USMC Fundamentals of Martial Arts
Technique if Person Grabs Weapon Under-handed:

1. Slide your left hand up the hand guards, trapping the opponent's closest finger above the knuckle with your thumb so they cannot release their grip.
2. Apply **bone pressure on the...
Technique if Person Grabs Weapon Under-handed:

1. Slide your left hand up the hand guards, trapping the opponent's closest finger above the knuckle with your thumb so they cannot release their grip.
2. Apply bone pressure on the opponent's finger to initiate pain compliance.
- Bone pressure is the application of pressure on a bone against a hard object (e.g., the weapon) to initiate pain compliance.
- It is very painful when pressure is applied to the fingers against the hardness of the weapon, particularly on the handguards of the rifle.
3. While maintaining pressure on the opponent's hand, step back with your right foot.
4. At the same time, lower the muzzle and raise the buttstock of the weapon in a swimming motion to redirect the opponent to the rear of the Marine executing the technique.
5. These actions drive the person to the deck where they can be further controlled or cause them to release their grip on the weapon.
6. If the opponent releases the weapon, pull the rifle into your shoulder into the ready weapons carry aiming at the opponent.
under-handed grab, bone pressure, pain compliance

Front Breakfall from a Kneeling Position

1. Assume a two-kneed kneeling position.
2. Bend your elbows and place your palms facing out in the position that will allow you to spread and absorb the impact of the fall.
3. Fall forward, breaking your fall with your forearms and palms. The forearms and hands, down to the fingertips, should strike the deck simultaneously. Fingers and thumb will be extended and joined.
4. Offer resistance with your forearms and hands to keep your head raised off the deck.

Executing a Side Breakfall from a Standing Position
Reference Source: MA 1.02 USMC Fundamentals of Martial Arts
Side Breakfall from a Standing Position

1. Assume a standing position with the feet shoulder width apart.
2. Bring your right arm across your body so your hand is next to your left shoulder with your palm facing inboard.
3. Fall on your right...
Side Breakfall from a Standing Position

1. Assume a standing position with the feet shoulder width apart.
2. Bring your right arm across your body so your hand is next to your left shoulder with your palm facing inboard.
3. Fall on your right side by sliding your right foot to the left and collapse to the right onto your right thigh, buttocks, and lat muscle.
4. Break your fall with your right arm, slapping the deck, making contact from your shoulder or forearm down to your hand. The arm should strike the deck at a 45° angle with respect to your body. At the same time, tuck your chin and keep your head raised off the deck.
5. To spread and absorb the impact, stretch out your right leg to make contact with the deck. Bend your left leg and make contact with the deck with your foot.
6. Practice this step as many times as necessary to ensure proper arm placement to break the fall.

### Planning Fire Support Operations
Planning is the continual process of selecting targets on which fires are prearranged to support a phase of the commander’s plan. The principles of planning follow:

• Consider what the commander wants to do.
• Plan early and continuously.
• Exploit all available targeting assets.
• Use all available lethal and nonlethal fire support means.
• Use the lowest echelon able to furnish effective support.
• Observe all fires.
• Use the most effective fire support asset available.
• Provide adequate fire support.
• Avoid unnecessary duplication.
• Provide for safety of friendly forces and installations.
• Provide for flexibility.
• Furnish the type of fire support requested.
• Consider the airspace.
• Provide rapid and effective coordination.
• Keep all fire support informed.

Ambush Operations (2) -

Conduct a Hasty Ambush
High Priority Source: Ranger Handbook 2006
Objective: Conduct a hasty ambush to engage an enemy force.

Steps:
1. Alerting the Unit:
- A Soldier uses visual signals to alert the unit that an enemy force is in sight.
- The Soldier continues monitoring the location and...
Objective: Conduct a hasty ambush to engage an enemy force.

Steps:
1. Alerting the Unit:
- A Soldier uses visual signals to alert the unit that an enemy force is in sight.
- The Soldier continues monitoring the location and activities of the enemy until relieved by the team or squad leader, who provides the enemy’s location and direction of movement.

2. Halting and Positioning:
- The platoon or squad halts and remains motionless.
- The Patrol Leader (PL) gives the signal to conduct a hasty ambush without alerting the enemy.
- The leader determines the best nearby location for the ambush, using arm-and-hand signals to direct unit members to covered and concealed positions.

3. Establishing the Kill Zone:
- The leader designates the location and extent of the kill zone.

4. Moving to Positions:
- Teams and squads move silently to covered and concealed positions, ensuring they are undetected and have good observation and fields of fire into the kill zone.

5. Security Elements:
- Security elements move out to cover each flank and the rear of the unit.
- The leader directs security elements to move a given distance, set up, and rejoin the unit on order or after the ambush (when firing ceases).
- At squad level, the two outside buddy teams provide flank security as well as fires into the kill zone. At platoon level, fire teams make up the security elements.

6. Assigning Sectors of Fire:
- The PL assigns sectors of fire and issues any other necessary commands such as control measures.

7. Initiating the Ambush:
- The PL initiates the ambush using the greatest casualty-producing weapon available when the largest percentage of the enemy is in the kill zone.
- The PL:
- Controls the rate and distribution of fire.
- Employs indirect fire to support the ambush.
- Orders cease fire.
- If necessary, orders the patrol to assault through the kill zone.

8. Processing Enemy Personnel and Equipment:
- The PL designates personnel to conduct a hasty search of enemy personnel and process enemy prisoners and equipment.

9. Withdrawing from the Ambush Site:
- The PL orders the platoon to withdraw from the ambush site along a covered and concealed route.

10. Reorganization and Reporting:
- The PL gains accountability, reorganizes as necessary, disseminates information, reports the situation, and continues the mission as directed.
hasty ambush, ambush tactics, kill zone, security elements, patrol leader, fire distribution, enemy engagement

4. Withdraw from Objective:
- The patrol withdraws all personnel and equipment from the objective on order, within the time specified in the order.

5. Obtain PIR and Continue Operations:

- Continue follow-on operations as directed.

Purpose: Create a visual terrain model to aid in patrol planning and communication of routes and actions on the objective.

Materials Needed:
• Cardboard or paper (e.g., 3 x 5 card, MRE box)
• String, colored tape, or yarn
• Moss, green/brown spray paint, pine needles, crushed leaves, grass
• Blue chalk, blue spray paint, blue yarn, tin foil, MRE creamer
• Sharpened twigs, pencils, or colored yarn for north-seeking arrows
• Red yarn, M-16 rounds, toy Rangers, poker chips for enemy positions
• M-16 rounds, toy Rangers, poker chips, small MRE packets for friendly positions
• Small pieces of cardboard or paper for target reference points and indirect fire targets
• Colored string/yarn for key phase lines and trench lines
• Spiral notebook for perimeter wire
• Tongue depressors/sticks for bunkers/buildings

Steps:
1. Create a checklist to ensure all necessary elements are included:
- North-seeking arrow
- Scale
- Grid lines (use string or colored tape, labeled with numbers)
- Objective location
- Exaggerated terrain relief and water obstacles
- Friendly patrol locations
- Targets (indirect fires, including grid and type of round)
- Routes: primary and alternate
- Planned RPs (ORP, L/URP, RP)
- Danger areas (roads, trails, open areas)
- Legend for all symbols used
- Blowup of objective area
2. Construct the terrain model using field-expedient techniques:
- Use a 3 x 5 card or MRE box to label the objective or key sites.
- Create grid lines with string from 550 cord or colored tape, labeled with numbers on small pieces of paper.
- Replicate trees and vegetation using moss, green/brown spray paint, pine needles, crushed leaves, or cut grass.
- Designate water obstacles with blue chalk, blue spray paint, blue yarn, tin foil, or MRE creamer.
- Mark the north-seeking arrow with sharpened twigs, pencils, or colored yarn.
- Use red yarn, M-16 rounds, toy Rangers, or poker chips to represent enemy positions.
- Represent friendly positions (security elements, support by fire, assault elements) using M-16 rounds, toy Rangers, poker chips, small MRE packets of sugar and coffee, or pre-printed acetate cards.
- Use small pieces of cardboard or paper to identify target reference points and indirect fire targets. Ensure grids are shown for each point.
- Mark breach, support by fire, and assault positions with colored yarn or string for easy identification.
- Construct bunkers and buildings using MRE boxes or tongue depressors/sticks.
- Create perimeter wire from a spiral notebook.
- Use colored string or yarn to mark key phase lines.
- Replicate trench lines by digging a furrow and coloring it with colored chalk or spray paint.
3. Ensure all symbols are clearly identified in the legend for clarity during briefings.

Danger Area Crossing (2) -

Crossing a Linear Danger Area (LDA) as a Platoon
Critical Source: SH 21 76 Ranger Handbook
### Step-by-Step Procedure for LDA Crossing by a Platoon:

STEP 1: The lead squad halts the platoon and signals the presence of a danger area.

STEP 2: The platoon leader moves forward to confirm the danger area, determining whether...
### Step-by-Step Procedure for LDA Crossing by a Platoon:

STEP 1: The lead squad halts the platoon and signals the presence of a danger area.

STEP 2: The platoon leader moves forward to confirm the danger area, determining whether the current location is a suitable crossing site.

STEP 3: The platoon leader confirms the danger area and establishes near and far side rally points for coordination.

STEP 4: On the platoon leader’s signal, A team of the lead squad establishes an overwatch position to the left of the crossing site. Prior to crossing, the compassman with the lead two squads confirms azimuth and pace data.

STEP 5: B team of the lead squad establishes an overwatch position to the right of the crossing site.

STEP 6: Once overwatch positions are established, the platoon leader gives the second squad in movement the signal to bound across by fire team.

STEP 7: Once across, the squad becomes the lead in movement and continues on azimuth.

STEP 8: After conducting SLLS (Stop, Look, Listen, Smell), the squad leader signals the platoon leader that it is all clear:
• Daytime: Use a hand and arm signal such as thumbs up.
• Nighttime: Use a clandestine signal, such as an IR or red lens.

STEP 9: The platoon leader receives the all-clear signal and crosses with the radio operator, FO (Forward Observer), WSL (Weapons Squad Leader), and two gun teams.

STEP 10: Once across, the platoon leader signals the third squad in movement to cross.

STEP 11: The PSG (Platoon Sergeant) with the medic and one gun team crosses after the second squad is across, sterilizing the central crossing site.

STEP 12: The PSG signals the security squad to cross at their location.

### Notes:
• The platoon leader must plan for fires at all known LDA crossing sites.
• Nearside security in overwatch will sterilize signs of the patrol, ensuring no trace is left behind.
platoon lda crossing,overwatch positions,slls,sterilizing site,fire planning

• Open areas

2. Move all personnel and equipment across the danger area safely.
3. Avoid decisive engagement by the enemy during crossing.

2. Secure the near side, left and right flanks, and rear security before crossing.
3. Reconnoiter and secure the far side of the danger area prior to movement.

Surveillance (2) -

Conduct Day and Night Surveillance for Enemy Detection
High Priority Source: STP 21 1 Warrior Skills Level 1
Procedure for Conducting Day and Night Surveillance

Overview: This procedure outlines how to conduct effective day and night surveillance to detect enemy soldiers and vehicles.

### Day Surveillance Steps:
1. **Identify Improperly...
Procedure for Conducting Day and Night Surveillance

Overview: This procedure outlines how to conduct effective day and night surveillance to detect enemy soldiers and vehicles.

### Day Surveillance Steps:
1. Identify Improperly Camouflaged Enemy Soldiers:
- Look for inconsistencies in camouflage patterns or unnatural movements.
- Focus on fighting positions where enemies may be hiding.
2. Differentiate Between Wheeled and Tracked Vehicles:
- Observe the shape and movement of vehicles.
- Wheeled vehicles typically have a more rounded profile, while tracked vehicles are more angular.

### Night Surveillance Steps:
1. Detect Moving Enemy Soldiers:
- Use night vision devices or natural light sources (e.g., moonlight).
- Watch for silhouettes against the skyline or unnatural movement patterns.
2. Identify Stationary Enemy Soldiers:
- Look for heat signatures using thermal imaging if available.
- Pay attention to subtle changes in terrain or shadows that may indicate a hidden soldier.

### Additional Notes:
• Frequent training is essential to master this skill, as it is difficult to detect the use of surveillance techniques without practice.
• Become familiar with common field environment sounds (e.g., vehicles, weapons fire) and smells (e.g., gasoline, campfires, deodorants).

### Evaluation Criteria:
• During day surveillance: Identify 50% of improperly camouflaged enemy soldiers in fighting positions and differentiate between wheeled and tracked vehicles.
• During night surveillance: Identify moving and stationary enemy soldiers.
surveillance, enemy detection, day and night, tactical training, camouflage identification

2. Ensure Anchor Availability: There must be good primary and secondary anchors above the departure point.
3. Check for Platforms: Ensure suitable loading and off-loading platforms are available at the site.
4. Equal Tension on Anchors: Distribute tension evenly between all anchor points to prevent failure.
5. Use Double Rope When Possible: Employ double rope systems if feasible to increase safety.
6. Verify Rope Length: Ensure that ropes extend to the off-loading platform.
7. Secure Personnel Near Edges: Tie in personnel working near edges for added safety.
8. Select a Safe Route: Choose a smooth route free of loose rock and debris.

Warnings:
• Poor site selection can lead to anchor failure or injury.
• Always inspect the area for hazards before setting up.

Combat Movement (2) -

Move Under Direct Fire as a Two-Man Team
High Priority Source: STP 21 1 Army Warrior Skills Level 1 Soldiers Manual of Common Tasks
### Moving Under Direct Fire

As a member of a two-man team, you must approach an enemy position from a distance of 250 to 300 meters across varied terrain. You will be equipped with an M16A1 rifle or M203 grenade launcher and load-carrying...
### Moving Under Direct Fire

As a member of a two-man team, you must approach an enemy position from a distance of 250 to 300 meters across varied terrain. You will be equipped with an M16A1 rifle or M203 grenade launcher and load-carrying equipment (LCE). The objective is to move within 100 meters of the enemy position while using correct individual tactical fire and movement techniques.

### Implementation Steps
1. Select a movement route within your team's or squad's axis of advance, ensuring it allows for cover and concealment.
2. Coordinate with your teammate to ensure synchronized movement and covering fire.
3. Use tactical fire techniques (e.g., controlled bursts, suppressive fire) as dictated by terrain features.
4. Move in a low profile, using natural cover and concealment to avoid exposure.
5. Maintain communication with your teammate throughout the approach.
6. Provide covering fire for each other when necessary, ensuring both members can advance safely.
7. Continue moving until within 100 meters of the enemy position or until the mission is complete.

### Notes
• This task requires precise coordination and discipline to avoid exposure and maintain tactical advantage.
• Always be aware of your surroundings and adjust movement based on terrain features.
direct fire movement, two-man team, tactical approach, enemy position, cover and concealment
Moving Across Open Areas with Precautions
High Priority Source: STP 21 1 Warrior Skills Level 1
Procedure for Moving Across Open Areas with Precautions:

Objective: Reduce exposure to enemy fire when moving across open areas.

Steps:
1. Conduct a Visual Reconnaissance of the Area and Position:
- Assess potential threats,...
Procedure for Moving Across Open Areas with Precautions:

Objective: Reduce exposure to enemy fire when moving across open areas.

Steps:
1. Conduct a Visual Reconnaissance of the Area and Position:
- Assess potential threats, cover/concealment options, and possible enemy positions.
2. Select a Route with Cover or Concealment:
- If no natural cover is available, use smoke or covering fire provided by other members of your element to reduce exposure.
3. Move Directly and Rapidly to the Selected Position:
- Minimize time in the open area to reduce the chance of being targeted.
- Moving rapidly denies the enemy the opportunity for accurate targeting.
4. Maintain Covering Fire During Movement:
- Ensure that covering fire is not masked during your movement.
5. Be Ready to Cover Others When Reaching Your Position:
- Once in position, prepare to cover the movement of other members of your fire team or squad (see figure 071-326-0541-2).
6. Move in Groups if Necessary:
- If two or more Soldiers must move at the same time:
- Prepare the group to position themselves for movement.
- Use a planned signal to initiate movement simultaneously.
- Maintain approximately 5 meters between each Soldier during movement (see figure 071-326-0541-3).
7. Move Parallel to Buildings:
- When possible, move parallel to buildings to reduce exposure and increase the likelihood of finding cover.

Purpose: To clear a narrow lane of fire while maintaining concealment of the defensive position.

Steps:

2. Leave a thin natural screen of vegetation to hide the defensive position and avoid revealing your location through excessive or careless clearing.

- Start near your position, working forward.
- Work in an irregular pattern so as not to reveal the weapon's position.
- Prune trees forward of your position:
- Remove lower branches of large trees in wooded areas.
- Cover cuts on trees and bushes with mud, dirt, or snow.
- Remove or thin dense brush (brush is never a suitable obstacle and obstructs field of fire).
- Cut weeds only where they obstruct your view.
4. Drag away cut brush, limbs, and weeds to points where they will not be detected by the enemy or provide concealment.
5. Ensure no trails are made in your sector of fire as lanes are cleared.

Notes: Proper clearing ensures optimal field of fire while maintaining concealment.

Steps to Sketch Terrain on a Range Card:

1. Roughly sketch the terrain in front of the position on the range card.
- Center the machine gun position at the bottom of the sketch.
2. Include any prominent natural and man-made features that a target could use to take cover.
3. Determine the location of the gun position relative to a prominent terrain feature:
- Use a hilltop, road junction, or building (either a man-made or natural terrain feature).
- If no such feature exists within 1,000 meters of the gun, write in the eight-digit map coordinates for your position near the gun position on the sketch.
4. Use a compass to determine the azimuth in mils or degrees from the terrain feature to the gun position or from the gun position to the terrain feature.
- Compute the back azimuth from the gun to the feature by adding or subtracting 3,200 mils or 180 degrees.
5. Determine the distance between the gun and the feature by pacing or looking at a map.
6. Draw the terrain feature in the lower left- or right-hand corner of the card, whichever better shows the terrain feature's position relative to the gun.
