• To Assemble: Replace in reverse order, ensuring that the indentation on the side of the wind guard containing the control valve stop rod is placed over the control valve handle.

Details for Cook Stand:
• The cook stand includes a wind guard with a small rod acting as a control valve stop.
• Extension arms can be swung outwards and locked into slots in the wind guard to support cooking utensils.

Steps for Generator:
• To Strip:
- Remove the cook stand.
- Remove the burner head.
- Unscrew the jamb nut with the cup attached and lift off.
- Keep the control valve handle at the OFF position.
- Lift up the generator tube far enough to see the lower end of the automatic cleaning needle.
- Disengage this needle from the hole in the eccentric block.
• To Assemble:
- Pull down the lower or hooked end of the cleaning needle.
- With the control valve handle at the OFF position, insert the hooked end of the needle into the hole at the top of the eccentric block.
- Hold the generator upright with one hand and place the jamb nut with attached cup over the top and screw down.
- Tighten with a wrench.

Details for Generator:
• The generator includes an automatic cleaning needle that must be disengaged during stripping.

Steps for Pump Assembly:
• To Strip:
- Unscrew the pump cap clip and remove the pump assembly from the stove.
- To separate the two brass tubes, unscrew the two milled head retaining rings.
- Remove the inner tube from the outer tube.
- To remove the leather pump plunger from the bottom end of the inner tube:
- Unscrew the pump screw and remove the brass washer and pump leather plate.
- The pump leather will now be loose.
- From the top of the inner tube, unscrew the pump handle.
• To Assemble: Reverse the above stripping sequence.

Details for Pump Assembly:
• Spare parts included in the inner tube:
- One rubber washer for sealing the pump assembly to the filling hole.
- One air valve assembly complete with spring.
- One length of graphite.
- One pump leather.
- One generator.
• When packing spare parts, the leather and rubber washers should be packed last.

Conduct and Equip Units for Operations on Permanent Ice and Snow-Covered Areas

Operations on permanent ice and snow-covered areas may be required for the establishment of support facilities, and protection of specialized activities. In such instances operations will normally involve small units but the total effect required...
Operations on permanent ice and snow-covered areas may be required for the establishment of support facilities, and protection of specialized activities. In such instances operations will normally involve small units but the total effect required will be large because of the extreme difficulties of operating in such areas.

Operations on an ice cap are so different from other northern areas that different techniques of operations are required. Troops require specialized training for operations in this area of crevasses and high winds. The absence of usable resources except ice and snow necessitate that every item required must be transported into the operating area. The construction of storage and maintenance shelters from snow and ice is feasible.

Specialized equipment for negotiating the area is required. This equipment will include:
• Oversnow vehicles,
• Tractors,
• Crevasse detectors,
• Trail marking equipment,
• Navigational aids,
• Living wanigans,
• Crampons,
• Ice axes,
• Ropes, and related items.

Rope Tying Techniques (1) -

Fisherman’s Knot and Double Fisherman’s Knot
Standard Source: FM 3 97 61 Military Mountaineering
Procedure for Tying a Fisherman’s Knot and Double Fisherman’s Knot:

Fisherman’s Knot:
1. Take the two ends of the rope and cross them over each other, forming an X.
2. Pass one end under the other and bring it up through the loop on...
Procedure for Tying a Fisherman’s Knot and Double Fisherman’s Knot:

Fisherman’s Knot:
1. Take the two ends of the rope and cross them over each other, forming an X.
2. Pass one end under the other and bring it up through the loop on the opposite side.
3. Repeat this process with the second end, creating a second overhand knot in the opposite direction.
4. Tighten both knots fully, ensuring that they are snug against each other.

Double Fisherman’s Knot:
1. Take the two ends of the rope and cross them over each other, forming an X.
2. Pass one end under the other and bring it up through the loop on the opposite side, creating an overhand knot.
3. Repeat step 2 with the second end, creating a second overhand knot in the same direction as the first.
4. Tighten both knots fully, ensuring that they are snug against each other.

Use: Both knots are used for joining two ropes of similar thickness together, especially in situations where the rope may be wet or slippery.
Warning: These knots can slip if not properly tied or under heavy load.

Roped Climbing Techniques (1) -

Roped Climbing Safety and Techniques
Reference Source: FM 3 97 61 Military Mountaineering
Overview: Roped climbing is essential for steep or difficult terrain where the risk of falling is high. Use this procedure to ensure safe roped climbing:

1. When to Use Ropes:
• Ropes must be used when the angle, length, or difficulty of a...
Overview: Roped climbing is essential for steep or difficult terrain where the risk of falling is high. Use this procedure to ensure safe roped climbing:

1. When to Use Ropes:
• Ropes must be used when the angle, length, or difficulty of a route exceeds the climber's safety margin (typically on class 4 and usually on class 5 terrain).
• Roped climbing is only safe if performed correctly with proper training and practice.

2. Rope Safety:
• A rope is completely useless for climbing unless the climber knows how to use it safely.
• Do not assume that reading this manual equates to skill with ropes; extensive training is required before using ropes in real situations.
• Ropes are generally not used in training until basic climbing principles are covered.

3. Tying-In Procedures:
• Over the years, climbers have developed various knots and procedures for tying-in to the rope.
• Older methods of tying directly into the rope may be easier to inspect but offer little support.

4. Top-Roped Climbing for Training Purposes:
• Top-roped climbing is used for training purposes only. This method of climbing is not used for movement due to the necessity of pre-placing anchors at the top of a climb. If you can easily access the top of a climb, you can easily avoid the climb itself.

### Benefits of Top-Roped Climbing:
• Allows climbers to attempt climbs above their skill level or hone present skills without the risk of a fall.
• Can be used to increase the stamina of a climber training to climb longer routes.
• Useful for a climber practicing protection placements.

### Belayer Positioning:
1. The belayer is positioned either at the base of a climb with the rope running through the top anchor and back to the climber or at the top at the anchor.
2. The belayer takes in rope as the climber moves up the rock, giving the climber the same protection as a belay from above.
3. If this is accomplished with the belayer at the bottom, the instructor is able to keep an eye on the belayer while he coaches the climber through techniques and safety procedures.
roped climbing, safety, military mountaineering, top-roped climbing, training, belayer positioning

Rope Safety And Equipment Use (1) -

Using and Improvising a Full-Body Harness for Safety and Comfort
Reference Source: FM 3 97 61 Military Mountaineering
Full-body harnesses combine the features of both chest and seat harnesses into one assembly, making them the safest option for climbing and rope movement. They are especially useful when carrying heavy packs or in situations where a fall may...
Full-body harnesses combine the features of both chest and seat harnesses into one assembly, making them the safest option for climbing and rope movement. They are especially useful when carrying heavy packs or in situations where a fall may occur.

### Key Features:
• Safety: A full-body harness relocates the tie-in point higher on the body (at the chest), reducing the chance of an inverted position when hanging on the rope.
• Body Positioning: The harness promotes an upright position only when hanging on the rope from the attachment point, but it does not prevent a fall head first during a fall.

### Improvising a Full-Body Harness:
1. Combine Seat and Chest Harnesses: Integrate a chest harness and seat harness into one assembly using a short loop of webbing or rope.
2. Position Tie-In Point at Chest: Ensure the tie-in point is relocated higher, at the chest level, to reduce the chance of an inverted hanging position on the rope.
3. Secure Assembly: Use appropriate knots and carabiners to connect the chest and seat components securely. The two harnesses must be fixed as one piece using webbing or rope for proper function and safety. The weight should be supported by the seat harness through the connecting material.

### Safety Considerations:
• A full-body harness will not prevent head injury in a fall. Body position during a fall is affected by the forces that generated the fall.
• Always ensure that the harness fits correctly and securely before use.
• Simply tying the rope into both harnesses does not create a true full-body harness.
full-body harness, improvised harness, safety, rope movement, military mountaineering

Ice Ax Techniques (1) -

Using an Ice Ax for Self-Arrest and Stability
Reference Source: FM 3 97 61 Military Mountaineering
Procedure:

1. When traveling through steep terrain, soldiers should be trained in the use of the ice ax for self-arrest.
2. The ice ax can be used to arrest a fall on:
- Solid ground
- Grass
- Scree
- Snow
3. It may also be used...
Procedure:

1. When traveling through steep terrain, soldiers should be trained in the use of the ice ax for self-arrest.
2. The ice ax can be used to arrest a fall on:
- Solid ground
- Grass
- Scree
- Snow
3. It may also be used as a third point of contact on difficult terrain.
4. When not in use, the ice ax should be:
- Carried in or on the rucksack with its head down.
- Secured to prevent accidental deployment.
5. Recognize the fall and prepare for self-arrest. If a climber falls, they must first gain control of their body using either the ice ax or brute force to stop any rolling or spinning.
6. Assess your position after the fall. You may end up in one of four positions:
- Head upslope, stomach on the slope, and feet pointed downslope.
- Head upslope, back to the slope, and feet pointed downslope.
- Head downslope, stomach on the slope, and feet pointed upslope.
- Head downslope, back to the slope, and feet pointed upslope.
7. Adjust your body position for self-arrest based on your fall position:
- If in the first position (head upslope, stomach on the slope), you are already in a proper position for arrest.
- If in the second position (head upslope, back to the slope), rotate your body from face up to face down by rolling toward the head of the ax.
- If in the third position (head downslope, stomach on the slope), place the pick of the ice

River Or Stream Crossing Safety (1) -

River or Stream Crossing Safety Procedures
Standard Source: FM 3 97 61 Military Mountaineering
Procedure:

1. Before conducting a river or stream crossing, identify all individuals who are weak swimmers or nonswimmers. Ensure that stronger swimmers are available to provide assistance during the crossing if needed.

2. **Evaluate the...
Procedure:

1. Before conducting a river or stream crossing, identify all individuals who are weak swimmers or nonswimmers. Ensure that stronger swimmers are available to provide assistance during the crossing if needed.

2. Evaluate the river or stream crossing site to determine if it can be crossed safely. Consider factors such as water depth, current speed, bottom configuration, and width of the stream. If a safe crossing is not possible at the selected site, consider crossing at a different time, place, using a different technique, or selecting another route.

3. Post a lookout 50 to 100 meters upstream from the crossing site. The lookout should monitor for any obstacles that may be carried downstream and interfere with the crossing.

4. When a rope installation is required, ensure at least two life vests or other personal flotation devices (PFDs) are available. These should be provided for the strong swimmer who must establish the far anchor and the last person across who retrieves the system.

Order Clarification And Legal Obligations (1) -

Ask a Superior for Clarification of an Order Presumed to be Criminal or Illegal
Standard Source: STP 21 24 Warrior Leader Skills Level 2 3 4 + STP 21 24 Army Warrior Leader Skills Level 2 3 and 4
Procedure:

1. Recognize the situation: If you receive an order that you believe may be criminal or illegal, you must take action.
2. Assess the order: Determine whether it may violate the Law of War, Geneva Conventions, or Hague...
Procedure:

1. Recognize the situation: If you receive an order that you believe may be criminal or illegal, you must take action.
2. Assess the order: Determine whether it may violate the Law of War, Geneva Conventions, or Hague Conventions.
3. Request clarification: You are responsible for asking your superior for clarification regarding the order.
4. Document the request: Ensure that the request is documented in writing if possible, to provide a record of your actions.
5. Follow up: If no clarification is provided or if the order remains unclear, continue to seek guidance from higher authorities until you have sufficient information to make an informed decision.
6. Report concerns: If the order is confirmed to be illegal or criminal, the Soldier must report it through proper channels as outlined in the Law of War procedures.

Important Notes:
• This procedure applies only when there is reasonable suspicion that an order may be illegal or criminal.
• Soldiers are not required to follow orders that they believe violate the Law of War or other legal obligations.
• Failure to seek clarification on a potentially illegal order may result in consequences.
order clarification, illegal orders, Law of War, Geneva Conventions, Hague Conventions, soldier responsibility

Law Of War Procedures (1) -

Procedures for Reporting and Processing Violations of the Law of War
Standard Source: STP 21 24 Warrior Leader Skills Level 2 3 4 + STP 21 24 Army Warrior Leader Skills Level 2 3 and 4
Procedure:

1. Understand CINC guidance: The combatant commander-in-chief (CINC) provides specific guidance for handling suspected or actual violations of the Law of War.
2. Immediate reporting: All suspected violations must be reported...
Procedure:

1. Understand CINC guidance: The combatant commander-in-chief (CINC) provides specific guidance for handling suspected or actual violations of the Law of War.
2. Immediate reporting: All suspected violations must be reported immediately to the appropriate authority (e.g., chain of command, legal officer).
3. Gather and preserve evidence: Collect and maintain all relevant evidence such as photographs, witness statements, or other documentation related to the incident.
4. Follow proper channels: Reports should be submitted through the chain of command or directly to legal authorities, ensuring compliance with established protocols.
5. Ensure no further violations: Prevent additional violations during the investigation process.
6. Legal review and accountability: Ensure that reports are reviewed by legal personnel to determine if a violation has occurred, and follow CINC guidance for investigation protocols and accountability measures.

Important Notes:
• The CINC’s guidance is a critical reference point in processing Law of War violations.
• Compliance with these guidelines ensures that all actions taken are consistent with international law and military regulations.
• In cases involving serious war crimes, reports may be submitted to international tribunals or other legal bodies as appropriate.

War Crimes And Accountability (1) -

Concept of Command Responsibility in War Crimes
Standard Source: STP 21 24 Warrior Leader Skills Level 2 3 4 + STP 21 24 Army Warrior Leader Skills Level 2 3 and 4
Command Responsibility:

• Military commanders are responsible for the actions of their subordinates during combat operations.
• If a commander fails to prevent or punish war crimes committed by subordinates, they may be held personally...
Command Responsibility:

• Military commanders are responsible for the actions of their subordinates during combat operations.
• If a commander fails to prevent or punish war crimes committed by subordinates, they may be held personally accountable.
• This principle ensures that leaders take responsibility for ensuring compliance with international law and the Law of War.

### Describe the Concept of Command Responsibility in Relation to War Crimes

• Definition:
- Command responsibility refers to the legal accountability of a military commander for war crimes committed by subordinates under their command.
• Key Elements:
- The commander must have had effective control over the subordinate who committed the crime.
- The commander knew or should have known that the crime was being committed.
• Consequences:
- Commanders can be held personally responsible for war crimes, even if they did not directly commit them.
- This principle is a cornerstone of international law and ensures accountability at all levels of command.

Combat Training Safety (1) -

Implement Safety Precautions During Combatives Training
High Priority Source: FM 3 25 150 Combatives
To prevent injuries during combatives training, follow these procedures:

Supervision:
• Supervise all practical work closely and constantly. Never leave a group unsupervised.

Instruction and Demonstration:
• Familiarize soldiers with each...
To prevent injuries during combatives training, follow these procedures:

Supervision:
• Supervise all practical work closely and constantly. Never leave a group unsupervised.

Instruction and Demonstration:
• Familiarize soldiers with each maneuver by providing a complete explanation and demonstration before they attempt the moves.
• Do not allow soldiers to get ahead of the instruction.

Training Execution:
• Ensure the training partner offers no resistance, but allows the maneuver to be freely executed during the learning stages and while perfecting the techniques.
• Ensure there is adequate space between soldiers during all practical work. Allow at least an 8-foot square for each pair of soldiers.
• Ensure that soldiers empty their pockets, remove their jewelry, and identification tags before training.

Strikes and Signals:
• Stress that only simulated strikes to vital points (e.g., head, neck, groin) are to be executed. Soldiers may use light blows to other vulnerable areas but must exercise caution at all times.
• Ensure soldiers understand the use of both physical tapping and verbal signals to indicate to the partner when to stop the pressure in grappling and choking techniques.

Warm-Up and Safety:
• Make sure soldiers warm up and stretch properly before practical work.
• Teach and practice falls before conducting throws.

Disarming Techniques:
• Ensure that the soldier to be disarmed does not place his finger in the trigger guard during rifle and bayonet disarming.
• Make sure soldiers keep scabbards on knives and bayonets firmly attached to rifles while learning bayonet disarming methods.
• Use bayonet scabbards or rubber knives during knife disarming training.

Sawdust Pit Safety:
• If utilizing a sawdust pit, inspect all sandbags on the retaining wall before conduct of training. Ensure that all bags are serviceable, at least 75 percent full, and that the entire retaining wall is covered with sandbags.
• Any bag placed where personnel are likely to fall will be filled with the same consistency filler as the sawdust in the pit and will also provide a minimum of 6 inches of sawdust.
• Maintain a buffer zone of 6 feet from the retainer wall and demonstration area during all training, especially training requiring throws and takedowns by students.

Pit Maintenance:
• Rake the training pit to loosen sawdust and remove all sharp objects. Properly inspect the pit so that all safety hazards are removed before instruction or demonstrations are executed.
• Perform inspections of the depth of sawdust with enough time before training to resurface the pit. Remember that new sawdust will need to be raked and inspected for foreign objects that may cause injuries.

Combat Defense (1) -

Defend Against a Rifle with Fixed Bayonet Using an Entrenching Tool (Straight Configuration)
High Priority Source: FM 3 25 150 Combatives
Objective: Use the entrenching tool in its straight position to defend against an attacker wielding a rifle with a fixed bayonet.

Steps:
1. The attacker lunges with a thrust to the stomach of the defender along a low No. 5 angle of attack...
Objective: Use the entrenching tool in its straight position to defend against an attacker wielding a rifle with a fixed bayonet.

Steps:
1. The attacker lunges with a thrust to the stomach of the defender along a low No. 5 angle of attack (see Figure 7-31, Step 1).
2. The defender moves just outside to avoid the lunge and meets the attacker’s arm with the blade of the fully extended entrenching tool (Figure 7-31, Step 2).
3. The defender gashes all the way up the attacker’s arm with the force of both body masses coming together.
4. The hand gripping the entrenching tool is given natural protection from the shape of the handle.
5. The defender continues pushing the blade of the entrenching tool up and into the throat of the attacker, driving him backward and downward (Figure 7-31, Step 3).

Cold Weather Weapons (1) -

Cold Weather Firing Procedures for Recoilless Rifles
High Priority Source: FM 31 70 Basic Cold Weather Manual
Cold Weather Firing Procedures for Recoilless Rifles

• Action Required: When firing recoilless rifles in cold weather:
- Zero the weapon for the specific temperature it is being fired at, as propellants burn slower in cold.
- Allow a...
Cold Weather Firing Procedures for Recoilless Rifles

• Action Required: When firing recoilless rifles in cold weather:
- Zero the weapon for the specific temperature it is being fired at, as propellants burn slower in cold.
- Allow a minimum of 60 seconds between firing and reloading to avoid premature explosion of rounds due to afterburn.

Additional Considerations:
• Ice fog will form during firing; frequently displace the weapon to regain visibility and avoid enemy detection.
• Triple the back blast danger area for safe operations in cold areas compared to temperate zones.
• The Spotter-Tracer Rifle on the 106mm recoilless rifle may have trajectory issues with the main round, requiring careful coordination.
• Metal parts of the spotter rifle are subject to breakage and should be lubricated with LOW or fired dry.

Notes:
• Barrel deformation due to solar radiation can occur if the weapon is foresighted before sunrise. Correct this by boresighting after firing several rounds.
• Crews must not rely entirely on firing tables in low temperatures; adjust based on experience and available data.

Core Values (1) -

Understand and Uphold the Marine Corps Core Values
High Priority Source: MA 1.02 USMC Fundamentals of Martial Arts
The Marine Corps Core Values are Honor, Courage, and Commitment. These values govern the behavior of Marines both on and off the battlefield, and they form the foundation of a Marine’s character.

### Honor
• Marines must be...
The Marine Corps Core Values are Honor, Courage, and Commitment. These values govern the behavior of Marines both on and off the battlefield, and they form the foundation of a Marine’s character.

### Honor
• Marines must be trustworthy. Trust is essential for unit cohesion and combat effectiveness. Once lost, trust is difficult to restore.
• Marines must respect human dignity, recognizing the diversity within the Corps and Nation as a source of strength. This includes respecting other cultures and people even in conflict situations.
• Marines must be accountable. They take responsibility for their actions, duties, and mistakes without blaming others or shirking obligations.

### Courage
• Marines must demonstrate moral courage, which involves making unpopular decisions that are right despite criticism.
• Marines must also display physical courage, facing fear in combat situations to overcome threats.

### Commitment
• Marines must be determined and dedicated to completing missions, even when faced with challenges or the temptation to take shortcuts.
• Commitment leads to professionalism, mastery of the art of war, discipline, pride, concern for others, and excellence in all endeavors.
• It also implies loyalty to the organization, expressed by adhering to Marine Corps requirements and showing discipline 24 hours a day.

These Core Values serve as a moral compass that guides every action a Marine takes. They are essential for character development, leadership, and maintaining the reputation of the Marine Corps as the world’s premier fighting force.
honor,courage,commitment,marine corps core values,tactical discipline,character development

Martial Arts Program (1) -

Provide Brief History of Marine Corps Martial Arts Program
Standard Source: MA 1.02 USMC Fundamentals of Martial Arts
Objective: To provide a brief historical overview of the development of the Marine Corps Martial Arts Program.

1. Historical Development:
- The Marine Corps was born during the battles that created the United States, with a martial...
Objective: To provide a brief historical overview of the development of the Marine Corps Martial Arts Program.

1. Historical Development:
- The Marine Corps was born during the battles that created the United States, with a martial culture unrivaled in the world today.
- The legacy includes fighting prowess and the character and soul unique to Marines.
- From the Continental Marines as sharpshooters on Navy ships to their skill as boarding parties using swords and bayonets, Marines have continued to develop their martial skills through history.

2. World War I:
- The skill of the bayonet was supplemented with training in unarmed techniques to meet the challenges of trench warfare.

3. World War II:
- Exposure to far eastern martial arts systems such as judo and karate influenced Marine training during this period.
- Specialized training based on experiences from the interwar years included systems like Combat Hitting Skills, the O’Niel System, and those of the Marines Raiders.

4. Post-World War II to Vietnam Era:
- Marines tested and refined new techniques, adapting to technologies and innovations of a new generation.
- During the 1970’s and 1980’s, focus was on professional military education and structured leadership training.

5. Development of LINE System:
- The Linear Infighting Neural Override Engagement (LINE) system was developed in response to a perceived need for a standardized close combat system.

6. Marine Corps Close Combat Program:
- In 1996, the Marine Corps Close Combat Program was developed by combining input from 10 subject matter experts (SMEs) from numerous martial arts disciplines with existing programs such as LINE, combat hitting skills, and pugil stick training.

7. Formalization of Core Values Training:
- In 1996, a formalized development of a Core Values training program was also initiated.

8. Vision of General James L. Jones:
- Upon assuming the Commandancy in June 1999, General James L. Jones detailed his vision for the Marine Corps Martial Arts Program.
- The program evolved by combining combat-tested martial arts skills, time-honored Close Combat training techniques, and proven Marine Corps Core Values and Leadership training.
Marine Corps history, LINE system, martial arts development, core values, General James L. Jones

3. If the person lunges at or tries to grab you, block them with your weapon by thrusting it out firmly, with your elbows still bent.

Ranger Communication Guidelines (1) -

Report Accurate Information as a Ranger
High Priority Source: Ranger Handbook 2006

Planning And Execution (1) -

Follow Troop-Leading Procedures (TLP) for Tactical Operations
Standard Source: Ranger Handbook 2006
Procedure:

The troop-leading procedures (TLP) are a set of steps that leaders use to prepare their unit to accomplish a tactical mission. The TLP consists of the following steps, which can be performed in any order or simultaneously:

1....
Procedure:

The troop-leading procedures (TLP) are a set of steps that leaders use to prepare their unit to accomplish a tactical mission. The TLP consists of the following steps, which can be performed in any order or simultaneously:

1. Receive the mission – This may come via warning order, operation order (OPORD), or fragmentary order (FRAGO). Use no more than one-third of available time for planning and issuing OPORD.
2. Issue a warning order – Provide initial instructions that mirror the five-paragraph OPORD format. Include:
- Mission statement
- Time and place for issuance of operation
- Who is participating in the operation
- Timeline of the operation
3. Make a tentative plan – Use METT-TC to develop an estimate of the situation, which will form the basis of your tentative plan.
4. Initiate movement – Begin moving toward the objective based on the tentative plan.
5. Reconnoiter – Conduct a reconnaissance mission or map reconnaissance as needed.
6. Complete the plan – Finalize all aspects of the operation, including coordinating with subordinates and ensuring resources are in place.
7. Issue the complete order – Provide full details to the unit based on the completed plan.
8. Supervise – Monitor execution and ensure that the mission is carried out as planned.
troop leading procedures, TLP, tactical operations, mission planning, warning order, OPORD, FRAGO, reconnaissance, supervision

1. Assess the Situation
- Identify enemy forces, including their weather-related factors (e.g., wind) and terrain features...
Objective: Execute a stream crossing operation with proper planning and coordination.

### Steps:
1. Assess the Situation
- Identify enemy forces, including their weather-related factors (e.g., wind) and terrain features (river width, depth, water temperature, current, vegetation, obstacles).
- Determine friendly forces providing support.
- Note any attachments or detachments.

2. Define the Mission
- Clearly state the objective and purpose of the stream crossing operation.

3. Execute the Operation
- Develop a concept of operation, including:
- Maneuver: Movement strategy and tactics.
- Fires: Use of weapons and fire support.
- Assign tasks to combat units, such as:
- Elements, teams, and individuals involved in the crossing.
- Provide coordinating instructions, including:
- Crossing procedure/techniques (e.g., use of ropes, rafts).
- Security measures during the operation.
- Order of crossing for units and individuals.
- Actions on enemy contact (response plan).
- Develop an alternate plan in case of obstacles or enemy interference.
- Designate rallying points for regrouping.
- Plan for rehearsals to ensure readiness.
- Establish a time schedule for all phases of the operation.

4. Service Support
- Ensure availability of ration, weapons, and ammunition.
- Distribute uniforms and equipment as needed.

5. Command and Signal
- Define the location of patrol leader, assistant patrol leader, and CP (command post).
- Establish emergency signals, including code words for communication.

Fire Adjustment Procedures (1) -

Announce DANGER CLOSE During Fire Adjustments
High Priority Source: Ranger Handbook 2006
When adjusting fire during combat operations, follow these steps:

1. Announce DANGER CLOSE in the Method of Engagement portion of the call for fire when:
- The target is within 600 meters of any friendly troops (for mortars and field...
When adjusting fire during combat operations, follow these steps:

1. Announce DANGER CLOSE in the Method of Engagement portion of the call for fire when:
- The target is within 600 meters of any friendly troops (for mortars and field artillery).
- Adjusting 5-inch or smaller naval guns on targets within 750 meters.
- Adjusting larger naval guns on targets within 1,000 meters.

2. Failure to adhere to these guidelines can result in fratricide, which is the unintentional killing of friendly forces by fire from your own side.

3. Avoid using the bracketing method of adjustment during DANGER CLOSE missions because it increases the risk of injury or death.

4. Use only the creeping method of adjustment during DANGER CLOSE missions.
- Make corrections of no more than 100 meters by creeping the rounds to the target.

Objective: Ensure successful mission accomplishment by using effective land navigation techniques and avoiding detection.

Procedure:
1. Designate primary and alternate compass and pace men for the patrol:
- These individuals are responsible for maintaining accurate direction and distance traveled during movement.
2. Assign responsibilities clearly:
- The point man is solely responsible for forward security; they should not be tasked with compass or pacing duties.
3. Use stealth and terrain advantages to avoid detection:
- Move through cover and concealment as much as possible.
- Use limited visibility conditions (e.g., night) to maximize the use of night vision devices and hinder enemy detection.
4. Time movements strategically:
- Coordinate patrol timing with other operations that may distract or divert the enemy’s attention.
5. Use appropriate movement techniques based on threat level and terrain:
- Fire teams maintain visual contact but remain spaced to avoid full engagement if enemy contact is made.
- Spread formations as needed for better observation of flanks, while maintaining relative positions within wedges or files.
6. Rotate lead squad responsibilities when necessary:
- The platoon leader may rotate the lead squad during long movements to maintain control and reduce fatigue.
7. Assign rear security responsibilities:
- The fire team/squad in the rear is responsible for rear security during movement.

Combat Identification (1) -

Identify Combat Vehicles by Observing Characteristics
High Priority Source: STP 21 1 Warrior Skills Level 1
### Identify Combat Vehicles by Observing Characteristics

Procedure Steps:

1. Observe the vehicle.

2. Observe vehicle characteristics.

3. Compare observed vehicle characteristics with known vehicle attributes. Four areas of...
### Identify Combat Vehicles by Observing Characteristics

Procedure Steps:

1. Observe the vehicle.

2. Observe vehicle characteristics.

3. Compare observed vehicle characteristics with known vehicle attributes. Four areas of characteristics are used to identify vehicles. Most armored vehicles have all four areas of characteristics although not all vehicles do.

- a. Track and suspension system: Many tanks can be recognized by their track and suspension systems. However, recognizing a vehicle by this feature alone is often difficult. Grass, dirt, terrain, dust, or other factors often obscure the tracks. To identify the track and suspension system, check to see whether it has support or return rollers. Few threat vehicles, except the T-10, T-64, T-72, BMD, BMP, SP-122, and SP-152, have either.

- (1) Characteristics of most Warsaw Pact vehicles include a flat Christie suspension system, without support or return rollers, without torsion bars, and with unevenly spaced road wheels.

- (2) Characteristics of most North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) vehicles include a suspended track, support or return rollers, torsion bars, shock absorbers, and evenly spaced road wheels.

- b. Turret: Most turrets can be grouped into three categories:

- (1) Big bulky turrets—older models.

- (2) Well sloped turrets—newer models.

- (3) Streamlined turrets—newer models.

- c. Main gun: Armament varies from machine guns to large cannons. In turreted vehicles, normally the heaviest armament is in the turret. Look for the main gun, the main gun bore evacuator, and its relative location on the main gun.

- (1) Types of main guns:

- (a) Smooth main gun without bore evacuator or blast deflector.

- (b) Main gun with bore evacuator.

- (c) Main gun with bore evacuator and muzzle brake or blast deflector.

- (2) Types of muzzles:

- (a) Single baffle.

- (b) Double baffle.

- (c) Multibaffle.

- d. Cupolas: The cupola is a small, turret-like projection normally on top of the turret, which is used by the vehicle commander. It usually mounts a machine gun.

4. Eliminate any vehicle that lacks an observed, characteristic attribute.

5. Record the actual vehicle.
identify combat vehicles, track and suspension system, turret types, main gun characteristics, cupola identification

Weapon Zeroing (1) -

Zero an M249 Machine Gun
Standard Source: STP 21 1 Army Warrior Skills Level 1 Soldiers Manual of Common Tasks
Conditions: Given an M249 machine gun on a live-fire range or safe terrain; a 300-meter target located 300 meters from the firing position; and a 30-round belt of ammunition.

Standards: Using no more than 30 rounds, adjust the sights on an...
Conditions: Given an M249 machine gun on a live-fire range or safe terrain; a 300-meter target located 300 meters from the firing position; and a 30-round belt of ammunition.

Standards: Using no more than 30 rounds, adjust the sights on an M249 machine gun to correct the sight picture and cause a fired round to impact the target at the point of aim.

Performance Steps:

1. Set sights for initial firing.

a. Elevation: Using the elevation knob, index the known range (300 meters) to the target. Center the peep sight by rotating it clockwise (right) as far as it will go and then rotate it counterclockwise (left) five clicks.

_Note: The elevation range-scale wheel has range settings from 300 to 1,000 meters. The even-numbered range settings are on the left side of the scale wheel and the odd-numbered range settings are on the right._

b. Windage: Rotate the windage knob toward the muzzle until the peep sight is completely to the right and then rotate the windage knob back toward the buttstock 12 clicks to the left. This will place the peep sight in the approximate center of the sight.

2. Assume a good, stable firing position (figures 071-312-4030-2 and 071-312-4030-3).

3. Fire a three-round burst at the center base of the target. Note where the burst strikes.

4. Adjust sights so that the rounds impact the target area.

Title: Identify Visual Indicators of an Improvised Explosive Device (IED)

Description: This procedure outlines the steps for identifying visual indicators of an improvised explosive device (IED) to ensure safety and prevent detonation.

Steps:
1. Look for any suspicious objects or packages that appear out of place in the environment.
2. Check for wires, timers, or other components commonly associated with IEDs.
3. Observe any unusual markings or symbols on objects that may indicate they are explosive devices.
4. Be aware of any signs of tampering, such as broken seals or damaged packaging.
5. Use binoculars or other tools to examine suspicious items from a safe distance.
6. Document all observations and report them immediately to the appropriate authorities.

Notes: This procedure is essential for identifying potential IED threats before they can be activated.

Fire Support Operations (1) -

Spotting and Correcting Deviation in Fire Missions
High Priority Source: STP 21 24 Army Warrior Leader Skills Level 2 3 and 4
Procedure for Spotting and Correcting Deviation in Fire Missions

Steps:
1. Spot each round when it impacts as right or left, over or short of your target.
2. Determine corrections for deviation left or right of the target.
-...
Procedure for Spotting and Correcting Deviation in Fire Missions

Steps:
1. Spot each round when it impacts as right or left, over or short of your target.
2. Determine corrections for deviation left or right of the target.
- Measure deviation using the reticle pattern in binoculars or hand measurement.
- Calculate horizontal angle in mils.
- Estimate range to the target and divide by 1,000 to get the observer-target (OT) factor:
- If OT distance is 1,000 meters or greater, express the OT factor as a whole number.
- If OT distance is less than 1,000 meters, express the OT factor to the nearest 1/10th (e.g., 800 = 0.8).
- Multiply the OT factor by the deviation in mils to get correction in meters.
3. When the first range spotting is observed, make a range correction that would result in a range spotting in the opposite direction.
- Example: If the first round is short, add enough to get an over on the next round (called successive bracketing).
4. Continue splitting the range bracket until a 100-meter bracket is split or range correct spotting is observed, maintaining deviation on line.
5. Transmit corrections to the FDC in meters:
- The initial correction should bracket the target in range.
- Keep rounds on the observer-target line during adjustment phase.
6. Use the following guide to establish a bracket:
- If estimated round impact distance is more than 400 meters, add or drop 800 meters.
- If estimated round impact distance is more than 200 but less than 400 meters, add or drop 400 meters.

Example:
• Target at 2,100 meters. Round impacts 50 mils left of the target with an OT factor of 2 (OT distance = 2,100 meters). Deviation correction is 100 meters left (50 mils × 2). Range correction: drop 400 meters to start successive bracketing. Correction to FDC: Right 100, Drop 400, Over.

Warning:
• DO NOT BRACKET when DANGER CLOSE—it could result in friendly casualties; use the creeping fire procedure (all corrections are 100 meters or less).
spotting, deviation correction, fire mission, bracketing, OT factor, FDC, tactical operations

Protective Equipment Testing (1) -

Conduct a Mask Fit Test Using the M41 Protection Assessment Test System (PATS)
Standard Source: STP 21 24 Warrior Leader Skills Level 2 3 4
Conditions: You are given an M41 PATS; M17-, M40-, M42- or M45-series protective masks; PATS operator's manual; TC 3-41; DA Form 2404 (_Equipment Inspection and Maintenance Work Sheet_ ), and any of the following situations:

1. You are directed...
Conditions: You are given an M41 PATS; M17-, M40-, M42- or M45-series protective masks; PATS operator's manual; TC 3-41; DA Form 2404 (_Equipment Inspection and Maintenance Work Sheet_ ), and any of the following situations:

1. You are directed by the commander to conduct a mask fit test.
2. You have a Soldier(s) who requires an initial issue, an annual verification, or a replacement mask issue.

Note: This task will not be performed in mission-oriented protective posture (MOPP) 4.

Standards: Conduct a mask fit test. Perform all the steps in sequence to verify the fit of a protective mask to an individual's face.

## Performance Steps

### 1. Prepare the M41 PATS for operation.
• a. Unpack all equipment without causing damage.
• b. Inventory the equipment using the operator's manual, and note any missing equipment on DA Form 2404.
• c. Perform setup procedures:
- (1) Attach the tube marked A to the ambient port and the tube marked S to the sample port.
- (2) Connect the alternating current (AC) power supply, or install the battery.
- (3) Install the alcohol cartridge.
• d. Perform a systems check:
- (1) Prepare the protection assessment test instrument (PATI).
- (2) Conduct troubleshooting on the PATS.

### 2. Prepare the mask for the fit test (M40, M42, or M45 series):
• a. Attach the drink tube sampling adapter to the drink tube quick-disconnect coupling.
• b. Have the Soldier sit down for the fit test.
• c. Have the Soldier don the mask.
• d. Instruct the Soldier to blow as hard as possible several times into the internal drink tube mouthpiece to remove any trapped fluids or foreign matter. Ensure that the drink tube is clear so that foreign matter will not be drawn into the PATI. Ensure that the PATI will be able to draw air from inside the mask. This is a critical step.
• e. Have the Soldier adjust the face piece and tighten the head harness. Ensure that the face piece is properly fitted.

### 3. Prepare the mask for the fit test (M17 series):
• a. Attach the drink tube sampling adapter to the drink tube quick-disconnect coupling.
• b. Attach the drink valve retaining lever to hold the drink valve open.
• c. Have the Soldier sit down for the fit test.
• d. Have the Soldier don the mask.
• e. Instruct the Soldier to blow as hard as possible several times into the internal drink tube mouthpiece to remove any trapped fluids or foreign matter. Ensure that the drink tube is clear so that foreign matter will not be drawn into the PATI. Ensure that the PATI will be able to draw air from inside the mask. This is a critical step.
• f. Have the Soldier remove the mask. Insert the sample tube extension into the internal drinking tube mouthpiece.
• g. Remove the drink valve retaining lever from the drink valve lever.

WARNING: Have the Soldier close his/her eyes while putting on the mask to prevent the sample extension tube from injuring his/her eyes.

Knife Skills (1) -

Perform the Mumbly Peg Knife Throwing Game - Step 1 (Right Hand)
Reference Source: Boy Scout Handbook 1911
Procedure:

1. Hold your right fist with the back of your hand to the ground.
2. Place the jack-knife on top of your closed fingers, with the blade pointing to the right.
3. Swing your hand to the right, up and over, describing a semicircle so...
Procedure:

1. Hold your right fist with the back of your hand to the ground.
2. Place the jack-knife on top of your closed fingers, with the blade pointing to the right.
3. Swing your hand to the right, up and over, describing a semicircle so that the knife falls point downward and sticks upright in the ground.
4. If there is room to slip two fingers, one above the other, beneath the handle of the knife, and if the point of the knife is hidden in the ground, it counts as a fair stick or throw.
